[ANSWER]: Classic reinforcement‑learning formulations assume that a reward function is given a priori, yet in real‑world deployments specifying such a function is notoriously difficult.  Prior work therefore explores how agents can acquire reward information from humans, either by asking for direct scalar feedback or by observing other signals.  Our contribution builds on this line by treating natural language as a rich, structured source of reward information and by formally analysing when different linguistic forms are most useful for the learner.

When the desired behavior is observable but the underlying reward is hidden, inverse reinforcement learning (IRL) has been the dominant approach.  Existing IRL methods infer a reward that rationalizes observed actions, but they suffer from fundamental identifiability issues and often require additional queries to disambiguate among many compatible rewards.  We extend this tradition by showing how a cooperative speaker can deliberately choose utterances that reduce ambiguity, and we provide a formal characterization of the optimal trade‑off between instruction‑type and description‑type language under varying autonomy horizons.

A growing body of work has examined language‑based instruction as a means of shaping agent behaviour.  These studies typically treat instructions as cues about specific actions or goals and use them either to bias policy learning or to recover latent reward preferences.  Our paper situates these approaches within a unified framework that predicts when a human will prefer instructions over more abstract language.  Specifically, we prove that low‑autonomy agents benefit most from short, action‑oriented utterances, whereas high‑autonomy agents profit from longer‑horizon, reward‑descriptive statements, thereby offering a principled guide for designing instruction‑based interfaces.

Learning from descriptive language—textual or free‑form explanations of reward structure—has received comparatively less attention because of the grounding challenge it poses.  Existing methods either assume a fixed mapping between words and features or focus on extracting task‑relevant concepts from large corpora.  By assuming known groundings, we are able to isolate the informational value of descriptions and to quantify their advantage in settings where the learner must act on novel states.  This theoretical analysis complements empirical work on description‑driven teaching and clarifies the conditions under which such language can be safely leveraged.

Recent advances in pragmatic reasoning, particularly the Rational Speech Act (RSA) framework and inverse reward design (IRD), treat human data as intentionally informative rather than merely observational.  These approaches have been applied to reference games, captioning, and instruction following, but they have not been extended to the full spectrum of natural‑language reward communication.  We unify RSA‑style pragmatic inference with IRD and adapt it to both instructions and descriptions, yielding a pragmatic listener that jointly infers the speaker’s horizon and reward function.  This joint inference mitigates the model‑mis‑specification vulnerabilities identified in earlier pragmatic learning work.

Finally, while many prior studies evaluate language‑based learning in simulation or with synthetic speakers, we validate our models through a behavioral experiment with human participants.  We demonstrate that our speaker model accurately predicts human utterance choices and that the pragmatic listener reliably recovers the underlying reward functions.  Moreover, we show that integrating this social inference with conventional reinforcement learning accelerates learning and reduces regret.  Together, these contributions advance the field from agents that merely obey language to agents that actively learn from it, positioning our work at the intersection of reward learning, linguistic pragmatics, and value alignment.

[ANSWER]: The extensive body of work on defending classifiers against adversarial perturbations demonstrates that most heuristic defenses have been defeated by stronger adaptive attacks, and that even the most successful scalable approach—PGD‑based adversarial training and its variants—still achieves limited robust accuracy on benchmark datasets such as CIFAR‑10. In contrast, our paper does not aim to propose a new defense; instead, it provides a diagnostic tool that explains why existing defenses fall short by revealing that the error regions of state‑of‑the‑art models exhibit high label uncertainty, a phenomenon that current robustness evaluations overlook. This perspective clarifies the gap between reported robust accuracies and the intrinsic difficulty of the classification task, thereby offering a complementary explanation to the empirical shortcomings of current defenses.  

Certified defenses based on linear programming, semidefinite programming, interval bound propagation, and randomized smoothing have shown that provable robustness can be attained for small networks, yet they often sacrifice empirical performance and do not scale to the larger models used in practice. Our contribution differs from these works in that we do not seek to certify robustness for a particular model; rather, we introduce a label‑uncertainty‑aware concentration framework that can be applied to any classifier to assess whether the underlying data distribution itself permits high‑accuracy robust classification. By incorporating label information into the concentration measure, we provide a more realistic intrinsic robustness limit that is applicable to the large‑scale models typically evaluated by certified methods.  

Theoretical analyses that connect concentration of measure with intrinsic robustness limits have established that, in concentrated metric probability spaces, adversarially robust classifiers cannot exist. These results, however, treat the input distribution as label‑agnostic and therefore yield limits that may be overly pessimistic for supervised learning tasks. Our work builds directly on this line of research by identifying the insufficiency of label‑agnostic concentration and formally defining label uncertainty as the average ambiguity of label assignments within a region. We then integrate this notion into the concentration function, yielding a label‑uncertainty‑constrained concentration measure that refines existing theoretical limits and makes them directly relevant to classification problems.  

Empirical methods for estimating concentration, such as the data‑driven estimator of Mahloujifar et al. and its later refinements, have enabled practitioners to compute intrinsic robustness bounds for image benchmarks. Nevertheless, these estimators ignore the relationship between the geometry of input regions and their associated labels, which leads to underestimates of the true robustness barrier. By adapting the Mahloujifar estimator to incorporate label uncertainty, we propose a novel algorithm that more accurately quantifies the intrinsic robustness of CIFAR‑10 and CIFAR‑10H. Our experiments demonstrate that the resulting bounds are tighter than those obtained by standard concentration estimates and align better with observed clean and robust accuracies, highlighting the practical impact of accounting for label information.  

Finally, prior works that estimate lower bounds on concentration via generative modeling or half‑space approximations have advanced the methodological toolbox but still operate without label awareness. Our results show that label information is essential for understanding intrinsic robustness limits: error regions produced by contemporary robust classifiers systematically exhibit higher label uncertainty than random subsets, and models that explicitly consider this uncertainty—e.g., by abstaining on high‑uncertainty examples—can achieve improved robustness‑accuracy trade‑offs. Thus, our contribution not only extends existing intrinsic‑robustness estimation techniques but also opens a new research direction centered on label‑aware analysis and abstention strategies for adversarial defense.

Early work such as [1] introduced video layer decompositions that model temporally varying spatial warps, primarily for compression, while Flexible Sprites [2] added semi‑transparent full‑canvas layers limited to translational motion and solved for layers with expectation‑maximization. Subsequent extensions [3] broadened the motion model, yet retained global layers that become intractable when many elements are present. In contrast, our method introduces a dense grid of local anchors and learns a dictionary of small, possibly transparent sprites that are placed only within a limited neighbourhood of each anchor. This locality makes inference scalable to thousands of sprites, factorises both spatially and temporally recurring patterns, and yields a representation that is immediately amenable to editing and analysis.

Layered video decompositions that separate human actors into independent streams [4] and approaches that impose solid‑color layer priors in GANs [5] also rely on global layers, and they do not explicitly disentangle motion from appearance. Soft‑layer techniques based on texture, colour or semantics [6, 7] and deep‑image‑prior layer pairings [8] provide useful editing cues but remain implicit and lack a discrete, reusable component library. Recent differentiable compositing works [10] treat compositing as an inductive bias but still operate on whole‑image patches rather than a compact dictionary of reusable sprites. Our contribution lies in learning a finite set of sprite patches jointly with their placement on a canvas, thereby producing a sparse, explicit decomposition where each sprite is a reusable visual primitive that can be edited or re‑used across frames without recomputing the entire decomposition.

Neural synthesis has achieved remarkable realism [11, 12], yet controllability and interpretability remain limited [13–16]. Several studies have introduced differentiable domain‑specific functions to regain control: parametric photographic edits [17], differentiable imaging operators [18], ray‑marching priors for radiance fields [19], neural textures on 3D meshes [20], and spatial transformers for explicit geometric changes [21]. While these methods expose certain aspects of the generation process, they still rely on implicit feature maps and do not provide a clear, discrete representation of recurring visual elements. Our generator differs by composing frames exclusively from learned 2D sprites undergoing rigid translations, which makes both appearance and motion directly observable and manipulable, offering a level of interpretability and editing granularity that prior neural generators lack.

Object‑centric representation learning seeks to segment and track entities without supervision. Slot Attention [22] and SPACE [23] extract compositional object representations, yet their latent slots encode appearance and motion jointly and often embed recurring patterns into an undifferentiated background, limiting explicit control. MONet [24] uses attention to isolate object regions, and other recent works employ fixed parametric primitives as building blocks [25, 26]. Our approach builds on this line of research by learning a dictionary of sprites that are themselves interpretable visual primitives; motion is expressed through the explicit placement of these sprites on a grid, allowing us to scale to many more objects per scene and to train orders of magnitude faster while retaining direct access to both shape and dynamics.

Video‑game‑specific generation methods such as GameGAN [28] synthesize frames from controller inputs by splitting the scene into static and dynamic components, but they render full frames with deeply entangled appearance and dynamics, offering little insight into the underlying structure. By contrast, our sprite‑based decomposition discovers the recurring graphic elements that constitute game assets, enabling downstream agents to reason about dynamics and gameplay mechanics using an explicit, editable representation of each asset.

Finally, video compression traditionally exploits appearance consistency and motion compensation [29], with recent deep‑learning‑based codecs [30, 31] improving efficiency. Classical techniques like DjVu [32] and Digipaper [33] separate documents into background and foreground layers, compressing recurring glyphs or coloured text, while image epitomes [34] summarise content in a miniature texture that can be sampled to reconstruct the original. Our method shares the principle of factoring out redundancy by learning a dictionary of recurring sprites, but goes further by providing a differentiable, end‑to‑end trainable pipeline that yields a sparse sprite atlas and explicit placement maps, thereby delivering both compression benefits and fine‑grained editing capabilities absent from prior compression or epitome approaches.

[ANSWER]: Continuous parameter‑space symmetries have been identified in neural networks with homogeneous [1, 2] and radial activation functions [3]. The influence of symmetry transformations on gradients has been examined for translation, scale, and rescale symmetries [4]. 

Several studies exploit symmetry to facilitate optimization. Path‑SGD [5] improves optimization in ReLU networks by applying path regularization. Scale‑invariant SGD [6] performs weight updates in a scale‑invariant space, leveraging the symmetry present in ReLU networks. The effect of ℓ₂ regularization in batch‑normalized networks, which yields scale‑invariant functions, is analyzed in [7]. Transformations of parameters within symmetry orbits are used to address slow movement along directions of weakly broken symmetry and to locate optimal points that minimize the loss [8]. 

Natural gradient methods [9], adaptive gradient methods [10, 11], and their approximations [12, 13] modify the direction of parameter updates rather than directly transforming parameters. When a group acts transitively on a level set, moving to points with maximal gradient aligns the update direction with that of Newton’s method. Connections between such updates and second‑order optimization methods have been explored empirically. 

The concept of neural teleportation, introduced via quiver representation theory, appears in [14, 15]. These works provide tools for exploring loss level curves of neural networks and demonstrate that random teleportation can accelerate gradient descent both experimentally and theoretically. 

The impact of parameter initialization on convergence rate has been studied in several works [16, 17, 18]. Applying a group transformation at initialization, as in [17], can affect early‑stage convergence, while other approaches allow transformations at arbitrary points during training. 

Overparameterization in modern neural networks has been shown to improve generalization [19] and to affect optimization dynamics. Early analyses [20] indicate that depth‑induced overparameterization can accelerate convergence. Other perspectives highlight that the symmetry introduced by overparameterization imposes constraints on training trajectories in the form of conserved quantities [21] and generates additional trajectories. When symmetry‑related trajectories are equivalent, model compression by removing redundancy can reduce training time [3]; when they are not equivalent, gradient flow can be faster along certain paths. Research has thus focused on identifying and exploiting the more efficient trajectories created by overparameterization.

These contributions provide a consistent evaluation framework that directly addresses the shortcomings of earlier comparative studies.

The broader literature on anaphora and coreference resolution has documented a wide variety of datasets, tasks, and evaluation protocols, yet most of this work operates on surface‑level representations rather than on structured semantic graphs. By situating our research at the intersection of AMR parsing and coreference resolution, we extend the applicability of those insights to a graph‑based semantic formalism. Our unified document‑level representation and efficient evaluation metric enable future work to benchmark semantic parsing systems against established coreference benchmarks, thereby bridging the gap between traditional coreference research and graph‑oriented meaning representation.

Early works introduced deep policies that map raw images to motor commands for tasks such as grasping, pushing and object reorientation, demonstrating the feasibility of learning directly from pixels.  A number of studies subsequently employed eye‑in‑hand (hand‑centric) cameras to obtain close‑up views of the manipulated object, improving accuracy for fine‑grasping and insertion tasks.  Parallel lines of research on visual servoing, predating deep learning, combined eye‑in‑hand and third‑person viewpoints to stabilize control loops.  More recent investigations have begun to question the placement of cameras themselves, proposing limited analyses of how different visual perspectives affect learning performance, yet systematic comparisons of camera configurations remain scarce.  An emerging concurrent effort explores cross‑view attention mechanisms to fuse hand‑centric and third‑person streams, reporting strong sim‑to‑real transfer in manipulation domains.  

The influence of observation perspective on generalization has been examined in several contexts.  Studies of language‑guided agents in simulated environments found that egocentric (first‑person) observation spaces facilitate systematic generalization to novel noun‑verb combinations.  In embodied manipulation settings, research using wrist‑ and head‑mounted cameras together with abstracted grasping primitives showed improved transfer to unseen objects and room layouts, attributing the benefit to richer visual cues.  These works typically rely on memory‑augmented architectures to compensate for the partial observability inherent in egocentric views, a strategy common in navigation but less explored for tabletop manipulation where third‑person cameras are the norm.  

Data‑augmentation techniques from computer vision have also been adapted for reinforcement learning to induce invariance to image‑space transformations such as random crops, flips, and color jitter.  By augmenting training observations, these methods aim to make policies robust to low‑level visual variations and have been shown to improve sample efficiency and performance on a variety of benchmark tasks.  This line of work treats augmentation as a way to prescribe specific invariances, distinct from investigations that focus on how the underlying observation function—i.e., the camera perspective—shapes a policy’s ability to generalize across environmental changes.  

In this work we provide a comprehensive empirical study of visual perspective for vision‑based robotic manipulation.  We formulate concrete hypotheses about the benefits and limitations of hand‑centric versus third‑person viewpoints and evaluate them across multiple families of learning algorithms—including imitation learning, reinforcement learning, and adversarial imitation learning—on a suite of manipulation tasks drawn from the Meta‑World benchmark.  Our results show that, when the hand‑centric view supplies sufficient observability, it consistently reduces training time and out‑of‑distribution failure rates relative to a pure third‑person setup, both in simulation and on a real robot platform.  Conversely, when hand‑centric observability is inadequate, incorporating a third‑person view is necessary for successful learning but introduces detrimental effects on generalization.  To reconcile these opposing factors we introduce a variational information bottleneck that regularizes the third‑person stream, mitigating its negative impact while preserving the benefits of full observability.  Integrated into the state‑of‑the‑art DrQ‑v2 reinforcement‑learning algorithm, this approach yields a single agent that jointly exploits both perspectives and achieves superior out‑of‑distribution performance on six representative tasks with varying degrees of hand‑centric observability, establishing a new performance baseline for vision‑based manipulation.  By systematically addressing camera placement design, perspective‑driven generalization, and regularization of multi‑view inputs, our study bridges gaps identified in prior literature and offers practical guidelines for building more robust, data‑efficient robotic manipulators.

[ANSWER]: The problem of learning to achieve goals has a long history in both the control community [1] and the reinforcement‑learning (RL) community [2]. Many prior works treat goal‑conditioned RL as a reward‑driven, multi‑task learning problem, assuming access to a goal‑conditioned reward function. A distinctive aspect of goal‑conditioned RL, compared with other multi‑task settings, is that it can also be approached with reward‑free methods. Examples include goal‑conditioned behavior cloning [3–6] and RL methods that employ hindsight relabeling [7–9, 2]. Goal‑conditioned behavior cloning is simple to implement and has shown strong performance on several real‑world tasks [10, 11], but it does not guarantee recovery of the optimal policy without additional assumptions such as determinism or online data collection. Both behavior‑cloning and hindsight‑relabeling approaches excel on many control problems yet often struggle with tasks that have long horizons.  

To address longer‑horizon tasks, a line of research has combined goal‑conditioned RL with graph‑search techniques, noting that goal‑conditioned value functions can be interpreted as dynamical distances [6, 12–14]. These methods typically operate in two stages: first learning a goal‑conditioned policy, then integrating that policy with a graph‑search planner. This stage‑wise approach has yielded impressive results on challenging control problems, including real‑world robotic navigation [10, 11]. However, the post‑hoc use of graph search prevents the search procedure from influencing the underlying policy, and the quality of the collected data remains a critical factor for RL performance [15–17].  

Exploration is another central theme in goal‑conditioned RL. The effectiveness of exploration depends heavily on how goals are sampled, a problem addressed by numerous methods that craft objectives to optimize learning progress [12, 19–25]. These approaches have demonstrated robust performance across a variety of environments.  

A broader perspective treats reinforcement learning as an inference problem [26–31]. Within this framework, variational inference for certain classes of problems has been shown to correspond to graph‑search procedures [31]. Extensions of this inferential view to hierarchical models have also been explored, linking probabilistic inference, RL, and planning.

While most BO methods assume a uniform evaluation cost, many practical problems—such as hyper‑parameter tuning, materials simulation, and robotics—exhibit evaluation costs that vary across the domain and are often unknown beforehand. Our work addresses this gap by formulating the BO problem as a Markov decision process (MDP) that explicitly incorporates stochastic, heterogeneous costs and a hard budget constraint, thereby extending the classic BO framework to settings where cost heterogeneity cannot be ignored.

A large body of prior research on cost‑aware BO operates in the multi‑fidelity regime, where cheap approximations of the objective are available. These approaches rely on a hierarchy of fidelities rather than on a single, unknown cost function, and therefore do not directly apply to the single‑fidelity, cost‑heterogeneous scenario that we consider. By focusing on the single‑fidelity case, our contribution complements the multi‑fidelity literature and provides a principled solution for problems where only one, variably costly, evaluation is possible.

Methods that adapt a traditional acquisition function by dividing it by a cost estimate—most notably expected improvement per unit of cost (EI‑PUC) and its variant with cost cooling (EI‑PUC‑CC)—represent the most common heuristic for handling heterogeneous costs. Both methods assume the cost at a candidate point is known or replace it by a point estimate, and they ignore the uncertainty associated with learning the cost function. In contrast, our budgeted multi‑step expected improvement (B‑MS‑EI) acquisition function treats the cost as a random variable, incorporates its posterior uncertainty, and evaluates points based on the expected value of information under a budget constraint, thereby providing a theoretically grounded alternative to these heuristics.

A recent concurrent effort introduced a non‑myopic, budget‑aware acquisition function based on rolling out a heuristic base policy. That approach models the problem with a finite‑horizon constrained MDP and approximates the optimal policy by a limited rollout of EI‑PUC followed by a final EI step. Our formulation differs fundamentally: we model the problem with an MDP that has a random horizon determined by the remaining budget, which more naturally captures the stopping condition inherent to budgeted BO. Moreover, B‑MS‑EI directly approximates the optimal policy rather than improving upon a fixed heuristic, resulting in stronger performance guarantees and empirical gains.

The “value‑divided‑by‑cost” heuristic that underlies many cost‑aware BO methods is reminiscent of greedy algorithms for the knapsack problem, which enjoy provable approximation bounds when the objective is additive. However, BO’s objective—maximizing the best observed function value—is non‑additive, and the greedy ratio rule can be arbitrarily suboptimal in this context. Our theoretical analysis formalizes this limitation by proving that both EI and EI‑PUC can be infinitely worse than the optimal non‑myopic policy, thereby justifying the need for a genuinely non‑myopic acquisition function such as B‑MS‑EI.

The bandit literature also studies reward‑to‑cost ratios under heterogeneous costs, typically optimizing cumulative regret. Those algorithms are ill‑suited for BO, where the performance metric is the quality of the best solution found rather than cumulative reward. By casting budgeted BO as an MDP with a random horizon and focusing on the expected improvement of the maximum observed value, our method aligns the decision‑making criterion with the true BO objective, distinguishing it from bandit‑style approaches.

Finally, non‑myopic BO methods aim to anticipate the benefit of future evaluations, yet only a few can handle unknown, heterogeneous costs. The existing non‑myopic work that does so (the aforementioned concurrent rollout method) is limited to a finite‑horizon MDP and relies on a heuristic base policy. Our contribution advances the state of the art by introducing a random‑horizon MDP formulation and a novel look‑ahead acquisition function—B‑MS‑EI—that approximates the optimal policy without resorting to heuristic rollouts. Empirically, B‑MS‑EI consistently outperforms both myopic cost‑aware baselines and the prior non‑myopic rollout approach on synthetic benchmarks and real‑world applications, confirming its practical advantage.

The third category exploits ensembles of classifiers to achieve fairness, either by aggregating models trained under different constraints ([11]) or by selecting subsets that satisfy fairness criteria ([12]). Our approach differs fundamentally: rather than combining multiple black‑boxes, we construct a single, lightweight α‑tree that directly modifies the output of any black‑box. Our empirical evaluation on conditional value‑at‑risk, equality of opportunity, and statistical parity further confirms that the proposed α‑tree boosters outperform existing baselines across diverse datasets.

Theoretical and empirical studies have shown that diversity among ensemble members is a prerequisite for attaining performance gains. Because each constituent network is trained independently, this paradigm readily exploits parallel computation without inter‑model dependencies.

Beyond predictive accuracy, ensembles of neural networks have been advocated for improving estimates of predictive uncertainty. Several works propose that deep ensembles approximate Bayesian inference, thereby delivering well‑calibrated probability estimates and enhanced out‑of‑distribution (OOD) detection. A parallel line of research disputes a direct equivalence between ensembles and Bayesian neural networks, emphasizing that the relationship remains an open question. Nevertheless, empirical evidence consistently shows that deep ensembles attain superior calibration and OOD detection performance compared with single deterministic networks.

Empirical studies report that deep ensembles often surpass alternative methods in preserving performance on shifted or OOD data, although subsequent analyses have identified scenarios where this advantage diminishes. The purported source of this robustness is frequently attributed to the diversity between ensemble members, which is believed to mitigate the impact of covariate shift on individual predictions.

Homomorphic‑encryption‑based solutions for federated matrix factorization allow arithmetic on encrypted data, yet often rely on a semi‑honest server and lack formal security proofs. Differential‑privacy mechanisms have been employed to protect user attributes such as location in transfer‑learning scenarios, but the injected noise degrades model utility and the guarantees are not composable with other cryptographic primitives. Collectively, these approaches illustrate a trade‑off between privacy, efficiency, and recommendation quality.

The SeSoRec framework introduced a protocol that computes social regularization terms while reducing communication costs; however, it achieves efficiency by revealing aggregated rows or columns of the social matrix, which can leak fine‑grained relationship information, especially when social ties are binary. Moreover, SeSoRec treats the social adjacency matrix as dense, leading to substantial overhead in realistic settings where social graphs are extremely sparse (densities often below one percent). Subsequent work on secure computation over sparse data, such as the ROOM framework, provides protocols for column‑ or row‑sparse matrices but requires pre‑generated correlated randomness and is limited to specific sparsity patterns. Other proposals combine homomorphic encryption with secret sharing to multiply a sparse matrix by a dense one, yet their performance deteriorates when the dense operand is large.

By integrating these primitives, recent protocols have achieved lower communication complexity for sparse‑matrix operations under both insensitive and sensitive sparsity assumptions, where either the pattern of non‑zeros or merely the count of zeros is public. These advances lay the groundwork for efficient, privacy‑preserving collaborative learning on highly sparse social data.

Our contributions are threefold: (1) we devise a general protocol for securely computing the social regularization term between a rating platform and a social platform under a semi‑honest threat model; (2) we propose two novel secure sparse matrix multiplication protocols—one for insensitive sparsity, where both parties know the non‑zero locations, and one for sensitive sparsity, where only the density is public—leveraging PIR and homomorphic encryption to avoid reliance on pre‑generated correlated randomness; and (3) we empirically demonstrate that the proposed framework attains recommendation accuracy comparable to existing social recommendation models while reducing computation time and communication volume by large margins relative to the state‑of‑the‑art secure solution, thereby addressing both the privacy and efficiency challenges identified in prior work.

Our contribution differs fundamentally: we address image‑goal navigation in completely unseen environments, require no prior map or panoramic input, and train an episodic distance function that aggregates all past observations to infer distances to the goal. [ANSWER]: Structure learning for Bayesian networks has long been recognized as an NP‑hard problem, motivating two principal families of methods.  Constraint‑based approaches infer conditional independences from data and then search for a DAG that is consistent with those independences.  Score‑based methods assign a numerical score reflecting goodness‑of‑fit—often combined with a complexity penalty—to each candidate DAG and then search the combinatorial space for a high‑scoring structure.  Over the years, a variety of scoring functions have been proposed, each incorporating either an implicit or explicit regularization term to avoid overfitting.  Approximate algorithms with probabilistic guarantees have been developed to produce high‑scoring graphs despite the exponential size of the search space, while exact algorithms exploit structural restrictions such as a bound on the number of parents per node, extending classic results like the Chow‑Liu tree construction to more general settings.  Sampling techniques that operate over node orderings rather than directly over DAGs have also been introduced, and once a graph structure is fixed, a range of methods exist for estimating edge weights, including scenarios with latent variables.

Continuous‑relaxation approaches address the difficulty of directly optimizing over discrete DAGs by embedding the adjacency matrix in a continuous space and enforcing acyclicity through differentiable penalties.  Early work formulated the problem as a least‑squares fit of a linear‑Gaussian structural equation model, augmenting the loss with a term that vanishes only when the relaxed matrix corresponds to an acyclic graph.  Subsequent contributions have refined the acyclicity penalty, proposing alternatives that improve optimization stability and convergence.  The GOLEM framework specifically targets linear‑Gaussian SEMs, showing that the squared loss aligns with the log‑likelihood and that a suitably designed penalty can replace the augmented‑Lagrangian scheme of earlier methods, enabling more efficient gradient‑based optimization over the relaxed adjacency matrix.

Learning a suitable ordering of variables is closely related to structure discovery in SEMs, as a DAG can be represented by a permutation of nodes together with a lower‑triangular weight matrix.  Autoregressive models illustrate this connection: the value of a variable depends on its predecessors in a given ordering, and certain permutations yield higher likelihoods.  Methods for discovering beneficial orderings have therefore been explored, ranging from heuristic searches to algorithms that treat the permutation as a latent variable.  Recent approaches employ continuous relaxations of permutations to enable gradient‑based learning; however, earlier latent‑permutation models relied on hard assignments and the REINFORCE estimator, which suffers from high variance compared with reparameterized gradient techniques.

Bayesian causal discovery seeks a full posterior distribution over DAGs rather than a single point estimate, offering a principled quantification of uncertainty.  Classical Bayesian methods, often based on exact or Monte‑Carlo inference, encounter scalability limits in high‑dimensional settings, prompting the development of approximate schemes such as Markov chain Monte Carlo and variational approximations.  While these approaches improve tractability, challenges remain in representing the discrete, combinatorial nature of graph structures and in achieving low‑variance stochastic optimization.

In this work we introduce Bayesian Causal Discovery Nets, a variational inference framework that produces a posterior distribution over DAGs for linear‑Gaussian SEMs.  The method defines an expressive, factorized variational family that jointly models edge weights and node orderings, leveraging the decomposition of a DAG into a permutation matrix and a lower‑triangular weight matrix.  Continuous relaxations of permutations are employed to obtain reparameterized, low‑variance gradient estimators, while a horseshoe prior on edge weights encourages sparsity.  By integrating these design choices, the approach scales to high‑dimensional problems, quantifies uncertainty in the inferred graph, and achieves superior performance on standard causal‑discovery benchmarks—particularly in low‑sample regimes—relative to existing maximum‑likelihood and Bayesian baselines.

Early models such as ViT introduced a simple patch‑embedding pipeline and a class token, while subsequent works (e.g., DeiT, PVT, CONTAINER) improved efficiency, scalability, and transferability. In contrast to prior efforts that redesign the architecture or prune tokens, our work tackles the compression challenge from the quantization perspective, seeking to retain the original transformer design while drastically reducing its bit‑width.

Quantization of neural networks has been explored extensively for convolutional architectures, with methods ranging from ternary weight networks and DoReFa‑Net to more recent techniques that jointly learn quantization intervals, minimize task loss, or employ KL‑divergence‑based regularization. While these approaches demonstrate impressive speed‑ups for CNNs, they have not been directly applicable to vision transformers, especially at ultra‑low precision (≤ 4 bits). These mechanisms directly target the bottleneck identified in low‑bit ViTs—namely, the distorted attention distributions—thereby achieving state‑of‑the‑art accuracy at dramatically reduced bit‑widths.

By integrating IRM and DGD within a fully quantized training pipeline, our method establishes the first systematic solution for accurate ultra‑low‑bit vision transformers. Extensive experiments on DeiT and Swin backbones show that Q‑ViT not only outperforms prior quantization baselines but also surpasses the full‑precision counterparts on ImageNet, confirming that precise attention‑level correction and distribution‑aware distillation are essential for viable transformer quantization. This positions our work as a bridge between the flourishing literature on vision transformers and the mature field of network quantization, opening a new direction for deploying high‑performance transformers on resource‑limited hardware.

Early works introduced single‑prototype representations, while later methods extended this idea to multiple prototypes per class and incorporated mechanisms such as attention [1, 7], relation networks [5], reweighting that accounts for between‑class and within‑class interactions [4], and latent clustering [6]. Multimodal prototype construction has also been explored [3]. Because prototype classifiers are simple to implement, they have been adapted to domains beyond image classification, including semantic segmentation [13], text classification [14], and speech recognition [15].

Another line of research focuses on transforming extracted feature spaces into representations that are more discriminative for novel classes. Approaches that learn such transformations include metric learning techniques and feature‑space adaptation methods [9‑12]. 

Update‑based meta‑learning approaches differ from prototype methods by adjusting model parameters at test time to enable rapid adaptation. Model‑agnostic meta‑learning (MAML) and its variants [16‑18] aim to find initial parameters that can be fine‑tuned with a few labeled examples and gradient steps. Alternative strategies learn explicit update rules for a base learner through episodic training [19, 20]. These methods typically involve additional hyper‑parameter learning and increased training time, which can limit their speed of adaptation.

Fine‑tuning of a linear classifier on features extracted from a model trained with standard cross‑entropy loss has been shown to achieve performance comparable to meta‑learning methods [21, 22]. Subsequent work has proposed enhancements for few‑shot fine‑tuning, such as calibrating the support‑set distribution [23], applying self‑supervised learning on query samples [24], and distilling knowledge to obtain improved embeddings [25]. Investigations into pre‑training objectives have revealed that incorporating a negative margin in cross‑entropy loss can boost few‑shot performance [26]. While effective, these fine‑tuning approaches also introduce extra hyper‑parameters and require additional adaptation steps.

Theoretical analyses of few‑shot learning remain limited. Information‑theoretic lower bounds on minimax convergence rates for algorithms trained on multiple sources and evaluated on novel data have been established [28]. For a given set of inducing points \( \mathbf{Z} \) and a base kernel \( k(\cdot,\cdot) \), the inducing‑point kernel can be written in its most basic form as  

\[
k_{\text{IP}}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{x}') = k(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{Z})\,k(\mathbf{Z},\mathbf{Z})^{-1}\,k(\mathbf{Z},\mathbf{x}').
\]

Sparse Gaussian Process Regression (SGPR) selects a subset \( \mathbf{Z} \) of inducing points and then uses the low‑rank approximation  

\[
K \approx K_{\mathbf{X}\mathbf{Z}}\,K_{\mathbf{Z}\mathbf{Z}}^{-1}\,K_{\mathbf{Z}\mathbf{X}},
\]

which yields computational efficiency because the matrix \( K_{\mathbf{Z}\mathbf{Z}} \) is low rank. The predictive mean and covariance admit compact expressions that incorporate observational noise \( \sigma^{2} \):

\[
\mu_{\star}=K_{\star\mathbf{Z}}K_{\mathbf{Z}\mathbf{Z}}^{-1}\mathbf{y},
\qquad
\Sigma_{\star}=K_{\star\star}-K_{\star\mathbf{Z}}K_{\mathbf{Z}\mathbf{Z}}^{-1}K_{\mathbf{Z}\star}+\sigma^{2}I .
\]

The sparse variational kernel introduced in [3] is also low rank and uses inducing points. The sparse variational GP (SVGP) arises from a variational‑inference formulation that depends on inducing points \( \mathbf{Z} \), data points \( \mathbf{X} \), and observed function values \( \mathbf{y} \). While many treatments assume a zero prior mean, the SVGP framework can accommodate a non‑zero prior mean together with a kernel \( k(\cdot,\cdot) \) and mean function \( m(\cdot) \). Because the variational posterior is defined through the joint dependence on \( \mathbf{Z} \) and the data, it does not constitute a true probability distribution over the entire function space. The variational objective also provides a principled way to select the inducing points, as discussed in [4].

An inducing‑point kernel with \( m \) inducing points defines an \( m \)-dimensional reproducing‑kernel Hilbert space (RKHS). The dimensionality of the RKHS governs the expressivity of the kernel. In contrast, a binary‑tree kernel yields an RKHS whose dimension grows exponentially with the number of leaves, yet can be constructed in linear time and space, offering a substantial improvement over traditional inducing‑point methods. The binary‑tree construction admits \( 2^{L} \) linearly independent functions of the form \( f_{l}(\mathbf{x}) \), one for each leaf of the tree.

Methods for accelerating inducing‑point approaches, especially in low‑dimensional settings, are developed in [5]. These techniques exploit structure in the data or the kernel matrix to reduce computational overhead.

Inducing‑frequency kernels constitute an alternative to inducing points. Given a set of \( m \) inducing frequency vectors \( \mathbf{w} \), the kernel can be expressed as  

\[
k_{\text{IF}}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{x}') = \sum_{i=1}^{m} \phi_{i}(\mathbf{x})\,\phi_{i}(\mathbf{x}'),

A parallel line of research seeks to retain the advantages of ensembles while reducing computational costs at training or inference time. Techniques such as model compression, snapshot ensembles, and weight‑sharing schemes aim to approximate ensemble performance with fewer resources [27]–[30]. Related efforts exploit the geometry of the loss landscape of a single model to generate multiple, diverse predictions without training separate networks, thereby achieving ensemble‑like results with lower computational overhead [27], [28].

[ANSWER]: Extensive research has pursued the construction of classifiers that remain reliable under adversarial perturbations. Early heuristic defenses—such as gradient masking, input preprocessing, and defensive distillation—were initially promising but were later shown to be vulnerable to stronger adaptive attacks. In contrast, adversarial training based on projected gradient descent (PGD) has emerged as the most scalable approach that resists adaptive adversaries. Numerous variants of PGD‑based training have been proposed, incorporating alternative loss functions or leveraging additional unlabeled data to improve robustness. Despite these advances, the best adversarially‑trained models on standard benchmarks such as CIFAR‑10 still achieve only modest robust accuracies (approximately 45 % against ℓ∞ perturbations of size 8/255), even when supplemented with extra training data.

To provide formal guarantees, certified defenses have been developed using a variety of techniques, including linear programming relaxations, semidefinite programming, interval bound propagation, and randomized smoothing. These methods can certify that a classifier’s prediction will not change within a prescribed perturbation radius, thereby offering provable robustness for individual inputs. However, most certified approaches scale only to relatively small networks and often incur a substantial drop in empirical robustness, especially for larger perturbation budgets, limiting their applicability to large‑scale image classification tasks.

A complementary line of work seeks to explain adversarial vulnerability from a theoretical standpoint by linking it to the concentration of measure phenomenon. Under this framework, if the input distribution is sufficiently concentrated with respect to the perturbation metric, no classifier can achieve non‑trivial robust accuracy. Early results demonstrated model‑independent robustness upper bounds for inputs uniformly distributed on high‑dimensional spheres by invoking the Gaussian isoperimetric inequality. Subsequent generalizations extended these bounds to arbitrary metric probability spaces that exhibit concentration. While these analyses illuminate fundamental limits, they rely on assumptions about the concentration properties of natural image distributions that remain unverified.

Recognizing the gap between theory and practice, several studies have proposed empirical methods for estimating the concentration function of real‑world data. One approach introduced a data‑driven estimator that measures concentration from samples and uses it to infer an intrinsic robustness limit for popular image benchmarks; this work highlighted a sizable disparity between the estimated limit and the robustness achieved by state‑of‑the‑art adversarial training. Later refinements employed half‑space constructions to improve estimation accuracy, and additional techniques approximated concentration lower bounds via generative modeling of the data distribution. Notably, these empirical investigations have largely ignored the role of class labels, treating the input space as unlabeled.

Building on these observations, the present work identifies the insufficiency of standard concentration‑of‑measure analyses for characterizing intrinsic robustness in supervised classification. It introduces a formal notion of label uncertainty that quantifies the average ambiguity of class assignments within a region of the input space, and incorporates this quantity into a label‑aware concentration framework. An adapted estimator for the label‑uncertainty‑constrained concentration function is proposed, accompanied by asymptotic theoretical guarantees and a practical heuristic algorithm for common perturbation metrics. Empirical studies on CIFAR‑10 and CIFAR‑10H reveal that error regions of contemporary robust models exhibit markedly higher label uncertainty than random subsets, confirming the relevance of the proposed measure. Compared with existing concentration‑based estimators, the new method yields tighter intrinsic robustness limits for benchmark datasets, and experiments suggest that leveraging label uncertainty—e.g., via an abstain option—offers a promising direction for enhancing adversarial robustness.

[ANSWER]: Imitation learning (IL) addresses the inverse problem of reproducing observed behavior without access to an explicit reward signal, contrasting with reinforcement learning (RL) which relies on reward feedback.  Early IL methods cast the problem as supervised learning, mapping states directly to actions via behavioral cloning (BC).  More recent distribution‑matching approaches align state‑action distributions between demonstrator and learner through adversarial training, often yielding higher fidelity imitation. Several extensions of IL and IRL have been proposed for fully‑offline learning in partially observable environments, a setting common in clinical decision making.  RNN‑based architectures have been used to infer belief states from observation histories, enabling BC in the presence of hidden information.  IRL has likewise been adapted to operate with belief‑state representations and to function without interactive data collection.  Although these methods achieve strong action‑matching performance, they rely on opaque neural networks, making the resulting policies difficult to interpret.  Consequently, many works impose additional constraints—such as assuming Markovian dynamics or low‑dimensional state spaces—to permit more transparent models, but at the cost of reduced scalability, limited expressiveness, and weakened identifiability of the underlying policy.

Interpretability has also been pursued by shaping the reward function rather than the policy itself.  By defining expressive, human‑readable reward structures, IRL can reveal an agent’s preferences over counterfactual outcomes or over information‑gathering value under time pressure.  Nevertheless, because the final policy is still extracted by a black‑box RL algorithm, the mapping from raw observations to concrete actions remains hidden.  Alternative approaches directly parametrize the policy with interpretable structures, such as high‑level programming languages or outcome‑based explanations, thereby exposing the decision logic.  These representations have been explored primarily for static or low‑dimensional problems, with limited attention to sequential, time‑series data.

Tree‑based models provide a natural avenue for interpretable decision making.  Soft and differentiable tree architectures have shown success on image classification tasks, where learned thresholds operate on latent feature embeddings.  Extensions to representation learning incorporate intermediate projections or cascade multiple trees, yet the resulting decision criteria often involve abstract variables that are unintuitive to domain experts.  Work on probabilistic decision trees for dynamic, heterogeneous, and sparse time‑series data remains scarce, and existing methods typically sacrifice interpretability by relying on transformed or auxiliary features rather than directly on raw observations.

In light of these gaps, we introduce a framework that learns policies as incrementally grown, probabilistic decision trees whose splits are defined on native observation variables, preserving clinical interpretability.  The trees are fully differentiable and adapt their depth and breadth during optimization, allowing the model complexity to match the intricacy of the task.  By embedding recurrent connections within the tree structure, the approach captures temporal dependencies in patient histories, enabling the policy to evolve as new information becomes available.  The method operates entirely offline and tolerates partial observability, leveraging belief‑state representations without requiring explicit reward signals.  Moreover, the framework supports the incorporation of domain knowledge as inductive biases, facilitates the formal quantification of abstract behavioral concepts such as uncertainty or low‑value actions, and demonstrates superior performance to state‑of‑the‑art baselines on both synthetic and real‑world medical datasets in terms of policy fidelity and explanatory power.

Convolutional, recurrent, and transformer‑based architectures have achieved strong performance on benchmark datasets, yet they largely ignore the latent correlations among event types and therefore provide limited robustness when training data are scarce. Early ontology‑based zero‑shot models, however, construct the ontology solely from intra‑event structure, overlooking richer inter‑type relationships that could further support knowledge transfer.  

To exploit correlations among event types, recent work has introduced graph‑based representations that connect event categories through shared entities and relational paths, allowing multi‑hop reasoning over a structured schema. Such designs, however, depend on extensive entity and relation annotations, which can be costly to obtain. Parallel efforts in relation extraction have demonstrated the benefits of logic‑based, ontology‑driven learning, where inductive logic programming yields symbolic rules that capture class‑level dependencies and support explicit reasoning. These approaches illustrate the potential of combining ontological knowledge with statistical models to encode inter‑type correlations.  

Building on these observations, the present work proposes an ontology‑driven event‑detection framework that simultaneously encodes intra‑event features and inter‑type correlations. A rule‑based correlation inference component augments the ontology with additional event‑event relations, enhancing reasoning capability without requiring exhaustive entity annotations. A newly constructed dataset supports comprehensive evaluation, and experiments demonstrate consistent gains over prior neural, meta‑learning, and ontology‑based baselines in overall, few‑shot, and zero‑shot settings, confirming the effectiveness of integrating structured ontological knowledge with deep representations for low‑resource event detection.

[ANSWER]: This work builds on the emerging field of machine‑learning engineering, which seeks to understand the practical challenges of developing, deploying, and maintaining complex model pipelines [1, 2, 3]. While prior surveys have catalogued engineering problems such as reproducibility, testing, and model versioning [4], they treat models as largely independent components. In contrast, our paper identifies and formalizes a new class of failure mode—self‑defeating improvements—arising from the entanglement of models within a system. By providing a systematic error decomposition and empirical evidence from a realistic stereo‑based detection pipeline, we extend the engineering literature beyond isolated model concerns to the holistic behavior of interconnected systems.

The notion of entanglement, often summarized as “changing anything changes everything” [4, 5, 6], has been explored in the context of backward‑compatible learners that aim to preserve downstream performance when upstream models evolve [7, 8, 9]. Those works primarily focus on preserving functional compatibility or guaranteeing monotonic performance under specific update rules. Our contribution differs in two respects: first, we demonstrate that even when downstream models are fully retrained, improvements to an upstream component can still degrade overall system performance; second, we categorize the underlying error mechanisms (distributional shift, error propagation, and objective misalignment) that explain why backward‑compatibility guarantees may be insufficient in practice.

A related line of research investigates how improvements to machine‑learning systems can unintentionally impair human operators [10]. Those studies emphasize human‑in‑the‑loop performance and cognitive load, whereas our analysis concentrates on purely algorithmic interactions among models. By isolating the algorithmic source of self‑defeating improvements, we provide a complementary perspective that can be combined with human‑centric studies to assess end‑to‑end system robustness.

The impact of upstream model changes on downstream tasks has also been framed as a domain‑shift problem [11, 12]. Existing domain‑shift mitigation techniques, such as importance weighting of training examples [13], assume a shared input space between source and target models. Our experiments show that in typical multi‑model pipelines the input spaces differ (e.g., depth maps versus raw images), rendering those techniques inapplicable. Consequently, we argue that self‑defeating improvements constitute a distinct phenomenon that requires new methodological tools beyond traditional domain‑adaptation approaches.

Transfer‑learning literature has reported cases where techniques that improve a source model’s accuracy hurt its usefulness for downstream tasks [14, 15, 16]. For example, regularization methods that boost ImageNet performance can reduce transferability to other recognition problems [15]. These observations are aligned with our findings, but prior work treats the source‑target relationship as a one‑shot transfer, whereas we examine iterative, co‑evolving pipelines where both upstream and downstream models are periodically updated. Our error decomposition clarifies why improvements that appear beneficial in isolation may undermine the downstream learning dynamics in such evolving systems.

Finally, differentiable programming approaches [17, 18] propose to resolve incompatibilities by back‑propagating loss signals through the entire model graph. While this strategy can, in principle, align upstream updates with downstream objectives, it presupposes differentiability and tractable gradients throughout the pipeline—assumptions that often fail in real‑world settings (e.g., when models are gradient‑boosted trees or are maintained by distinct teams). By explicitly demonstrating scenarios where downstream retraining alone cannot prevent performance degradation, our work delineates the limits of differentiable programming as a universal remedy and motivates research on alternative coordination mechanisms for entangled model systems.

[ANSWER]: Ensembling has long been recognized as an effective strategy for reducing generalization error by aggregating the predictions of multiple models. Classical results demonstrate that diversity among ensemble members is a prerequisite for achieving performance gains, and a variety of mechanisms—including random sub‑sampling of data or features, boosting‑based reweighting, heterogeneous model families, and joint training objectives—have been proposed to induce such diversity. Our work builds on this foundation but challenges the prevailing assumption that diversity itself confers unique benefits for uncertainty quantification and robustness; we show that the improvements attributed to diverse ensembles can be matched by a single, larger neural network when in‑distribution performance and individual model uncertainty are controlled.

In the context of deep learning, ensembles are typically constructed by training several instances of the same architecture with different random initializations and minibatch orderings, leveraging the stochasticity of SGD and the non‑convex loss landscape to obtain sufficiently diverse predictors. While this procedure is computationally attractive because the models can be trained and evaluated in parallel, prior studies have treated the resulting diversity as the source of enhanced predictive performance and reliable uncertainty estimates. By systematically varying model capacity and isolating the contribution of individual‑model uncertainty, we demonstrate that the apparent advantages of such “deep ensembles” do not stem from the stochastic diversity of their members but rather from the higher capacity that a comparable single model can provide.

Recent literature has highlighted deep ensembles as a practical alternative to Bayesian neural networks for predictive uncertainty, citing improved calibration and out‑of‑distribution (OOD) detection. Some works argue that ensembles approximate Bayesian inference, while others dispute this connection. Our analysis clarifies this debate by revealing that ensemble diversity does not increase OOD uncertainty beyond what is already expressed by each constituent network. Moreover, we establish a strong correlation between per‑example ensemble disagreement and the expected gain from scaling up a single model, indicating that the uncertainty benefits of ensembles are replicable without ensembling.

The robustness of deep ensembles under dataset shift has also been emphasized, with several studies reporting superior accuracy and calibration on OOD data relative to single models and other baselines. This robustness has been attributed to the diversity of ensemble members. Contrasting with those findings, we provide evidence that OOD performance is tightly coupled to in‑distribution accuracy, a relationship that holds equally for ensembles and for single networks of comparable capacity. Consequently, ensembles do not offer “effective robustness” beyond what can be achieved by a suitably sized single model, even when evaluated with probabilistic metrics such as NLL, Brier score, or calibration error.

Finally, a growing body of work seeks to obtain ensemble‑like gains with reduced computational overhead, either by compressing trained ensembles, distilling their knowledge into a single network, or exploiting the optimization landscape of a solitary model. Our results substantiate the intuition behind these efforts: since the performance, uncertainty quantification, and robustness advantages of deep ensembles can be reproduced by a larger single model, methods that aim to emulate ensembles with fewer resources are fundamentally sound. By explicitly quantifying the limits of ensemble‑specific benefits, we provide a principled benchmark for future approaches that target efficiency without sacrificing the desirable properties traditionally ascribed to deep ensembles.

[ANSWER]: Classic reinforcement‑learning formulations assume that a reward function is given a priori, yet in real‑world deployments specifying such a function is notoriously difficult.  Prior work therefore explores how agents can acquire reward information from humans, either by asking for direct scalar feedback or by observing other signals.  Our contribution builds on this line by treating natural language as a rich, structured source of reward information and by formally analysing when different linguistic forms are most useful for the learner.

When the desired behavior is observable but the underlying reward is hidden, inverse reinforcement learning (IRL) has been the dominant approach.  Existing IRL methods infer a reward that rationalizes observed actions, but they suffer from fundamental identifiability issues and often require additional queries to disambiguate among many compatible rewards.  We extend this tradition by showing how a cooperative speaker can deliberately choose utterances that reduce ambiguity, and we provide a formal characterization of the optimal trade‑off between instruction‑type and description‑type language under varying autonomy horizons.

A growing body of work has examined language‑based instruction as a means of shaping agent behaviour.  These studies typically treat instructions as cues about specific actions or goals and use them either to bias policy learning or to recover latent reward preferences.  Our paper situates these approaches within a unified framework that predicts when a human will prefer instructions over more abstract language.  Specifically, we prove that low‑autonomy agents benefit most from short, action‑oriented utterances, whereas high‑autonomy agents profit from longer‑horizon, reward‑descriptive statements, thereby offering a principled guide for designing instruction‑based interfaces.

Learning from descriptive language—textual or free‑form explanations of reward structure—has received comparatively less attention because of the grounding challenge it poses.  Existing methods either assume a fixed mapping between words and features or focus on extracting task‑relevant concepts from large corpora.  By assuming known groundings, we are able to isolate the informational value of descriptions and to quantify their advantage in settings where the learner must act on novel states.  This theoretical analysis complements empirical work on description‑driven teaching and clarifies the conditions under which such language can be safely leveraged.

Recent advances in pragmatic reasoning, particularly the Rational Speech Act (RSA) framework and inverse reward design (IRD), treat human data as intentionally informative rather than merely observational.  These approaches have been applied to reference games, captioning, and instruction following, but they have not been extended to the full spectrum of natural‑language reward communication.  We unify RSA‑style pragmatic inference with IRD and adapt it to both instructions and descriptions, yielding a pragmatic listener that jointly infers the speaker’s horizon and reward function.  This joint inference mitigates the model‑mis‑specification vulnerabilities identified in earlier pragmatic learning work.

Finally, while many prior studies evaluate language‑based learning in simulation or with synthetic speakers, we validate our models through a behavioral experiment with human participants.  We demonstrate that our speaker model accurately predicts human utterance choices and that the pragmatic listener reliably recovers the underlying reward functions.  Moreover, we show that integrating this social inference with conventional reinforcement learning accelerates learning and reduces regret.  Together, these contributions advance the field from agents that merely obey language to agents that actively learn from it, positioning our work at the intersection of reward learning, linguistic pragmatics, and value alignment.

[ANSWER]: Bayesian optimization (BO) originated from early work on global optimization of expensive black‑box functions and has since become a standard tool for problems where evaluations are scarce.  It has been successfully applied to hyper‑parameter tuning of machine learning models, materials discovery, drug design, and robot locomotion, among many other domains.  

A substantial strand of the BO literature addresses the fact that evaluation costs may vary across the search space.  Much of this research is situated in the multi‑fidelity setting, where cheaper approximations of the objective are available and algorithms exploit correlations between fidelities to trade off information gain against cost.  In the single‑fidelity case, only a few approaches explicitly model heterogeneous costs, focusing on incorporating cost information into the acquisition function while retaining the standard BO framework.

Robustness obtained by training or fine‑tuning on one type of shift (e.g., Gaussian noise) often does not transfer to another (e.g., salt‑and‑pepper noise), even for visually similar perturbations [1], [2]. A common practice to mitigate this issue is to broaden the training distribution—by collecting more data or applying extensive data augmentation—so that it hopefully encompasses the test distribution [3], [4], [5].

A related, but more restrictive, setting assumes the availability of unlabeled data from the target (test) distribution in addition to labeled source data. This approach leverages the observation that most distribution shift occurs in the inputs rather than the labels, allowing the model to observe the test inputs during training. However, the resulting model is typically effective only for the specific target distribution for which data have been prepared [6]–[13].

The use of unlabeled test data dates back to transductive learning in the 1990s [14]. Vapnik characterized transduction as “trying to get the answer that you really need but not a more general one” [15]. Early transductive methods applied this principle to support‑vector machines by incorporating test instances as additional constraints on the decision‑boundary margin [16]–[18]. A parallel line of work on local learning trained a separate model on the nearest neighbors of each test input before making a prediction [19], [20].

In computer‑vision research, several works have explored continued training at deployment. For example, face detection can be improved by bootstrapping difficult faces from easier ones within the same test image [21]; personalized generative models have been obtained by fine‑tuning on a few images of an individual [22]; super‑resolution networks have been trained from scratch on each test image [23]; and video‑segmentation efficiency has been increased by a student model that learns online from a teacher model on test videos [24].

Test‑time training (TTT) formalized the idea of adapting a model to each test input via self‑supervision, thereby addressing generalization under distribution shift [25]. The approach has been extended to diverse domains, including vision‑based reinforcement learning [26], legged locomotion [27], video object tracking [28], natural‑language question answering [29], and medical imaging [30]. The original TTT method employed rotation prediction as a self‑supervised pretext task, asking the model to classify the angle of a 90°‑multiple rotation [31]. This task can be overly easy for natural outdoor scenes—where horizon orientation suffices—or overly hard for top‑down views where many orientations appear equally plausible.

TTT can be interpreted as a one‑sample form of unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA), wherein only a single unlabeled target sample (often the test input itself) is used for adaptation. Subsequent works have considered broader settings, such as TTT++ which assumes access to an entire target dataset [32], and TENT which adapts over batches of test inputs from the same distribution [33].

Masked autoencoders (MAE) in particular partition an image into many patches, mask a large proportion (e.g., 75 %), and train the model to reconstruct the missing patches by minimizing pixel‑wise mean‑squared error [36]. MAE pre‑trains a large ViT encoder together with a smaller decoder; downstream tasks typically use only the encoder, attaching a task‑specific linear projection head. Two common strategies for downstream fine‑tuning are (1) end‑to‑end fine‑tuning of both encoder and head, and (2) linear probing, where the encoder is frozen and only the head is trained.

[ANSWER]: Most continual learning approaches are formulated for the class‑incremental setting, where a model is trained on disjoint sets of classes that arrive in successive increments and is evaluated on all classes learned so far. Early methods mitigate catastrophic forgetting by storing a subset of exemplars from previously seen classes and replaying them together with new data (e.g., iCaRL, GEM). Although effective, exemplar storage scales poorly because memory capacity becomes a bottleneck as the number of classes grows. To avoid explicit replay, regularization‑based techniques such as Elastic Weight Consolidation and Synaptic Intelligence constrain updates to important parameters, thereby reducing forgetting without additional storage. These methods, however, typically lag behind replay‑based approaches in accuracy. More recent work on few‑shot class‑incremental learning (FSCIL) tackles the additional challenge of learning new categories from only a few labeled examples while maintaining a limited memory budget. Despite these advances, the majority of CL methods assume that the full training set for each increment is available and fully labeled, an assumption that conflicts with the streaming, often unlabeled data encountered in real‑world robotic deployments where online learning is required.

Active learning research has focused on reducing labeling effort by allowing models to query the most informative unlabeled instances. A common strategy is uncertainty sampling, where predictive entropy, margin, or variance is used to select samples for annotation. Recent deep‑learning‑based active learning methods augment the training objective with auxiliary loss terms that encourage well‑calibrated uncertainty estimates. Nonetheless, these approaches are designed for batch learning: the model is trained on a static labeled set before querying, and the learned classifier is not updated continually. When applied in a continual setting, such methods suffer from catastrophic forgetting because they lack mechanisms to preserve knowledge of earlier tasks. Moreover, traditional active learning pipelines assume a closed‑world scenario; they can detect unknown classes only in the initial batch, after which newly encountered unknowns are forced into previously learned categories, eroding the ability to recognize novel objects in later increments.

A complementary line of research investigates open‑set recognition and out‑of‑distribution (OOD) detection, where a model trained on a known set of classes must identify samples that belong to unseen categories at test time. Techniques based on calibrated confidence scores, generative modeling, or distance‑based thresholds have been proposed to flag unknown inputs. While effective for post‑hoc detection, these methods generally do not incorporate the newly discovered samples into the model’s knowledge base, limiting their usefulness for lifelong learning. Several surveys have highlighted the conceptual overlap between open‑set recognition, active learning, and continual learning, suggesting that open‑set detection could serve as a natural interface for selecting informative unknown samples to be labeled and incorporated incrementally. However, an integrated solution that simultaneously addresses few‑shot learning, active querying, and continual knowledge consolidation remains underexplored.

In this work we introduce a unified framework for Few‑Shot Continual Active Learning (FoCAL) that bridges these gaps. We represent each learned class with a uniform Gaussian mixture model, enabling compact generative replay of past data without storing raw images. Pseudo‑rehearsal is performed by sampling from these mixtures, thereby preserving class representations while avoiding memory overload. To select the most informative unlabeled instances, we combine predictive entropy with a viewpoint‑consistency metric computed on the GMM‑based representations, yielding an uncertainty measure tailored to the continual setting. Extensive experiments on the CORe‑50 benchmark demonstrate state‑of‑the‑art performance under strict labeling budgets, and deployment on a real humanoid robot validates the method’s practicality for long‑term object learning in unstructured environments. Subsequent studies by Vakili and Zhao refined the analysis under alternative risk metrics and completed the regret bounds for the same objective. All of these contributions assume a discrete set of actions and independence across arms, and therefore do not address settings where decisions involve continuous mixtures of correlated options.  

A distinct body of literature has studied bandit problems in which the learner has access to covariance information among arms.  In the stochastic setting, Degenne and Perchet considered combinatorial semi‑bandits with correlated rewards, assuming a known upper bound on the covariance matrix and designing algorithms that exploit this prior knowledge.  Perrault and colleagues extended this line of work by removing the explicit covariance bound and operating under sub‑exponential reward distributions, achieving tight asymptotic regret guarantees for combinatorial semi‑bandits.
