A frequently used alternative to the exponential mechanism is the report‑noisy‑max technique, which perturbs each quality score with noise and returns the item with the largest noisy score. Empirical studies have shown that report‑noisy‑max can be competitive with the exponential mechanism, but the two methods do not dominate each other in a Pareto sense: report‑noisy‑max performs better on certain score vectors, while the exponential mechanism is superior on others. Several additional mechanisms have been proposed for private selection that exploit specific assumptions or special cases, offering improved utility under those conditions [2,5–9].

To address settings where quality scores have heterogeneous sensitivity, a generalization of the exponential mechanism was introduced in [10]. This approach constructs a modified quality function that balances the raw score against its sensitivity and then applies the exponential mechanism to the transformed function, thereby preserving differential privacy while adapting to varying sensitivities. Separate work [11] refined the privacy analysis of multiple sequential executions of the exponential mechanism, showing that leveraging the range of the score function rather than its sensitivity can tighten composition bounds. These refinements are orthogonal to the core selection mechanism and can be incorporated into alternative designs.

When the quality functions themselves are differentially private mechanisms, a distinct selection problem arises. Study [12] presented a mechanism that operates on such private candidates, removing the need for bounded‑sensitivity assumptions on the scores. This formulation is particularly relevant for applications like hyper‑parameter optimization, where the scores are derived from private learning procedures.

The optimality of the exponential mechanism has also been examined. In [3] the authors formulated linear‑programming characterizations of mechanisms that are optimal on average, focusing on graph‑structured input–output universes where each node corresponds to a database. They proved that any optimal mechanism must satisfy privacy constraints with equality on adjacent nodes and that the exponential mechanism attains optimality up to a constant factor of two in this setting.

Beyond private selection, a line of research has derived optimal mechanisms for other privacy‑constrained tasks by carefully analyzing the underlying constraints. Results include optimal constructions for predicate‑counting queries [15], mechanisms that achieve information‑theoretic limits under differential privacy [16], and generic approaches for low‑sensitivity functions [17].

Building on this body of work, we introduce the permute‑and‑flip mechanism as a drop‑in replacement for the exponential mechanism in the private selection problem. The new mechanism retains the simplicity, linear‑time runtime, and ease of implementation of the exponential mechanism while guaranteeing that its expected utility is never lower and can be up to twice as high. By explicitly respecting the privacy constraints, the permute‑and‑flip mechanism is Pareto optimal among selection mechanisms and, under a natural condition on the score distribution, achieves overall optimality. Comparative analysis shows that it matches or exceeds the performance of report‑noisy‑max on all examined score vectors. Moreover, the mechanism is compatible with the sensitivity‑balancing transformation of [10] and can be analyzed under the refined composition framework of [11] with minimal modification. It also extends naturally to the setting of private candidates considered in [12], offering utility gains without requiring bounded sensitivity. Consequently, the permute‑and‑flip mechanism provides a universally applicable, higher‑utility alternative to the exponential mechanism, with immediate practical impact for any differential‑privacy pipeline that relies on private selection.

[ANSWER]: Mapping‑based bilingual lexicon induction (BLI) has become a dominant paradigm because it requires only limited bilingual supervision and can therefore be applied to low‑resource languages and domains. Early work introduced linear mappings learned from a small seed dictionary of word translation pairs (Mikolov et al., 2013) and later extended the approach to incorporate orthogonal constraints (Artetxe et al., 2018; Ruder et al., 2019) and iterative self‑learning loops that progressively refine the dictionary and the mapping (Artetxe et al., 2018; Karan et al., 2020). In addition to linear projections, several studies explored non‑linear mapping functions (Mohiuddin et al., 2020) and adversarial training (Lample et al., 2018; Hoshen and Wolf, 2018) to align monolingual static word embeddings. Comparative analyses have shown that weakly supervised setups with a few thousand seed pairs consistently outperform fully unsupervised methods, especially for typologically distant language pairs (Vulić et al., 2019). Nevertheless, performance gaps remain for lower‑resource languages and for language pairs with substantial lexical divergence, motivating further refinements of the mapping and self‑learning components.

Contrastive learning has emerged as a powerful technique for shaping semantic representation spaces in natural language processing. By pulling together embeddings of semantically similar inputs while pushing apart those of dissimilar inputs, contrastive objectives have yielded state‑of‑the‑art sentence encoders (Reimers and Gurevych, 2019; Carlsson et al., 2021; Gao et al., 2021). The same principle has been applied to downstream tasks such as summarisation (Gao et al., 2021) and named‑entity recognition (Zhang et al., 2022), where contrastive fine‑tuning improves task‑specific representations. In the context of cross‑lingual learning, contrastive objectives have been used to align multilingual sentence embeddings, demonstrating that the approach can effectively bridge language gaps when appropriate positive and negative pairs are available.

A separate line of research has investigated how to expose the lexical knowledge embedded in large pretrained multilingual language models (PLMs) such as mBERT or mT5. Directly extracting word‑level representations from off‑the‑shelf PLMs often yields suboptimal results on lexical tasks (Vulić et al., 2020). To remedy this, several works have fine‑tuned PLMs with contrastive learning on curated or automatically mined phrase and word pairs, thereby converting the models into more effective lexical encoders (Liu et al., 2021; Wu et al., 2021). Similar strategies have been employed for phrase‑in‑context and word‑in‑context representation learning (Schwartz et al., 2022; Chen et al., 2022), confirming that PLMs contain rich lexical information that becomes accessible after targeted fine‑tuning. These findings suggest that combining the strengths of static embeddings with the contextual knowledge of PLMs could further enhance cross‑lingual lexical tasks.

Building on these strands of work, we propose a two‑stage contrastive learning framework for weakly supervised BLI. In the first stage, we refine linear cross‑lingual maps between static word embeddings using a contrastive objective that leverages progressively improved translation pairs and hard negatives, and we integrate this refinement into a self‑learning loop. In the second stage, we fine‑tune a multilingual pretrained language model with a BLI‑oriented contrastive loss, using the refined static mappings to generate positive and negative examples. After fine‑tuning, we extract word representations from the multilingual model and combine them with the static cross‑lingual embeddings obtained in the first stage. This combined representation yields substantial improvements over state‑of‑the‑art mapping‑based methods, achieves higher precision on a broad set of language pairs—including low‑resource and typologically distant languages—and demonstrates that contrastive fine‑tuning can unlock and complement the lexical knowledge stored in multilingual PLMs for the BLI task.

[ANSWER]: When training and test distributions differ, generalization becomes intrinsically difficult without access to training data from the test distribution. Robustness obtained by training or fine‑tuning on one type of shift (e.g., Gaussian noise) often does not transfer to another (e.g., salt‑and‑pepper noise), even for visually similar perturbations [1], [2]. A common practice to mitigate this issue is to broaden the training distribution—by collecting more data or applying extensive data augmentation—so that it hopefully encompasses the test distribution [3], [4], [5].

A related, but more restrictive, setting assumes the availability of unlabeled data from the target (test) distribution in addition to labeled source data. This approach leverages the observation that most distribution shift occurs in the inputs rather than the labels, allowing the model to observe the test inputs during training. However, the resulting model is typically effective only for the specific target distribution for which data have been prepared [6]–[13].

The use of unlabeled test data dates back to transductive learning in the 1990s [14]. Vapnik characterized transduction as “trying to get the answer that you really need but not a more general one” [15]. Early transductive methods applied this principle to support‑vector machines by incorporating test instances as additional constraints on the decision‑boundary margin [16]–[18]. A parallel line of work on local learning trained a separate model on the nearest neighbors of each test input before making a prediction [19], [20].

In computer‑vision research, several works have explored continued training at deployment. For example, face detection can be improved by bootstrapping difficult faces from easier ones within the same test image [21]; personalized generative models have been obtained by fine‑tuning on a few images of an individual [22]; super‑resolution networks have been trained from scratch on each test image [23]; and video‑segmentation efficiency has been increased by a student model that learns online from a teacher model on test videos [24].

Test‑time training (TTT) formalized the idea of adapting a model to each test input via self‑supervision, thereby addressing generalization under distribution shift [25]. The approach has been extended to diverse domains, including vision‑based reinforcement learning [26], legged locomotion [27], video object tracking [28], natural‑language question answering [29], and medical imaging [30]. The original TTT method employed rotation prediction as a self‑supervised pretext task, asking the model to classify the angle of a 90°‑multiple rotation [31]. This task can be overly easy for natural outdoor scenes—where horizon orientation suffices—or overly hard for top‑down views where many orientations appear equally plausible.

TTT can be interpreted as a one‑sample form of unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA), wherein only a single unlabeled target sample (often the test input itself) is used for adaptation. Subsequent works have considered broader settings, such as TTT++ which assumes access to an entire target dataset [32], and TENT which adapts over batches of test inputs from the same distribution [33].

MAE pre‑trains a large ViT encoder together with a smaller decoder; downstream tasks typically use only the encoder, attaching a task‑specific linear projection head. Two common strategies for downstream fine‑tuning are (1) end‑to‑end fine‑tuning of both encoder and head, and (2) linear probing, where the encoder is frozen and only the head is trained.

Attention‑based HGNNs [14, 17] introduced learnable weighting of hyperedges during aggregation, while methods that directly preserve proximity of nodes sharing a hyperedge [23] emphasized the preservation of higher‑order structure. The model jointly optimizes a subgraph classification objective and a regularization term that aligns node embeddings across hyperedges, employing a strongly dual‑attention message‑passing scheme that simultaneously updates gene and pathway representations. [ANSWER]: Structure learning for Bayesian networks addresses the inference of network structure from data, a problem known to be NP‑hard [1]. Two principal families of methods have emerged. Constraint‑based approaches infer conditional independences from the data and construct a graph consistent with those independences [2]. Score‑based methods assign a goodness‑of‑fit score to a candidate DAG and search the space of DAGs to maximize this score, despite the combinatorial size and discrete nature of the DAG space in high dimensions [3], [4]. Various scoring functions have been proposed, typically incorporating an explicit or implicit complexity penalty to mitigate overfitting [5], [6]. Recent efforts have focused on approximate algorithms that provide high‑scoring graphs with probabilistic guarantees [7] and on exact methods that exploit structural assumptions such as a bounded number of parents per node, extending ideas from the classic Chow‑Liu algorithm [8], [9], [10]. These techniques enable exhaustive search over graphs with limited parent sets in moderate dimensions [11]. Sampling strategies have also been investigated, including approaches that sample over variable orderings rather than directly over DAGs [12]. Given a fixed structure, several methods address the estimation of edge parameters, even in the presence of latent variables [13].

Continuous relaxations have been introduced to enable gradient‑based optimization for structure learning. While learning undirected graphical models can be cast as a convex optimization problem [14], the acyclicity constraint for directed graphs precludes a straightforward application of continuous methods. A line of work therefore relaxes the discrete adjacency matrix to a continuous matrix and optimizes over this surrogate space. The initial formulation employed a least‑squares loss to measure data fit and added a penalty that is active only when the relaxed matrix corresponds to a DAG, thereby encouraging acyclicity [15]. Subsequent studies have proposed alternative penalty terms and variants of the relaxation framework [16]. GOLEM extended this idea to linear‑Gaussian structural equation models, showing that the squared loss approximates the log‑likelihood and that the added term serves as an acyclicity penalty, enabling optimization without the augmented Lagrangian scheme used in earlier work [17].

Approximate algorithms with probabilistic guarantees have been developed to produce high‑scoring graphs despite the exponential size of the search space, while exact algorithms exploit structural restrictions such as a bound on the number of parents per node, extending classic results like the Chow‑Liu tree construction to more general settings.  Sampling techniques that operate over node orderings rather than directly over DAGs have also been introduced, and once a graph structure is fixed, a range of methods exist for estimating edge weights, including scenarios with latent variables.

Continuous‑relaxation approaches address the difficulty of directly optimizing over discrete DAGs by embedding the adjacency matrix in a continuous space and enforcing acyclicity through differentiable penalties.  Early work formulated the problem as a least‑squares fit of a linear‑Gaussian structural equation model, augmenting the loss with a term that vanishes only when the relaxed matrix corresponds to an acyclic graph.  Subsequent contributions have refined the acyclicity penalty, proposing alternatives that improve optimization stability and convergence.  The GOLEM framework specifically targets linear‑Gaussian SEMs, showing that the squared loss aligns with the log‑likelihood and that a suitably designed penalty can replace the augmented‑Lagrangian scheme of earlier methods, enabling more efficient gradient‑based optimization over the relaxed adjacency matrix.

Autoregressive models illustrate this connection: the value of a variable depends on its predecessors in a given ordering, and certain permutations yield higher likelihoods.  Methods for discovering beneficial orderings have therefore been explored, ranging from heuristic searches to algorithms that treat the permutation as a latent variable.  Recent approaches employ continuous relaxations of permutations to enable gradient‑based learning; however, earlier latent‑permutation models relied on hard assignments and the REINFORCE estimator, which suffers from high variance compared with reparameterized gradient techniques.

By formulating inference as a control problem on a message‑passing graph, we derive optimal policies that balance inference accuracy against the explicit costs of the messages themselves, a feature absent from prior Bayesian accounts.

Efficient coding theory addresses how sensory representations can maximize information transmission given limited biological resources ([9]–[13]), and predictive coding builds on this idea by using top‑down predictions to suppress already‑known components of the input ([14]–[20]). Recent efforts have sought to unify these perspectives with sparse coding and to relate them to deep learning architectures ([21]–[28]), and several works have begun to explore the joint optimization of coding efficiency and inference performance (e.g., Park et al. [29]; Chalk et al. [17]; Młynarski et al. [30]; Aitchison et al. [31]). However, all of these studies assume that the cost of transmitting predictions is either negligible or identical to that of feedforward signals, and they do not model noise on the feedback channel. Our contribution is to close this gap by introducing asymmetric cost functions for feedforward and feedback messages, derived from biological constraints such as Dale’s law, and by analyzing how these asymmetries reshape the optimal predictive feedback gain. This yields a principled account of when feedback is advantageous and when it is prohibitive, grounded in realistic metabolic and reliability considerations.

A growing body of work has highlighted the practical benefits of predictive feedback for artificial neural networks and for interpreting cortical dynamics ([21]–[28]), yet these investigations largely remain agnostic to the control‑theoretic structure of inference. By casting inference as a Linear‑Quadratic‑Gaussian (LQG) control problem, we obtain closed‑form solutions for the optimal predictive feedback gain and reveal non‑monotonic dependencies on both computational parameters and environmental dynamics. Importantly, our analysis predicts phase transitions in the utility of feedback—a qualitative shift that emerges only when feedback costs and noise are explicitly modeled. This theoretical advance not only clarifies the conditions under which predictive coding improves performance but also provides testable predictions about the organization of excitatory and inhibitory pathways in cortical circuits, positioning our work at the intersection of Bayesian inference, efficient coding, and biologically realistic predictive feedback.

A range of techniques has been proposed to mitigate language bias, including the use of extra annotations for accurate visual grounding [6], [7], synthetic data generation for augmentation [8]–[12], modifications to language modules [13], [14], and explicit formulation and exclusion of language priors [15]–[17]. By assuming that answers are always present in the text, the task reduces to predicting start and end positions, a formulation that has driven many influential models [19]–[25]. However, directly predicting positions can introduce a positional bias, where models learn to associate answers with specific locations in the passage [26]. Connections between robustness and large‑margin classification have also been investigated.  The support‑vector machine (SVM) and its variants constitute the classic large‑margin linear classifier, seeking to maximize the minimal distance between training points and the decision boundary.  More recent works have extended large‑margin ideas to nonlinear settings, for example by constructing Lipschitz‑constrained classifiers, by optimizing worst‑case margins for deep networks, or by learning metric embeddings that yield large‑margin nearest‑neighbor classifiers. [ANSWER]: Answering multi‑hop logical queries over knowledge graphs has been approached from two complementary perspectives.  Path‑based methods start from anchor entities and explicitly enumerate intermediate nodes, which yields accurate answers but incurs exponential computational cost as the query length grows.  Embedding‑based approaches sidestep this bottleneck by mapping entities and first‑order logic (FOL) queries into low‑dimensional spaces, where set‑theoretic operations are simulated with geometric or probabilistic constructs.  Prior geometric models embed queries as points, boxes, or other simple regions, yet they cannot represent the complement of these regions and therefore fail on queries that involve negation.  Probabilistic models such as those based on Beta distributions address negation but lose the intuitive region‑based decision rule that geometric shapes provide.  Our contribution is to introduce a unified geometric framework—Cone Embeddings (ConE)—that represents both entities and queries as Cartesian products of two‑dimensional cones.  By exploiting the closure properties of cones under intersection, union, and complement, ConE can faithfully model conjunction, disjunction, and negation within the same embedding space, making it the first geometry‑based QE model capable of handling the full spectrum of FOL operations while preserving the interpretability and efficiency of region‑based reasoning.

Geometric embeddings have become a cornerstone of modern knowledge‑graph representation, with families of models leveraging translation, rotation, and more complex transformations to capture relational patterns.  Recent work has explored boxes, convex cones, and non‑Euclidean manifolds such as Poincaré balls and hyperbolic entailment cones, demonstrating the expressive power of structured geometric regions.  Although several studies employ cone‑shaped objects, they are typically designed for tasks such as hierarchical classification or entailment modeling, and their cone definitions differ from the two‑dimensional Cartesian products we adopt.  In contrast, ConE defines cones whose complements remain within the same family, enabling a seamless geometric implementation of logical negation—a capability absent from existing cone‑based or hyperbolic approaches.  By integrating these geometric properties into a query‑embedding pipeline, ConE advances the state of the art in multi‑hop reasoning, offering a principled and computationally tractable alternative to both prior region‑based and distribution‑based methods.

[ANSWER]: Model-based reinforcement learning (MBRL) has attracted extensive attention because of its superior sample efficiency compared with model‑free approaches. Existing methods can be broadly grouped into four families according to how they exploit a learned dynamics model: (i) Dyna‑style algorithms that generate imaginary transitions and combine them with real experience to train a policy with off‑the‑shelf model‑free techniques; (ii) shooting methods that employ model predictive control to plan actions directly; (iii) analytic‑gradient approaches that back‑propagate through the model for policy search; and (iv) model‑augmented value‑expansion methods that use short model rollouts to refine temporal‑difference targets. Our work concentrates on the first family, where the interplay between model learning, imaginary‑data generation, and policy optimization creates a rich set of hyperparameters that must be scheduled throughout training. By focusing on this category, we are able to address the specific gap in theoretical understanding and automated scheduling of the real‑data ratio—a factor that prior work has treated only heuristically.

Within Dyna‑style MBRL, many studies have proposed improvements to individual components. Deep ensembles have become a standard technique for robust model learning, short rollout horizons are advocated to limit compounding model error, and uncertainty‑aware sampling schemes have been introduced to select reliable imagined transitions. Some works train the policy exclusively on imagined data, whereas others fix a constant mixture of real and imagined samples or adapt the mixture based on Q‑function uncertainty. Although these contributions advance the stability and performance of Dyna methods, they do not provide a principled way to coordinate multiple hyperparameters—such as model‑training frequency, policy‑training iterations, rollout length, and especially the proportion of real data—throughout the entire learning process. Our contribution lies in filling this void: we derive a theoretical return‑discrepancy bound that reveals why a gradually increasing real‑data ratio is advantageous, and we embed this insight into a joint hyperparameter‑scheduling framework (AutoMBPO) that automatically tunes all relevant knobs in model‑based policy optimization.

These approaches, however, either lack a theoretical justification for the scheduled parameters, assume unrealistic access to initial states without further interaction, or define a hyper‑MDP that differs substantially from the training dynamics of Dyna‑style methods. In contrast, our method formulates a hyper‑MDP that captures the full training state (including model error, policy performance, and data statistics) and designs a reward based on the actual return of the underlying RL task. By combining this formulation with the theoretical analysis of the real‑data ratio, AutoMBPO not only outperforms prior automatic tuning methods across a suite of continuous‑control benchmarks but also yields hyperparameter schedules that align with the derived theory, thereby offering both empirical gains and deeper insight into the design of Dyna‑style MBRL algorithms.

[ANSWER]: A large body of research has investigated embodied vision‑and‑language problems, including Vision‑Language Navigation (VLN) [1–3], Embodied Question Answering [4,5] and multimodal representation learning [6,7].  Early work on language grounding in embodied settings laid the foundation for agents that must interpret natural‑language cues while perceiving egocentric visual streams [8].  In VLN, which requires an agent to reach a goal location from a high‑level instruction, a series of methods have been proposed since the introduction of the R2R benchmark [1].  These approaches, often built on sequence‑to‑sequence or transformer architectures, have pushed unseen‑environment success rates up to roughly 61 % [9–11].

The more demanding task of Embodied Instruction Following (EIF) extends VLN by requiring agents to execute multi‑step plans that combine navigation and interaction actions.  Initial EIF systems employed end‑to‑end learning on concatenated language, visual, and trajectory inputs.  A Seq2Seq model equipped with an attention mechanism and a progress monitor served as a baseline [12], while later work replaced the sequence model with an episodic transformer [13].  Both families of methods predict the next low‑level action directly from the multimodal input, relying on large amounts of expert demonstration data.

Several subsequent approaches introduced a degree of modularity by first converting raw language and visual observations into structured representations before passing them to a separate action‑prediction module.  In these pipelines [14–16], the “action‑taking” component is still trained end‑to‑end and depends on neural memory (e.g., transformer embeddings or LSTM states) that implicitly encodes spatial layout, progress through the instruction, and the agent’s internal state.  This implicit tracking limits interpretability and makes it difficult to isolate the sources of failure.

A more explicitly structured line of work incorporated a persistent, spatially organized memory.  One notable method transformed language and visual inputs into high‑level actions and a 3D map, then used a value‑iteration network (VIN) to generate low‑level actions [17].  Navigation goals for the VIN were sampled from a model trained on interaction‑pose labels derived from expert trajectories, tying the system’s exploration behavior to supervised trajectory information.

Research on visual navigation with semantic mapping has also informed EIF solutions.  Classical Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (SLAM) techniques construct 2D or 3D obstacle maps [18–20].  More recent methods generate semantic maps through differentiable projection operations, mitigating the accumulation of egocentric prediction errors [21,22].  These works target object‑goal navigation, a simpler problem than EIF, and employ semantic exploration policies that guide agents toward large, easily detectable objects (e.g., a fridge) across rooms.  In contrast, other studies [23,24] applied semantic 2D maps to grounded‑language navigation for aerial platforms, where the field of view is nearly complete and the need for fine‑grained search is reduced; additionally, these settings involve only a single navigation subtask.

**This work introduces a fully modular architecture for embodied instruction following that (i) parses natural‑language commands into structured semantic representations, (ii) builds a metric semantic map from egocentric visual input, (iii) employs a language‑conditioned semantic search policy to propose candidate goal locations, and (iv) executes a deterministic navigation‑and‑interaction policy based on the predicted goal.  The design eliminates the requirement for expert demonstration trajectories and low‑level language instructions, although the latter can be incorporated as optional auxiliary input to obtain an additional performance gain.  Evaluated on the ALFRED benchmark, the system attains state‑of‑the‑art success rates of 24.46 % (an 8.17 % absolute improvement over the previous best) and 26.49 % when low‑level instructions are provided.  These results demonstrate that an explicit spatial memory coupled with a semantic search policy yields more robust state‑tracking and exploration than end‑to‑end approaches that rely on implicit neural memory.

[ANSWER]: Traditional event‑detection approaches have been dominated by neural‑network models that treat each event type independently. Convolutional, recurrent, and transformer‑based architectures have achieved strong performance on benchmark datasets, yet they largely ignore the latent correlations among event types and therefore provide limited robustness when training data are scarce. Consequently, these methods tend to overfit on well‑represented categories while failing to generalize to rare or unseen types.  

Low‑resource event detection has motivated a range of alternative strategies. Supervised methods that rely on abundant labeled instances struggle when the data distribution is long‑tailed, prompting researchers to explore meta‑learning techniques that cast event detection as a few‑shot learning problem and enable rapid adaptation to new types with minimal supervision. Knowledge‑enhancement approaches incorporate external trigger vocabularies or reformulate the task as machine‑reading comprehension to alleviate long‑tail effects, while zero‑shot frameworks map mentions to a predefined ontology without requiring any annotated examples of the target type. Early ontology‑based zero‑shot models, however, construct the ontology solely from intra‑event structure, overlooking richer inter‑type relationships that could further support knowledge transfer.  

To exploit correlations among event types, recent work has introduced graph‑based representations that connect event categories through shared entities and relational paths, allowing multi‑hop reasoning over a structured schema. Such designs, however, depend on extensive entity and relation annotations, which can be costly to obtain. Parallel efforts in relation extraction have demonstrated the benefits of logic‑based, ontology‑driven learning, where inductive logic programming yields symbolic rules that capture class‑level dependencies and support explicit reasoning. These approaches illustrate the potential of combining ontological knowledge with statistical models to encode inter‑type correlations.  

Building on these observations, the present work proposes an ontology‑driven event‑detection framework that simultaneously encodes intra‑event features and inter‑type correlations. By enriching a base event ontology with temporal, causal, and hierarchical links, the method learns ontology embeddings that propagate information from data‑rich to data‑poor categories and enable inference for previously unseen types. A rule‑based correlation inference component augments the ontology with additional event‑event relations, enhancing reasoning capability without requiring exhaustive entity annotations. A newly constructed dataset supports comprehensive evaluation, and experiments demonstrate consistent gains over prior neural, meta‑learning, and ontology‑based baselines in overall, few‑shot, and zero‑shot settings, confirming the effectiveness of integrating structured ontological knowledge with deep representations for low‑resource event detection.

[ANSWER]: Knowledge distillation has traditionally relied on access to the original training data, either by directly transferring soft predictions of a teacher [1, 2] or by matching intermediate representations [3, 4].  Recent data‑free distillation methods attempt to bypass this requirement by synthesizing images from scratch [5–8], yet they often suffer from low fidelity and limited diversity, which hampers performance on complex downstream tasks such as semantic segmentation [9, 10].  A complementary line of work explores the use of out‑of‑domain (OOD) samples for distillation, but naïve application of OOD data typically yields students that fail to generalize to the target domain [11, 12].  Our approach, **MosaicKD**, advances this literature by introducing the first dedicated framework for OOD‑KD that explicitly leverages the shared local statistics of OOD images to reconstruct approximate in‑domain samples.  By embedding the teacher’s guidance into a four‑player adversarial game, MosaicKD generates synthetic data with realistic patches and coherent global semantics, thereby achieving substantially higher student performance than prior data‑free and OOD‑based distillation methods.

Domain adaptation and generalization aim to bridge distribution gaps between source and target domains, often by aligning feature spaces [13–15] or by learning domain‑invariant representations [16, 17].  While unsupervised adaptation assumes access to unlabeled target data during training, domain‑generalization techniques restrict themselves to source data only and seek robustness to unseen domains [18–21].  These paradigms, however, are designed for supervised tasks and do not address the unique challenges of knowledge transfer from a fixed teacher when the original training data are unavailable.  MosaicKD situates itself at the intersection of these fields: it treats the teacher’s pre‑trained model as a source of privileged knowledge, yet discards any reliance on source or target data, instead synthesizing surrogate in‑domain inputs from OOD patches.  This novel formulation extends the scope of domain‑generalization ideas to the distillation setting, providing a principled solution to the OOD‑KD problem that outperforms both adaptation‑based and generalization‑based baselines.

Generative adversarial networks (GANs) have become the de‑facto tool for realistic image synthesis through a two‑player minimax game between a generator and a discriminator [22].  Subsequent work has focused on improving image quality [23, 24], enhancing diversity [25, 26], and stabilizing training [27, 28], as well as adapting GANs to low‑data regimes via transfer learning [29] or data augmentation [30].  Nonetheless, standard GAN formulations presume the availability of real samples from the target distribution, an assumption that breaks down in OOD‑KD where the original data are inaccessible.  MosaicKD augments the classic GAN framework with two additional participants—a pre‑trained teacher and a student network—forming a four‑player min‑max game.  The discriminator operates on local patches to enforce authenticity, while the generator is driven not only by adversarial loss but also by the teacher’s soft predictions, ensuring that the synthesized images possess globally meaningful semantics for effective distillation.  This extended adversarial scheme uniquely addresses data synthesis under strict OOD constraints and yields synthetic samples that are both locally realistic and globally useful for knowledge transfer, surpassing existing GAN‑based data‑free distillation approaches.

[ANSWER]: Learning action abstractions has been a central theme in hierarchical reinforcement learning.  Prior work on online skill discovery typically learns temporally extended primitives to improve exploration and sample complexity in an online setting, often by maximizing information‑theoretic objectives or by training continuous or discrete low‑level policies that higher‑level controllers invoke (e.g., [6]–[10], [11]–[13], [14]–[16]).  These methods rely on interactive data collection and assume that the learned skills are executed repeatedly during training.  In contrast, our contribution is to **learn a compact, single‑step action representation entirely offline from a fixed, potentially highly suboptimal dataset** and to show that this representation can be leveraged to dramatically reduce the amount of near‑optimal expert data required for imitation learning.  By decoupling the representation learning phase from any hierarchical execution structure, we avoid the need for temporal abstraction and enable the use of arbitrary offline trajectories, including those generated by random policies.

Offline skill extraction approaches aim to discover temporally extended actions from a static dataset, typically by fitting latent variable models and then using the induced latent space for planning, imitation, or reinforcement learning (e.g., [17]–[28]).  Theoretical analyses of these methods attribute performance gains mainly to the **temporal abstraction** they provide, assuming that the latent space contains richer, longer‑horizon behaviors than the raw action space ([19], [29]).  Our work departs from this line of research in two important ways.  First, we provide a **theoretical bound that isolates the benefit of a lower‑dimensional, reparameterized action space independent of any temporal hierarchy**, showing how it directly improves the sample efficiency of downstream behavioral cloning.  Second, because our method does not require the offline data to exhibit diverse, skill‑like structures, it remains effective even when the dataset is unimodal or consists of random actions—situations that have been reported as challenging for existing offline skill extraction techniques ([19]).  Thus, our analysis and algorithm broaden the applicability of offline representation learning to settings where only cheap, suboptimal trajectories are available.

A complementary strand of research has investigated state representation learning for accelerating reinforcement learning, often by learning latent dynamics models that compress high‑dimensional observations such as images into smaller state embeddings ([30]–[36]).  While these works demonstrate that a compact state space can ease policy learning, they do not address the **action‑space bottleneck** that persists even when states are low‑dimensional.  Our contribution fills this gap by **learning a factored transition model that yields a latent action space**, enabling the downstream imitation learner to operate on a simpler decision variable.  By jointly training an energy‑based transition model and an action decoder on offline data, and then reparameterizing expert actions through this model, we achieve up to a four‑fold improvement over standard behavioral cloning.  In this sense, our work complements state‑representation methods but focuses on the under‑explored problem of action‑space reduction for sample‑efficient imitation learning.

[ANSWER]: Most continual‑learning research has focused on the class‑incremental setting, where a model—typically a neural network—receives data from new classes in successive stages and is evaluated on all classes learned so far. Early class‑incremental learning (CIL) methods mitigate catastrophic forgetting by retaining a subset of exemplars from previously seen classes and interleaving them with new data during training. While effective, exemplar‑based approaches scale poorly because memory constraints become prohibitive as the number of classes grows, limiting their applicability in real‑world scenarios. To address memory limitations, a line of work adopts regularization‑based strategies that constrain parameter updates to preserve knowledge of earlier tasks. Although these techniques eliminate the need for stored examples, they generally lag behind exemplar‑based methods in terms of accuracy.

A smaller body of literature has examined few‑shot class‑incremental learning (FSCIL), which seeks to incorporate new classes from only a few labeled examples while operating under strict memory budgets. These studies explore various mechanisms—such as prototype adaptation, metric learning, and dynamic network expansion—to balance the competing demands of sample efficiency and stability. Nonetheless, a common assumption across most continual‑learning frameworks is that each incremental batch contains fully labeled data for the classes introduced at that stage. In many robotic and embodied settings, data arrive as a continuous stream, are often unlabeled, and must be processed online, highlighting a gap between existing methods and practical deployment.

Parallel to continual learning, active learning has been widely investigated for object recognition. Approaches based on uncertainty sampling train deep networks with specialized loss functions that encourage the model to assign high uncertainty scores to ambiguous samples, thereby guiding the selection of informative instances for annotation. These methods, however, are generally designed for batch learning and do not incorporate mechanisms to prevent forgetting when the model is updated repeatedly. Moreover, while active‑learning systems can identify unknown classes during an initial batch training phase, they tend to lose this capability in subsequent increments, as newly learned categories absorb previously unknown samples.

Open‑set recognition and out‑of‑distribution (OOD) detection constitute another related research area. In this setting, a model trained on a known set of classes must identify test samples that belong to unseen categories. Numerous OOD detection techniques have been proposed, ranging from confidence‑based thresholds to generative‑model approaches, enabling the recognition of unknown inputs during inference. However, these methods typically treat unknown samples as static test‑time anomalies and do not incorporate them into the training process for continual improvement. Comprehensive surveys have highlighted the conceptual overlap among continual learning, active learning, and open‑set recognition, suggesting that integrating insights from these domains could provide a natural bridge for systems that must both select informative unlabeled data and adapt continuously to newly encountered classes.

[ANSWER]: The literature on exploiting redundancy in deep networks can be organized into several strands. Tensor decomposition methods have been widely explored for reducing the computational burden of convolutions. A Generalized SVD approach was introduced to factorize a convolution tensor into a sequence of smaller convolutions, while Spatial SVD decomposes kernels into spatially separated components. Subsequent work presented a non‑iterative low‑rank decomposition technique, and CP‑decomposition as well as tensor‑train decomposition have been applied to high‑dimensional tensors to achieve similar reductions.  

Structured pruning approaches focus on removing redundant channels across layers. Various selection criteria have been proposed, including lasso‑based channel selection and group‑lasso regularization that penalizes unimportant groups at multiple granularity levels. Comprehensive surveys compare structured pruning with tensor‑decomposition techniques, highlighting their respective trade‑offs.  

Semi‑structured and unstructured pruning methods operate at finer granularities. Block‑wise sparsity, also called semi‑structured pruning, removes groups of weights within channels, whereas unstructured pruning eliminates individual parameters, often achieving higher compression ratios at the cost of hardware‑friendly deployment.  

Using prefixed bases to represent convolutional filters constitutes another line of work. Basis representations such as wavelet bases and Fourier‑Bessel bases have been employed to extract features and reduce computational complexity. Tensor decomposition can be interpreted as learning such basis representations, and binary mask‑based bases have been proposed to directly decrease the number of multiplications required.  

Orthogonal to these compression strategies, shift‑based operations and addition‑dominant network designs have been investigated to replace costly multiplications with cheaper additions, leveraging the disparity between multiplication and addition costs in modern hardware.

[ANSWER]: Vision Transformers (ViTs) introduce self‑attention mechanisms to vision tasks, extending the Transformer architecture originally proposed for natural language processing. The seminal work of Dosovitskiy et al. demonstrated that a pure Transformer can achieve strong image‑classification performance when trained on large datasets. Subsequent studies have enriched the ViT design by integrating convolutional operations to capture local inductive biases, by constructing hierarchical pyramidal feature maps that enable multi‑scale representation, and by enhancing locality through specialized token‑mixing strategies. Neural architecture search (NAS) techniques have also been employed to discover efficient ViT configurations, while token‑pruning methods aim to reduce the number of processed tokens during inference, thereby accelerating model execution.

Efficient attention mechanisms address the quadratic time and memory complexity of standard multi‑head self‑attention (MSA). In natural language processing, approaches such as low‑rank decomposition, kernel‑based approximations, memory‑augmented attention, and sparsity‑inducing patterns have been proposed to alleviate this burden. Directly transferring these techniques to computer vision often yields suboptimal results due to the distinct spatial characteristics of image data. Vision‑specific efficient attentions include spatial‑reduction attention, which compresses the key/value tensors; local window attention, which restricts attention to non‑overlapping regions; and Twins attention, which combines shifted windows with global tokens. Methods that attempt to capture both local and global interactions within a single layer, such as focal attention and QuadTree attention, introduce additional operations (e.g., multi‑scale window partitioning, recursion) that are not hardware‑friendly and can degrade practical throughput on GPUs despite favorable theoretical FLOP counts.

Frequency‑domain analysis has long been used to understand visual information. Low‑frequency components tend to encode global structure, illumination, and coarse color patterns, whereas high‑frequency components capture fine details such as edges and textures. This decomposition has motivated a variety of applications, including image super‑resolution, robustness and generalization studies, image re‑scaling, and network compression techniques that exploit spectral properties. By recognizing the complementary roles of different frequency bands, recent works have explored ways to process or emphasize specific frequency ranges to improve efficiency or performance in visual models.

In this work, we present a vision‑Transformer backbone that emphasizes practical inference speed on modern hardware while preserving competitive accuracy across classification, detection, and segmentation benchmarks. Building on the observation that existing efficient attentions often sacrifice either locality or global context, we introduce a novel self‑attention module that explicitly separates high‑ and low‑frequency processing within a single MSA layer. The high‑frequency branch performs localized windowed attention on full‑resolution feature maps, capturing fine‑grained details efficiently, whereas the low‑frequency branch aggregates average‑pooled representations from each window and conducts global attention over this compact set, preserving long‑range dependencies at reduced cost. This dual‑path design avoids hardware‑unfriendly operations and achieves superior throughput and memory utilization compared with prior efficient attentions. Additionally, we adopt a lightweight convolutional positional encoding within feed‑forward networks to replace costly interpolation‑based schemes, further enhancing speed on dense‑prediction tasks. Extensive experiments demonstrate that the proposed architecture outperforms state‑of‑the‑art ViTs in both accuracy and direct speed metrics on GPUs and CPUs, establishing a new baseline for efficient, frequency‑aware transformer models in computer vision.

Structured pruning strategies target redundancy at the granularity of entire channels or groups of filters. By measuring the importance of each channel—often via magnitude‑based criteria, ℓ₁ regularization, or learned sparsity masks—these methods eliminate whole feature maps and the associated weights, leading to substantial reductions in memory footprint and FLOPs. Variants employ group‑lasso penalties to encourage blockwise sparsity across layers, and surveys have cataloged a wide range of channel‑selection techniques, including optimization‑driven and heuristic approaches. While effective, such pruning explicitly removes parameters after training, relying on a separate selection step to determine which structures to discard.

Semi‑structured and unstructured pruning operate at finer resolutions. Block‑wise sparsity imposes patterns of zeros within individual filters, offering a middle ground between channel‑level removal and per‑parameter sparsity. Purely unstructured pruning zeroes out individual weights based on criteria such as magnitude or sensitivity, often achieving higher compression ratios. A complementary line of research replaces learned convolutional kernels with fixed basis expansions. By expressing filters as linear combinations of pre‑defined functions—such as wavelets, Fourier‑Bessel bases, or other analytical dictionaries—these approaches constrain the degrees of freedom of the weights while retaining expressive power. The choice of basis critically influences both the representational efficiency and the computational cost; for instance, Fourier‑Bessel bases have been shown to reduce FLOPs without sacrificing accuracy. [ANSWER]: Sparse depth completion targets the reconstruction of dense depth maps from sparse depth measurements together with a corresponding RGB image. The sparsity patterns encountered in practice differ markedly depending on the acquisition method. Stereo‑based approaches typically yield depth points concentrated along object contours while providing few measurements on texture‑less regions. Beyond these three common patterns, additional configurations have been explored: line‑based patterns simulate partial laser observations, removal of depth values on specular surfaces emulates the behavior of commodity depth cameras, and uniform grid sampling represents a simplified, artificial sparsity model.

Early deep‑learning methods for sparse depth completion treated the sparse depth map and the RGB image as a single four‑channel input, feeding the concatenated tensor into a ResNet‑style depth estimation network. This straightforward stacking improves performance relative to monocular depth estimation that relies solely on RGB. Subsequent works adopted a two‑branch encoder‑decoder architecture, reminiscent of networks used for RGB‑D segmentation, in which one branch processes the sparse depth and the other processes the RGB image. In many of these designs the two branches extract features independently and later fuse them through concatenation, addition, or by using RGB features to guide refinement of the depth prediction. Such approaches work well on benchmarks where the sparsity is moderate, but they may struggle when the depth measurements are extremely sparse.

Canonical Correlation Analysis (CCA) is a classical statistical technique for finding a shared subspace in which representations from two modalities are maximally correlated. To overcome the linearity constraint of traditional CCA, Deep CCA (DCCA) introduced nonlinear projections learned by deep neural networks, enabling more expressive cross‑modal mappings. DCCA and related extensions have been applied broadly to multimodal representation learning tasks, including audio‑visual correspondence, cross‑modal retrieval, and sensor fusion.

Standard (one‑dimensional) CCA suffers from singular covariance matrices when applied to high‑dimensional data with a limited number of samples, a situation known as the small‑sample‑size (SSS) problem. Two‑dimensional CCA formulations address this issue by constructing full‑rank covariance matrices directly on matrix‑valued inputs, an idea inspired by 2DPCA and 2DLDA and successfully employed in face‑recognition studies. By decomposing the input into observable depth‑RGB pairs and complementary RGB regions, the network learns a joint representation that bridges the two modalities. To capture this relationship we embed a two‑dimensional deep canonical correlation objective, which enforces the feature encoders to produce maximally correlated, nonlinear embeddings while avoiding the SSS singularity inherent in traditional DCCA. The proposed architecture combines a dual‑branch encoder‑decoder with feature‑level mutual transformation, enabling the reconstruction of missing depth values from complementary RGB cues. Extensive experiments across diverse sparsity patterns—including stereo‑derived contours, LiDAR‑structured scans, SLAM‑derived feature points, line‑based laser simulations, specular‑surface culling, and uniform grids—demonstrate state‑of‑the‑art performance on both indoor and outdoor datasets, confirming the effectiveness of the correlation‑driven design and the 2D deep CCA formulation.

Ensemble learning has been widely combined with knowledge distillation to further enhance generalization. Methods that distill from ensembles of independently trained teachers have reported notable gains, and online distillation frameworks have sought to increase the diversity among multiple models during training, thereby strengthening the ensemble effect. The prevailing view in these approaches remains that stronger ensembles, achieved through longer training or larger model capacities, are preferable for distillation.

A line of research has challenged the notion that the strongest possible teacher is always optimal. Empirical studies have shown that a large capacity gap between teacher and student can impede effective knowledge transfer. To mitigate this gap, several strategies have been explored: introducing an intermediate‑size assistant network, designing “tolerant” teachers via softened loss functions, or constructing student‑friendly teachers by embedding student branches during training. While these works demonstrate that reducing the teacher‑student mismatch can improve distillation, they typically lack a unifying theoretical explanation for the observed gap.

Self‑distillation frameworks provide another perspective by using a model’s own intermediate checkpoints as teachers for its later iterations. Building on this insight, we propose an algorithm that selects the optimal intermediate teacher by maximizing task‑related mutual information while minimizing nuisance information. Such approaches have been applied to point‑cloud generation, bounding‑box regression, and graph construction, but they inherit the “responsibility problem”: the loss is discontinuous because any permutation of the predicted elements is equally valid.  In contrast, our model explicitly respects permutation invariance by back‑propagating through a differentiable set encoder, yielding a smooth set‑wise objective that works for variable‑size outputs and eliminates the discontinuities that plague MLP decoders.  

Recurrent neural networks (RNNs) have also been used to emit set elements sequentially, relying on a manually imposed canonical order (e.g., breadth‑first traversal for graphs).  While this sidesteps permutation issues, it requires domain‑specific ordering heuristics and limits applicability to problems where such an order is natural.  Our approach does not depend on any predefined ordering; it directly maps a single feature vector to an unordered set, making it suitable for tasks like object detection where no intrinsic sequence exists.  

Mordatch’s iterative energy‑minimisation framework similarly differentiates through a forward‑pass optimisation, but it has only been demonstrated on small 2‑D point sets and employs an opaque learned energy whose relationship to the target set is unclear.  We extend the idea of differentiable optimisation to large‑scale, real‑world set prediction problems (e.g., detecting multiple objects in images) and replace the learned energy with a clear set‑distance objective, providing both scalability and interpretability that the original method lacks.

Because the decoder requires the encoder at test time, the architecture is limited to reconstruction tasks and cannot be used for pure set prediction from an external feature.  Our model decouples encoding and decoding: the set encoder is only used during training to define a differentiable loss, while inference relies solely on the learned vector‑to‑set decoder, enabling prediction from any upstream feature extractor.

Early approaches introduced binary discrete messages and later converged on one‑hot encodings, treating each possible token as an orthogonal basis vector that agents emit without sharing gradients or weights during training or execution.  

A recurring limitation of emergent protocols is their lack of interpretability for humans or for agents that have not co‑trained on the same communication system, which manifests as a “zero‑shot’’ learning problem.  Several studies have identified environmental and architectural factors that promote zero‑shot continuous communication, while other efforts adopt bottom‑up strategies that explicitly align emergent tokens with human language, demonstrating that people can infer the meaning of certain agent symbols in novel contexts. Parallel developments in natural‑language processing have transitioned from naïve one‑hot word representations to dense embedding methods such as Word2Vec and GloVe. The success of such continuous representations has motivated the view that emergent communication tokens might benefit from a similar embedding‑based treatment rather than remaining as isolated one‑hot symbols.  

Research on zero‑ and few‑shot classification further illustrates how side information—often derived from language—enables models to recognize novel classes with little or no labeled data. By aligning the emergent token space with pre‑trained word embeddings, the agents acquire zero‑shot capabilities: they correctly interpret novel human utterances and generate appropriate responses without additional training.  Human‑subject studies confirm that participants can reliably decode the unlabeled emergent symbols, outperforming prior one‑hot communication schemes.  Together, these contributions extend emergent discrete communication beyond orthogonal symbols, integrate ideas from modern word‑embedding and zero‑shot learning literature, and enable both agent‑agent and human‑agent interaction without reliance on external language models.

[ANSWER]: Interpretability research in deep NLP has traditionally focused on two complementary questions: (i) what linguistic or world knowledge is encoded in contextualized representations (concept analysis) and (ii) how that knowledge influences individual model decisions (attribution analysis).  Our study belongs to the first line of inquiry, but we move beyond the usual post‑hoc decomposability approaches by explicitly treating clusters of hidden states as “encoded concepts” and by measuring their systematic overlap with a broad taxonomy of human‑defined linguistic categories.  This positioning lets us address the same overarching goal—understanding what a model knows—while providing a more fine‑grained, unsupervised view of the internal organization of knowledge.  

A large body of prior work probes representations by training auxiliary classifiers to predict specific linguistic properties (e.g., morphology, syntax, semantics) and interprets probe accuracy as a proxy for the amount of information stored in the model.  Although probing has yielded valuable insights, it inherits methodological concerns such as probe complexity, dependence on random seeds, and a focus on single properties in isolation.  In contrast, ConceptX does not rely on any downstream classifier; instead it discovers latent clusters directly from the representations and aligns them with dozens of pre‑defined concepts ranging from affixes to psycholinguistic categories.  By sidestepping probe‑training altogether, our framework avoids the confounds associated with probe design and offers a holistic picture of how multiple linguistic abstractions coexist across layers.  

Earlier investigations of latent concepts in language models have either visualized activation patterns, examined attention heads, or induced task‑specific concepts through supervised binary classification.  For example, studies that induced latent concepts with a binary task demonstrated the presence of both linguistically motivated and novel notions, yet they required supervision and were limited to a single downstream objective.  Our contribution extends this line of work by (a) operating fully unsupervised, (b) employing a novel alignment function that quantifies overlap between discovered clusters and a large, heterogeneous set of human‑defined concepts, and (c) scaling the analysis to seven distinct transformer architectures.  This enables a systematic comparison of how different model families distribute lexical, morphological, syntactic, semantic, and psycholinguistic information across their depth.  

Finally, while probing and our clustering‑based approach address different aspects of interpretability, they are not mutually exclusive.  ConceptX provides a complementary perspective that can be combined with probing results to validate findings or to pinpoint where probes succeed or fail.  By delivering both qualitative visualizations and quantitative alignment scores, our work supplies a new, scalable tool for the community to map the internal geometry of language models to interpretable linguistic constructs.

[ANSWER]: Deep clustering methods have leveraged the expressive power of neural networks to learn representations and cluster assignments jointly. Early approaches combined reconstruction objectives with clustering loss functions, while later works incorporated pairwise relationships, multi‑task learning, or other auxiliary signals. These joint frameworks typically optimize a weighted sum of several losses, which can be difficult to balance in practice when validation data are scarce, leading to sensitivity to hyper‑parameter choices.

Probabilistic deep clustering has been explored from both generative and discriminative perspectives. Generative models introduce latent variables and impose mixture‑of‑Gaussians priors on latent representations to model the data‑generation process. Although such assumptions can capture certain statistical regularities, they may be violated for complex visual data and do not always translate into superior clustering performance. Discriminative probabilistic methods, by contrast, model the direct mapping from inputs to cluster labels and often maximize mutual information, achieving higher cluster accuracy. However, these approaches tend to ignore instance‑specific details that could enhance representation learning and consequently benefit clustering.

Several recent works have combined the mixture‑of‑experts (MoE) paradigm with deep clustering. Methods such as MIXAE, DAMIC, and MoE‑Sim‑VAE integrate MoE with reconstruction‑based objectives, but they rely on additional mechanisms such as pre‑training stages, regularization terms, or auxiliary clustering losses to achieve good performance. These extra components increase algorithmic complexity and may limit scalability.

Contrastive learning has become a dominant paradigm for learning discriminative visual representations without labels. A variety of contrastive objectives have been proposed, ranging from instance discrimination with noise‑contrastive estimation to pretext tasks such as colorization and context auto‑encoding. Architectures like InstDisc, MoCo, and related extensions maintain memory banks or momentum encoders to compute efficient contrastive losses. While the resulting embeddings excel on downstream tasks after fine‑tuning, most contrastive frameworks are not directly optimized for clustering. Some recent attempts, such as PCL, augment contrastive learning with an auxiliary clustering objective (e.g., k‑means) to expose semantic structure, but they still require extra clustering steps and focus on learning transferable embeddings rather than discovering intrinsic data groups.

In this work we introduce a unified probabilistic clustering framework that integrates the strengths of contrastive representation learning and latent mixture modeling. By employing a gating network to assign data points to expert modules and training each expert with a contrastive objective, the method captures both fine‑grained instance discrimination and high‑level semantic partitioning within a single objective. A scalable Expectation‑Maximization algorithm is derived to handle the latent variables, with theoretical guarantees on the monotonic improvement and convergence of the evidence lower bound. Unlike prior MoE‑based clustering approaches, the proposed method does not rely on pre‑training, explicit regularization, or separate clustering losses. Compared with purely discriminative or generative probabilistic models, it preserves instance‑level detail while modeling cluster semantics. Extensive experiments on four widely used natural‑image benchmarks demonstrate that the approach consistently outperforms strong contrastive baselines and a broad range of existing deep clustering methods, establishing a new state‑of‑the‑art for unsupervised image clustering.

[ANSWER]: Prototype classifiers that rely on meta‑learning have become a cornerstone of few‑shot learning. Early work introduced the idea of constructing one or multiple class prototypes from support examples and classifying queries by measuring similarity to these prototypes [1–8]. Various extensions enrich the prototype representation or the similarity computation: attention mechanisms [1,7], relation networks [5], re‑weighting schemes that account for between‑class and within‑class interactions [4], latent‑cluster models [6], and multimodal prototype constructions [3]. Transformations of the feature space to enhance separability have also been explored [9–12]. Because of their simplicity, prototype‑based methods have been adapted to tasks beyond image classification, including semantic segmentation [13], text classification [14], and speech recognition [15].

Update‑based meta‑learning approaches take a different route by adapting model parameters at test time. Methods such as Model‑Agnostic Meta‑Learning (MAML) and its variants [16–18] learn initial parameters that can be quickly refined with a few gradient steps on the support set. Other techniques learn an explicit update rule for a base learner through episodic training [19,20]. While effective, these approaches introduce additional hyper‑parameters and require extra computation during adaptation, which can hinder rapid deployment to novel classes.

A line of research has demonstrated that fine‑tuning a linear classifier on features extracted by a standard cross‑entropy‑trained backbone can achieve performance comparable to meta‑learning methods [21,22]. Subsequent studies propose refinements for the few‑shot setting, such as calibrating the support‑set distribution [23], leveraging self‑supervised learning on query data [24], and distilling knowledge to obtain richer embeddings [25]. Investigations into the pre‑training phase revealed that employing a negative margin in the cross‑entropy loss can further improve few‑shot performance [26]. Despite these gains, fine‑tuning still requires hyper‑parameter selection and retraining whenever new classes appear, limiting its suitability for instant adaptation.

Theoretical analyses of few‑shot learning remain relatively sparse. Within the meta‑learning framework, risk bounds for the meta‑testing phase have been derived as functions of the amounts of meta‑training and meta‑testing data [27]. Information‑theoretic lower bounds on minimax convergence rates for algorithms trained on multiple source domains and evaluated on novel domains have also been established [28]. Specific to prototype classifiers, a bound was presented that links performance to the mismatch between the number of shots used during meta‑training and meta‑testing, assuming class‑conditional Gaussian distributions with shared covariance matrices [29]. This assumption restricts the applicability of the result to more realistic feature distributions.

In this work we (i) derive a novel generalization bound for prototype classifiers that does not rely on any specific distributional form or on equal class covariances, (ii) elucidate how the variance of feature‑vector norms influences the bound and consequently the classifier’s performance, and (iii) empirically validate that reducing this variance—via simple L₂ normalization or by directly minimizing the ratio of within‑class to between‑class variance—yields performance on par with fine‑tuned linear classifiers while requiring neither meta‑learning nor test‑time adaptation. Our analysis bridges the gap between prototype‑based methods, fine‑tuning approaches, and existing theoretical results, offering a principled and practical route to fast, hyper‑parameter‑free few‑shot classification.

The second strand concentrates on enhancing the decoder component, often by imposing syntactic or semantic constraints such as grammar‑based decoding, graph‑based generation, or domain‑specific validity checks. Markov chain Monte Carlo techniques have been employed to sample high‑probability regions of the space, while reinforcement‑learning approaches have trained policies to construct molecules atom by atom or to generate complete SMILES strings using autoregressive models. Although many of these methods can discover high‑performing compounds, they often require large numbers of function evaluations and therefore exhibit lower sample efficiency compared with Bayesian optimization‑based approaches.

Third, we design a transformer‑based encoder–decoder architecture built on a recent graph‑oriented molecular representation, which further improves the organization and validity of the latent space. Comprehensive experiments on six real‑world benchmark tasks demonstrate that the resulting algorithm achieves up to twenty‑fold improvements over state‑of‑the‑art latent‑space Bayesian optimization methods, while retaining the sample efficiency advantages of Bayesian optimization compared with evolutionary, MCMC, and reinforcement‑learning baselines.

While these models benefit from joint optimization, they still rely on a fixed factorization of the joint distribution over subjects, objects and predicates, imposing conditional independencies that may be suboptimal for certain visual contexts.  

The long‑tail nature of object and predicate distributions is a well‑known challenge for scene graph generation, as the combinatorial space of relationship triplets is heavily skewed toward a few frequent classes. In the broader literature, data‑sampling techniques—such as oversampling tail classes or undersampling head classes—have been widely employed to rebalance training sets [15‑21]. More recent approaches like [3] generate entities and predicates separately and then employ a graph‑assembly step to pair predicates with entity pairs, which limits the ability of predicate predictions to influence entity estimates. These designs illustrate the trade‑off between architectural simplicity and the degree of mutual conditioning among graph components.

[ANSWER]: Research on efficient computation of probabilistic queries has a long history in machine learning and artificial intelligence, originating from exact inference in multivariate graphical models. In this setting, two broad families of queries are distinguished. Conditional probability queries ask for the probability of a subset of variables given observed values of another subset, requiring marginalization over the remaining variables. Assignment queries, also known as most probable explanation (MPE) or maximum a posteriori (MAP) queries when no evidence variables are present, seek the highest‑probability assignment to a set of variables conditioned on observed evidence. Foundational works on these problems established the theoretical underpinnings and algorithmic approaches for both exact and approximate inference.

When the underlying model exhibits a sparse Markov dependence structure, a substantial body of work has leveraged this property to obtain efficient inference algorithms. In sequential settings, recursive computation techniques such as the forward‑backward algorithm and dynamic programming exploit the limited connectivity of Markov chains or hidden Markov models, enabling tractable evaluation of both conditional and assignment queries. However, autoregressive neural sequence models differ fundamentally from traditional Markovian models: their hidden state is a continuous vector that summarizes the entire history, producing a combinatorial tree of exponentially many future trajectories. Consequently, classic dynamic‑programming methods do not apply, and both conditional probability and assignment queries become computationally intractable in the worst case, with NP‑hardness results documented for related inference problems.

In natural language processing and related domains, a considerable literature has addressed assignment‑type queries for neural sequence models, focusing on the MAP problem of generating high‑quality sequences conditioned on a prefix or auxiliary context. Heuristic decoding strategies such as beam search, best‑first search, various sampling schemes, and hybrid approaches have been proposed and empirically validated for producing plausible outputs. These methods are primarily designed to approximate the most likely sequence rather than to estimate arbitrary conditional probabilities. While some decoding techniques can be repurposed to obtain lower‑bound estimates of probabilities, they inherently produce biased estimators and do not provide general solutions for the broader class of conditional probability queries.

Building on the gaps identified in prior work, this paper introduces a systematic framework for answering arbitrary predictive queries in neural autoregressive sequence models. By defining a typology that decomposes complex queries into elementary building blocks, the approach constrains the underlying model to restricted path spaces that satisfy a given query, thereby yielding a novel proposal distribution. Leveraging this distribution, we develop three estimation methods—beam‑search‑based importance sampling, pure importance sampling, and a hybrid of the two—that enable near real‑time computation of conditional probabilities for events occurring at any horizon. Extensive experiments on four large‑scale user‑behavior datasets, two language corpora, and the GPT‑2 language model demonstrate that the proposed methods make query answering tractable across exponentially large predictive path spaces, reveal distinct cost‑accuracy trade‑offs among the techniques, and illustrate how model entropy influences performance. This work thus fills a previously unaddressed niche in the literature by providing the first general-purpose solutions for conditional probability querying in neural autoregressive models.

In disease‑classification pipelines, the problem is typically framed as an image‑level categorization where each disease corresponds to a class. Various multi‑scale and multi‑instance convolutional architectures have been proposed to capture heterogeneous patterns in medical scans, such as lung nodule patches, diabetic macular edema, and myopic macular degeneration. Some approaches further predict disease severity or stage by mapping learned representations to ordinal status categories. Detection methods have adapted object‑detection frameworks originally designed for natural images, including Faster‑RCNN, Feature Pyramid Networks (FPN), and YOLO, to locate organs or lesions in 2‑D and 3‑D medical volumes.
