[ANSWER]: Research on cooperative multi‑agent reinforcement learning has largely focused on self‑play (SP) approaches, where a team of agents is trained jointly to maximise joint performance.  Early work introduced variations of SP for partially observable Dec‑POMDPs, demonstrating strong in‑team scores but also revealing that optimal SP policies often rely on arbitrary handshakes or conventions that break when agents are paired with independently trained partners (e.g., other AI agents or humans).  Empirical analyses have shown that these conventions limit the generality of SP policies and motivate the need for training regimes that produce coordination‑compatible behaviours.  

The zero‑shot coordination (ZSC) setting was proposed to address the incompatibility of SP policies by requiring agents to cooperate with previously unseen partners at test time.  Several families of algorithms have been developed for ZSC.  Other‑Play (OP) exploits known symmetries of the environment to constrain policy updates so that agents preserve these symmetries during training, yielding improved cross‑play and human‑AI performance in games such as Hanabi.  Ridge Rider (RR) leverages the relationship between environmental symmetries and repeated eigenvalues of the Hessian to encourage symmetry‑preserving policies without explicit symmetry information, though its computational cost has limited scalability to large‑scale RL problems.  Life‑Long Learning (LLL) approaches maintain a pool of pre‑trained agents and adapt new policies through continual interaction, often assuming access to symmetry information.  Off‑Belief Learning (OBL) trains agents with access to a simulator to infer and exploit belief structures, achieving strong ZSC results in Hanabi but requiring simulator‑level interactions during training.  

Parallel training techniques have been employed to improve robustness and sample efficiency in multi‑agent settings.  Population‑Based Training (PBT) was introduced for hyper‑parameter optimisation and later adapted to multi‑agent contexts, where a population of agents evolves jointly to avoid local optima and to produce less exploitable strategies in competitive or cooperative games.  PBT has also been applied to self‑play in Hanabi, demonstrating gains in policy quality.  These frameworks provide a natural infrastructure for synchronously training multiple agents or hierarchical levels, enabling periodic model exchange through a central server and facilitating scalable learning across many machines.  

Cognitive‑hierarchy models from behavioural game theory, particularly k‑level reasoning (KLR), describe agents that iteratively best‑respond to lower‑level opponents.  While KLR has successfully captured human behaviour in simple games, prior attempts to scale it to high‑dimensional cooperative tasks have encountered difficulties, and it has not been widely applied to large‑scale ZSC problems.  

In this work we extend the KLR framework to large‑scale partially observable coordination tasks by training all reasoning levels synchronously, thereby eliminating the linear wall‑clock overhead of sequential level‑by‑level training and providing a regularising effect that stabilises policy learning.  Leveraging a PBT‑style architecture, each level is trained on a separate worker and model parameters are periodically synchronised through a central server.  On top of the synchronized hierarchy we co‑train a best‑response policy that emphasises the highest reasoning levels, yielding a hybrid agent that can adapt on‑the‑fly to previously unseen partners.  Our method does not require explicit knowledge of environmental symmetries, unlike OP, nor does it depend on costly Hessian‑based computations as in RR, nor on pre‑trained pools or simulator access as in LLL and OBL.  Empirically, the synchronously trained KLR hierarchy and its best‑response achieve state‑of‑the‑art zero‑shot coordination scores in Hanabi, surpass existing ZSC baselines in cross‑play and ad‑hoc teamplay, and demonstrate superior performance when paired with a human‑like proxy without using any human data during training.  These results illustrate that simple, well‑engineered extensions of classic game‑theoretic reasoning can be scaled to modern deep MARL problems and provide a practical alternative to symmetry‑dependent or computationally intensive ZSC approaches.

[ANSWER]: Prototype classifiers that rely on meta‑learning have become a cornerstone of few‑shot learning. Early work introduced the idea of constructing one or multiple class prototypes from support examples and classifying queries by measuring similarity to these prototypes [1–8]. Various extensions enrich the prototype representation or the similarity computation: attention mechanisms [1,7], relation networks [5], re‑weighting schemes that account for between‑class and within‑class interactions [4], latent‑cluster models [6], and multimodal prototype constructions [3]. Transformations of the feature space to enhance separability have also been explored [9–12]. Because of their simplicity, prototype‑based methods have been adapted to tasks beyond image classification, including semantic segmentation [13], text classification [14], and speech recognition [15].

Update‑based meta‑learning approaches take a different route by adapting model parameters at test time. Methods such as Model‑Agnostic Meta‑Learning (MAML) and its variants [16–18] learn initial parameters that can be quickly refined with a few gradient steps on the support set. Other techniques learn an explicit update rule for a base learner through episodic training [19,20]. While effective, these approaches introduce additional hyper‑parameters and require extra computation during adaptation, which can hinder rapid deployment to novel classes.

A line of research has demonstrated that fine‑tuning a linear classifier on features extracted by a standard cross‑entropy‑trained backbone can achieve performance comparable to meta‑learning methods [21,22]. Subsequent studies propose refinements for the few‑shot setting, such as calibrating the support‑set distribution [23], leveraging self‑supervised learning on query data [24], and distilling knowledge to obtain richer embeddings [25]. Investigations into the pre‑training phase revealed that employing a negative margin in the cross‑entropy loss can further improve few‑shot performance [26]. Despite these gains, fine‑tuning still requires hyper‑parameter selection and retraining whenever new classes appear, limiting its suitability for instant adaptation.

Theoretical analyses of few‑shot learning remain relatively sparse. Within the meta‑learning framework, risk bounds for the meta‑testing phase have been derived as functions of the amounts of meta‑training and meta‑testing data [27]. Information‑theoretic lower bounds on minimax convergence rates for algorithms trained on multiple source domains and evaluated on novel domains have also been established [28]. Specific to prototype classifiers, a bound was presented that links performance to the mismatch between the number of shots used during meta‑training and meta‑testing, assuming class‑conditional Gaussian distributions with shared covariance matrices [29]. This assumption restricts the applicability of the result to more realistic feature distributions.

In this work we (i) derive a novel generalization bound for prototype classifiers that does not rely on any specific distributional form or on equal class covariances, (ii) elucidate how the variance of feature‑vector norms influences the bound and consequently the classifier’s performance, and (iii) empirically validate that reducing this variance—via simple L₂ normalization or by directly minimizing the ratio of within‑class to between‑class variance—yields performance on par with fine‑tuned linear classifiers while requiring neither meta‑learning nor test‑time adaptation. Our analysis bridges the gap between prototype‑based methods, fine‑tuning approaches, and existing theoretical results, offering a principled and practical route to fast, hyper‑parameter‑free few‑shot classification.

[ANSWER]: Reference-based translation evaluation assesses quality by comparing a candidate translation with a given reference, both written in the same language. Early approaches relied on statistical methods that measured surface similarity using linguistic features such as n‑grams [1], token overlap [2], and character‑level matches [3, 4]. Although these metrics were widely applicable across languages, later studies highlighted their low correlation with human judgments and limited ability to evaluate high‑quality machine‑translation systems [5‑7]. 

The advent of large pretrained language models (PLMs) shifted attention toward model‑based approaches. These methods typically derive sentence representations for similarity calculation [8] or estimate probabilistic confidence [9, 10]. Specialized PLMs have been pretrained for evaluation tasks, exemplified by BLEURT [12], while hybrid systems that combine statistical and representation‑based features, such as YiSi‑1 [11], have demonstrated improved alignment with human assessments relative to purely statistical metrics. 

Reference‑free evaluation, often termed quality estimation, addresses scenarios where no ground‑truth reference is available by taking the source sentence and the translation candidate as inputs. This setting requires modeling cross‑lingual semantic alignment. Approaches include statistical techniques [13], model‑based methods [13, 9], and combinations of statistical and learned features [14], each aiming to predict translation quality without external references. 

A third line of work incorporates both source and reference information (Src+Ref), allowing evaluators to leverage features from both sides of the translation pair. Recent progress in cross‑lingual PLMs has been especially beneficial for this paradigm; fine‑tuning such models on human‑annotated datasets has yielded state‑of‑the‑art results in recent WMT evaluation campaigns [6, 15].

[ANSWER]: Visual Question Answering (VQA) aims to answer a question given an image as visual context [1]–[3]. Early VQA models were found to exploit language priors present in the training data, leading to shortcut learning where answers could be predicted without proper visual grounding [3]–[5]. For instance, in the VQA v1.0 dataset roughly 40 % of sports‑related questions are answered with “tennis”, illustrating a strong bias toward certain answer patterns. While such biases can boost in‑distribution (ID) performance, they severely degrade out‑of‑distribution (OOD) robustness [4]. A range of techniques has been proposed to mitigate language bias, including the use of extra annotations for accurate visual grounding [6], [7], synthetic data generation for augmentation [8]–[12], modifications to language modules [13], [14], and explicit formulation and exclusion of language priors [15]–[17]. These approaches achieve notable OOD improvements on the VQA‑CP benchmark, which reverses answer distributions between training and test splits [4], although they often incur a drop in ID accuracy, highlighting the challenge of balancing both evaluations.

Extractive Question Answering (extractive QA) requires locating answer spans within a given passage [18]. By assuming that answers are always present in the text, the task reduces to predicting start and end positions, a formulation that has driven many influential models [19]–[25]. However, directly predicting positions can introduce a positional bias, where models learn to associate answers with specific locations in the passage [26]. For example, training on data where answers consistently appear in the first sentence can cause a model to overly focus on that region. To assess robustness to such biases, a variant of the SQuAD dataset was introduced that deliberately skews answer position distributions, enabling evaluation of models’ resistance to positional shortcuts [26].

Ensemble‑based debiasing methods explicitly model and remove shortcut biases from training data [15], [16], [8], [17], [27]. These approaches capture bias through a separate branch [15] or statistical priors [16], and many are interpreted within a causality framework [17]. While they often yield strong OOD performance, they can sacrifice ID accuracy because they assume substantial divergence between training and test distributions, sometimes even reversal of answer distributions.

Knowledge distillation, originally proposed for model compression by transferring knowledge from a large teacher to a smaller student, has been extended to debiasing in natural language understanding tasks [30], [31] and long‑tail classification problems [32]–[34] [28], [29]. Related ideas of “self‑distillation” or “introspection” treat a model as its own teacher across training epochs or stages [35]–[39]. Unlike traditional distillation that relies on fixed weighting hyper‑parameters, some recent work adapts weights dynamically based on introspective signals, aiming to incorporate blended knowledge without extensive hyper‑parameter tuning. This line of research differentiates itself from standard self‑distillation by emphasizing comparative reasoning between factual and counterfactual predictions rather than merely reinforcing in‑distribution knowledge.

[ANSWER]: The literature on learning with graph-structured data can be divided into two broad families. The first family comprises semi‑supervised methods that aim to predict labels for nodes, edges, or whole graphs by exploiting both the graph topology and node features. A large body of work in this category is based on graph convolutional architectures, which extend the convolution operation to irregular domains. Early spectral approaches defined convolutions in the eigenbasis of the graph Laplacian, while later spatial methods performed aggregation directly on neighboring nodes. Variants of these graph convolutional networks have been proposed to improve expressiveness, computational efficiency, or stability, including multi‑layer designs, attention mechanisms, and deeper architectures. Diffusion‑based techniques constitute another line of semi‑supervised learning, where information is propagated through the graph using random‑walk or heat‑kernel dynamics; some of these models are trained until a fixed‑point of the diffusion process is reached. Low‑rank approximations of convolutional operators have also been introduced to reduce the computational burden while preserving predictive performance. Collectively, these methods rely on the availability of label information during training and typically focus on local neighborhoods rather than explicitly modeling interactions between all pairs of nodes.

The second family consists of unsupervised graph embedding approaches that seek task‑agnostic vector representations preserving structural properties of the graph. Early methods directly factorized the adjacency matrix or related proximity matrices, producing embeddings that approximate pairwise relationships such as dot products. Subsequent work incorporated higher‑order connectivity patterns by simulating random walks and feeding the resulting node sequences to language‑model‑style encoders; examples include approaches that treat walks as sentences and learn embeddings via skip‑gram or hierarchical softmax objectives. Extensions of these random‑walk‑based models have introduced biased or context‑specific walk strategies, hierarchical context distributions, and joint optimization of walk parameters and embedding vectors. Other unsupervised techniques exploit graph autoencoders, variational frameworks, or contrastive objectives to capture both local and global structure without relying on explicit label information. These embeddings are subsequently used for downstream tasks such as link prediction, clustering, or visualization.

Recent surveys provide comprehensive overviews of both semi‑supervised graph neural networks and unsupervised graph embedding methods, situating individual contributions within the broader evolution of graph representation learning.

[ANSWER]: Van der Wilk et al. adapted Gaussian processes to image classification by defining a prior over functions that map an entire image to a scalar output. Their construction draws a function from a GP and then sums the outputs of that function evaluated on each convolutional patch of the image. The resulting convolutional kernel is applied to all pairs of patches from two images, which makes kernel evaluation expensive and necessitates inter‑domain inducing‑point approximations to remain tractable.  

Subsequent work built upon this idea by stacking several Gaussian processes that use the same convolutional kernel, thereby forming a “deep GP”. In this formulation the hierarchical structure is created by composing multiple GP layers rather than by deepening the underlying kernel itself.  

Deep kernel learning introduced the practice of preprocessing inputs with a deep neural network before feeding them to a conventional GP kernel (e.g., RBF). The neural‑network parameters are learned by maximizing the marginal likelihood, resulting in models that combine the expressive power of state‑of‑the‑art networks with GP uncertainty quantification. Because these approaches inherit the large parameter count of modern deep nets (often millions of weights), they tend to achieve performance comparable to the underlying network but at the cost of considerably more parameters than purely GP‑based kernels.  

Another line of research showed that a convolutional neural network can exhibit Gaussian‑process‑like behavior when the limit is taken with respect to filter size rather than the number of filters. Since real‑world images have finite spatial dimensions, taking the infinite‑filter‑size limit does not directly yield a practical model for typical image data.  

A series of papers analyzed the mean‑field dynamics of deep fully‑connected and convolutional networks to identify random initializations that avoid vanishing or exploding activations. These analyses focus on the variance of activations for a single training example, whereas constructing a Gaussian‑process kernel requires computing covariances between the outputs for different inputs, a more demanding statistical quantity.  

In this work we establish that a convolutional neural network (including residual architectures) with an infinite number of filters per layer defines an exact Gaussian‑process prior. By deriving the corresponding kernel directly from the infinite‑filter limit, we obtain a kernel that depends only on the original CNN hyper‑parameters and can be evaluated efficiently: the variance at every spatial location can be computed simultaneously as a convolution, and the contribution of each location decorrelates due to independent downstream weights, eliminating the need to track inter‑patch covariances. Consequently, evaluating the kernel for a pair of images incurs a cost comparable to a single forward pass through the original CNN with one filter per layer. Leveraging the translation‑invariant structure of the kernel, we achieve state‑of‑the‑art performance among non‑parametric GP models, attaining a 0.84 % error rate on MNIST without gradient‑based training or data augmentation. This positions the proposed approach as a bridge between the expressive, scalable architecture of modern CNNs and the exact Bayesian inference capabilities of Gaussian processes, addressing the computational and over‑parameterisation limitations of prior convolutional GP and deep‑kernel methods.

Recognizing that deterministic hidden representations may limit expressive power, a line of work introduced stochastic latent variables into recurrent architectures. The development of variational auto‑encoding techniques enabled broader adoption of stochastic recurrent models, leading to variants such as temporal sigmoid belief networks, deep Kalman filters, deep Markov models, and Kalman variational auto‑encoders. Despite successes in certain domains, the benefit of latent stochasticity does not uniformly translate across data modalities. In language modeling, some stochastic recurrent models have been observed to underperform deterministic baselines. Similarly, for image density estimation, fully deterministic auto‑regressive models like PixelCNN consistently surpass latent‑variable generative approaches. This mixed evidence has motivated investigations into the conditions under which stochastic latent variables provide practical advantages.  

Several studies have highlighted methodological factors that can affect comparative evaluations. Notably, the use of fully factorized output distributions restricts a model’s ability to capture intra‑step correlations, potentially biasing results in favor of stochastic models that can implicitly exploit such dependencies. Conversely, deterministic recurrent baselines constrained by the same factorization are prevented from modeling these correlations explicitly, leading to an uneven playing field.

Techniques that rely on post‑training fine‑tuning of the quantized weights have been shown to mitigate accuracy degradation, yet they are generally unsuitable for training networks from scratch and typically require several bits (e.g., 5‑bit weight precision) to retain performance comparable to full‑precision baselines.

A parallel line of research has targeted the quantization of activations, either jointly with weights or in isolation. Methods such as XNOR‑Net, DoReFa‑Net, and related binary‑network designs quantize both weights and activations to 1 bit, enabling extreme compression and speed‑up but often at the cost of large accuracy penalties (e.g., 8–12 % top‑1 loss on ImageNet). Some approaches alleviate this loss by employing layer‑wise reordering, specialized training tricks, or mixed‑precision schemes, yet they still rely on complex quantization pipelines and frequently demand extensive fine‑tuning to approach baseline performance. Recent work on low‑precision activations using 5‑bit uniform or logarithmic quantization has reported accuracy within 1 % of full precision, and further fine‑tuning can narrow the gap to 0.6 %, but these methods typically leave a subset of layers in higher precision and involve non‑trivial quantization schedules.

Beyond algorithmic considerations, hardware efficiency has emerged as a critical factor for low‑precision designs. Quantization schemes that produce operand values not aligned to powers of two can lead to irregular memory accesses and reduced utilization of DRAM or cache bandwidth, complicating the translation of theoretical gains into practical speed‑ups. Consequently, several studies have emphasized hardware‑friendly quantization, advocating for simple, uniform bit‑width reductions that preserve alignment and enable straightforward implementation on GPUs, FPGAs, and ASICs. Compared with prior binary and low‑precision methods, we achieve state‑of‑the‑art results for wide binarized ResNet‑34 and AlexNet variants while incurring lower overall compute cost. The quantization strategy is deliberately simple and uniform, ensuring alignment with hardware memory boundaries and facilitating efficient implementation across diverse platforms. Sani et al. formalized this setting and provided the first regret analysis for mean‑variance bandits.  Subsequent studies by Vakili and Zhao refined the analysis under alternative risk metrics and completed the regret bounds for the same objective.  A Thompson‑sampling approach for mean‑variance bandits was later proposed by Zhu and Tan.  Beyond variance, several lines of research have examined other risk measures.  Value‑at‑Risk (VaR) was investigated in one stream, while Conditional Value‑at‑Risk (CVaR) received attention in two separate works.  More generally, Cassel et al. introduced the empirical‑distribution performance measure (EDPM), a flexible risk functional, and presented an algorithmic framework for optimizing EDPM in bandit problems.  All of these contributions assume a discrete set of actions and independence across arms, and therefore do not address settings where decisions involve continuous mixtures of correlated options.  

A distinct body of literature has studied bandit problems in which the learner has access to covariance information among arms.  In the stochastic setting, Degenne and Perchet considered combinatorial semi‑bandits with correlated rewards, assuming a known upper bound on the covariance matrix and designing algorithms that exploit this prior knowledge.  Perrault and colleagues extended this line of work by removing the explicit covariance bound and operating under sub‑exponential reward distributions, achieving tight asymptotic regret guarantees for combinatorial semi‑bandits.  In the adversarial domain, Warmuth and Kuzmin examined online variance minimization, where at each round the learner selects a weight vector and observes a full covariance matrix; they developed exponentiated‑gradient‑type algorithms for this problem.  These studies differ from one another in several respects: the stochastic works focus on discrete combinatorial action spaces and typically aim solely at maximizing expected reward, while the adversarial works assume direct observation of covariance and do not consider stochastic reward generation.  Moreover, none of these papers address continuous decision spaces, risk‑aware objectives that combine reward and covariance, or feedback regimes beyond the semi‑bandit case.  

In contrast, the present work introduces a continuous‑mean‑covariance bandit framework that simultaneously captures reward and covariance‑based risk for actions represented by arbitrary weight vectors over a set of correlated base arms.  It extends the risk‑aware literature by moving beyond discrete, independent arm models to a continuous decision space where correlation directly influences risk.  It also builds on the covariance‑aware line of research by eliminating the need for prior covariance bounds, handling stochastic environments where the covariance must be estimated from indirect feedback, and incorporating three feedback settings—full‑information, semi‑bandit, and full‑bandit—thereby broadening the applicability of covariance‑aware bandits.  By deriving optimal regret bounds (up to logarithmic factors) for each feedback regime and establishing matching lower bounds, the contribution clarifies how arbitrary covariance structures affect learning performance, filling a gap left by prior combinatorial and adversarial studies.

[ANSWER]: Marginal‑likelihood approximations have long been a cornerstone of Gaussian‑process (GP) modeling. Early work on sparse GP approximations relied on selecting subsets of the training data to reduce the cubic cost of exact inference, a strategy formalized in the subset‑of‑data (SoD) and subset‑of‑regressors frameworks. The introduction of pseudo‑inputs (or inducing points) provided a more flexible alternative, allowing the inducing locations to be placed anywhere in the input space and leading to variational formulations that yield an evidence lower bound (ELBO) on the marginal likelihood. Stochastic approximations to the ELBO were subsequently proposed, enabling mini‑batch training and scaling to larger datasets. These stochastic ELBO methods can be viewed as Bayesian counterparts to earlier deterministic sparse approximations, preserving the probabilistic treatment while improving scalability.

Active‑set methods, which fix the inducing variables to be a subset of the training inputs, were investigated empirically and shown to produce stable approximations even when the active set comprised only a small fraction of the data. However, random selection of active points was observed to induce non‑smooth fluctuations in the objective, complicating convergence under exact gradient ascent. This instability motivated the development of pseudo‑input approaches, where the inducing variables are optimized continuously rather than chosen discretely, resulting in smoother optimization dynamics. Recent stochastic optimization techniques have revisited active‑set ideas, proposing to average over active‑set configurations rather than optimize a single deterministic subset, thereby mitigating the fluctuations associated with random selection.

The relationship between cross‑validation (CV) and GP marginal‑likelihood estimation has been explored as an alternative avenue for model selection. Initial studies highlighted CV as a practical tool for assessing predictive performance, while later theoretical work established an equivalence between exhaustive CV and the log‑marginal likelihood, offering a novel perspective on Bayesian model evidence. Building on this equivalence, recent research has integrated CV‑based objectives into GP training pipelines. In the context of GP latent‑variable models, back‑constraints have been introduced to regularize the latent space when using inducing points, employing doubly stochastic variational inference to handle the resulting intractabilities. Parallel advances in supervised GP settings have leveraged amortization networks to drastically reduce the number of required inducing points, further enhancing scalability.

In this work we introduce a stochastic active‑set (SAS) framework that unifies these strands of prior research. By exploiting the established link between exhaustive cross‑validation and the log‑marginal likelihood, we derive a stochastic estimator of the marginal likelihood that can be evaluated efficiently using randomly sampled active sets. Unlike traditional active‑set methods, SAS does not seek a single optimal subset; instead, it averages over many subsets, eliminating the non‑smooth fluctuations observed with random selection and obviating the need for costly combinatorial optimization. This stochastic estimation also sidesteps the optimization challenges associated with pseudo‑inputs, while retaining the computational benefits of fixed active points. Moreover, SAS integrates naturally with back‑constraint ideas, providing a principled way to encourage structure in the latent space without additional variational parameters. Empirically, the SAS‑GP decoder attains superior latent representations, scales to substantially larger datasets, and outperforms both variational autoencoders and competing GP‑based decoders in terms of robustness, computational efficiency, and representation quality.

[ANSWER]: Metric learning seeks a distance function that brings semantically similar examples together while pushing dissimilar ones apart. In deep metric learning, an explicit non‑linear mapping from raw inputs to a low‑dimensional embedding space is learned, after which Euclidean distance exhibits the desired behavior. Although unsupervised formulations exist, the majority of work follows a supervised paradigm in which positive pairs share a class label and negative pairs belong to different classes. Loss functions for deep metric learning can be categorized as pair‑based or proxy‑based. Pair‑based losses operate on direct relationships between data points and have been defined over pairs, triplets, quadruplets, or higher‑order tuples. These losses capture fine‑grained data‑to‑data relations but are sensitive to label noise and outliers, and they often contain terms that become inactive once constraints are satisfied, yielding zero gradients. Consequently, hard‑example mining strategies such as semi‑hard or distance‑weighted sampling are commonly employed to provide informative training signals. Proxy‑based losses introduce learnable class proxies in the embedding space, replacing data‑to‑data interactions with data‑to‑proxy relations. By summarizing global class structure, proxy‑based approaches reduce computational overhead, generate more consistently non‑zero gradients, and typically require less aggressive mining, leading to faster convergence.

Input mixup linearly interpolates between two or more examples in the input space to augment data. Numerous extensions exploit the structure of specific domains, particularly images, by performing non‑linear interpolations or applying mixup to transformed representations. Manifold mixup extends the idea to intermediate feature representations, sometimes coupled with decoding back to the input space. In both input‑ and feature‑level mixup, target labels are interpolated linearly, and most studies have focused on cross‑entropy loss for classification tasks. The application of mixup to pairwise loss functions, such as those used in metric learning, has received considerably less attention.

Within deep metric learning, several works have explored interpolation strategies compatible with pairwise objectives. Embedding expansion and symmetrical synthesis interpolate pairs of embeddings deterministically within the same class, making them applicable to pair‑based losses. Proxy synthesis, on the other hand, interpolates between class proxies and can be used with proxy‑based losses; however, it does not modify labels, which can lead to the inadvertent creation of false negatives when the interpolation factor approaches the extremes. In contrastive representation learning, MoCHi interpolates anchor embeddings with negative samples without altering labels and employs a threshold to mitigate false negatives. A similar thresholding concept appears in OptTransMix, which adjusts interpolation to avoid label ambiguity. The i‑mix approach interpolates anchor embeddings along with their virtual class labels in a linear fashion; it maintains a single positive per anchor while keeping all negatives clean, thereby limiting its ability to exploit interpolation for relative weighting of positives and negatives. These methods collectively illustrate a growing interest in leveraging interpolation for metric‑learning objectives, while highlighting challenges related to label handling and the balance between positive and negative contributions.

[ANSWER]: The data‑programming paradigm introduced a way to label data programmatically by combining multiple noisy labeling functions (LFs) and treating the true label as a latent variable in a generative probabilistic graphical model (PGM).  Early work focused on learning the parameters of this generative model, and a series of methods have been proposed to mitigate the computational burden of inference, including approximate sampling, variational approximations, and matrix‑based estimators.  A recurring limitation of many of these approaches is their reliance on strong independence assumptions among the LFs; popular libraries and several research studies adopt a conditionally independent model, which can lead to substantial performance degradation when the true dependencies and correlations among the sources are misspecified.  To address this, a line of work has explored learning the intra‑LF dependency structure, either by augmenting the PGM with latent dependency variables or by employing structure‑learning techniques that infer correlation patterns from the unlabeled data.  Separately, co‑training methods share the spirit of leveraging multiple views of the data but typically assume the availability of some labeled examples; recent extensions combine a small labeled set with multiple weak supervision sources, often relying on large pre‑trained language models to achieve strong results, though their applicability to non‑text domains or settings without such models remains uncertain.  

Aggregating noisy labels has also been extensively studied in the crowdsourcing literature, where the goal is to infer the unknown ground‑truth label while modeling worker reliability.  Classical approaches employ expectation‑maximization (EM) or related iterative algorithms to jointly estimate worker accuracies and the latent label, usually under the assumption that worker errors are independent and randomly distributed across instances.  Unlike weak‑supervision settings, crowdsourcing frameworks often consider dynamic task assignment and may optimize which workers label which items.  A number of end‑to‑end methods have been introduced for crowdsourced annotation, particularly for image labeling tasks, that integrate EM‑like worker models directly into the training of discriminative predictors.  These methods typically tailor their assumptions to the crowdsourcing scenario—such as fixed numbers of workers and specific error models—and therefore may not generalize to broader weak‑supervision contexts where the sources are heterogeneous rules, heuristics, or distant‑supervision signals.  

In contrast to the prior approaches described above, the present work proposes a fully end‑to‑end framework for learning downstream models directly from multiple weak‑supervision sources without any labeled data.  By re‑parameterizing the posterior distributions of traditional PGM‑based label models with a neural encoder that produces attention scores for each source, the method jointly optimizes the encoder and the downstream predictor using a shared loss that treats the other component’s predictions as constant targets.  This design eliminates the need for separate generative‑model learning, avoids costly sampling or matrix inversions, and does not rely on conditional independence or correctly specified dependency structures among the LFs.  The approach is also agnostic to the nature of the weak sources, handling both binary heuristics and probabilistic signals, and it remains robust when the sources are highly correlated or adversarial.  Empirical evaluations demonstrate consistent improvements over state‑of‑the‑art latent‑label modeling techniques across several benchmark datasets, including a crowdsourcing task where the method outperforms specialized EM‑based baselines.  An open‑source implementation compatible with arbitrary PyTorch models is released to facilitate adoption in diverse application domains.

[ANSWER]: Transfer learning aims to improve performance on a target task by leveraging knowledge from source domains. Early approaches reused features extracted by a pretrained model, while later studies demonstrated that fine‑tuning the entire network yields higher transfer performance. Empirical investigations have examined fine‑tuning across diverse downstream scenarios, including image classification, few‑shot learning, medical imaging, and object detection. More recent work has identified limitations of vanilla fine‑tuning and proposed enhancements such as parameter or feature regularization, auxiliary tasks that capture category relationships or intrinsic structures, and analyses of layer‑wise transferability. When multiple pretrained models are available, several lines of research have explored how to exploit them. One family estimates the transferability of each model and selects the most suitable one for a given target task, but accurate measurement of model transferability remains challenging and the approach discards the complementary knowledge present in other models. Another family aggregates information across models by concatenating features or merging parameters. However, these aggregation methods typically assume a model zoo in which all models share a common architecture or layer‑wise correspondence, an assumption that does not hold for heterogeneous collections of pretrained networks. This limitation motivates the study of more general settings where arbitrary pretrained models can be jointly leveraged without architectural constraints.

Conditional computation investigates mechanisms that activate only a subset of network components for each input example. Mixture‑of‑experts (MoE) architectures employ data‑dependent gating networks to select expert pathways, and sparsely‑gated MoE layers enable the training of extremely large models by activating a small number of experts per example. These works generally construct experts from homogeneous networks initialized randomly, rather than from a heterogeneous set of pretrained models that encode diverse knowledge.

In this work we address the general problem of transferring knowledge from a heterogeneous model hub. We introduce a Hub‑Pathway framework that generates data‑dependent pathway weights to (i) select which pretrained models are activated for each input, (ii) aggregate the predictions of the activated models, and (iii) fine‑tune the selected models on the data that trigger them. To promote diverse exploration of pathway configurations we employ a noisy pathway generator together with an exploration loss, while the task‑specific loss drives exploitation of the most beneficial pathways. By operating without any assumptions on model architecture, dataset, or training paradigm, our approach overcomes the limitations of single‑model fine‑tuning, model‑level selection, and existing aggregation techniques, and extends conditional computation concepts to the setting of heterogeneous pretrained experts. Experiments on vision and reinforcement‑learning benchmarks demonstrate that the proposed method achieves state‑of‑the‑art performance for model‑hub transfer learning.

In contrast, our Functional Ensemble Distillation (FED) explicitly models the full predictive distribution, preserving both mean and covariance structure, thereby enabling downstream applications that depend on inter‑prediction correlations.

[ANSWER]: Imbalanced classification has long been recognized as a pervasive challenge in real‑world applications, prompting extensive research on techniques that mitigate the adverse effects of skewed class distributions. Early work primarily addressed the quantity‑imbalance problem, where the number of training examples differs across classes, leading to models that favor majority categories. To rebalance datasets, researchers have explored data‑selection strategies such as active learning, which queries informative samples, and various resampling schemes—including oversampling of minority instances and undersampling of majority ones—to construct more balanced training sets. Complementary model‑training approaches have focused on re‑weighting loss contributions of samples according to class frequencies, thereby encouraging the learner to pay greater attention to under‑represented classes.

Beyond generic resampling and re‑weighting, a line of research has investigated instance‑level filtering methods that aim to reduce the negative influence of samples lying near decision boundaries. Techniques such as Tomek links, NearMiss, and One‑Sided Selection identify and remove borderline or noisy instances based on feature‑space similarity measures. While effective for vector‑based data, these methods rely on explicit feature distances, which can be unreliable in graph settings where the relational structure provides richer contextual information and labeled nodes are often scarce.

Graph‑structured data appear in diverse domains—including social networks, financial markets, e‑commerce, healthcare, and transportation—yet they inherit the same quantity‑imbalance difficulties observed in other modalities. To address this, several graph‑specific strategies have been proposed. DR‑GCN introduces class‑conditioned adversarial training together with constraints on the latent distribution of unlabeled nodes. RA‑GCN learns class‑wise sample weights within an adversarial framework, while AdaGCN applies boosting principles to emphasize minority‑class nodes during training. A complementary strand of work has sought to exploit the topology of graphs to infer node importance or proximity to decision boundaries. Approaches that select anchor nodes and compute distances or diffusion scores aim to locate absolute positions of all nodes relative to these anchors, thereby informing sampling or weighting decisions. In light of these gaps, the present study introduces the notion of topology‑imbalance in node representation learning, emphasizing how asymmetric placement of labeled nodes can shift decision boundaries independently of class frequencies. By analyzing the influence‑conflict phenomenon under label propagation, we propose a conflict‑detection metric that quantifies each labeled node’s relative position to class boundaries without requiring external anchors. Building on this metric, we develop a model‑agnostic re‑weighting framework that adaptively adjusts training contributions of individual nodes based on their structural roles, thereby addressing both quantity‑ and topology‑imbalance simultaneously. Comprehensive experiments across multiple imbalance scenarios, datasets, and graph neural network architectures demonstrate the effectiveness and generalizability of the proposed method, while also revealing varying sensitivities of GNN designs to topology‑imbalance—a perspective that offers new criteria for evaluating and selecting graph learning models.

[ANSWER]: Robust control focuses on designing feedback controllers that guarantee performance in the presence of modeling uncertainties and external disturbances. Classical approaches formulate robustness criteria as linear matrix inequalities (LMIs), which can be solved efficiently with interior‑point or gradient‑based algorithms for problems of moderate size. These techniques often rely on linear or low‑order controllers to obtain provable stability, which can limit average‑case performance when richer nonlinear policies might be beneficial.  

Reinforcement learning (RL), and in particular deep RL, removes the restriction to simple controller structures by learning policies represented by neural networks through direct interaction with an environment. This paradigm has achieved notable success on a wide range of complex control tasks, as documented in several recent benchmarks and surveys. Because deep RL optimizes expected return without explicit safety constraints, most applications have been confined to simulated settings or highly controlled real‑world domains where failures are tolerable.  

To mitigate the safety and stability shortcomings of RL, a number of research directions have emerged. One line of work integrates control‑theoretic concepts, especially robust control, with the expressive power of neural‑network policies. Examples include methods that jointly learn Lyapunov functions and control policies to enforce stochastic stability, and approaches that cast continuous‑time control synthesis as min‑max differential games in which the controller and disturbance play opposing roles. These hybrid strategies aim to retain robustness guarantees while exploiting nonlinear policy representations.  

Another strand of research is safe RL, which seeks to enforce safety during learning and deployment. Many safe‑RL algorithms constrain exploration to regions of the state space that satisfy safety criteria, often assuming smooth dynamics that can be modeled with Gaussian processes or that satisfy Lipschitz continuity. Such assumptions enable probabilistic safety certificates but can be restrictive when dynamics exhibit sharp discontinuities.  

A third category leverages constrained Markov decision processes (C‑MDPs), where the objective is to maximize a discounted reward while keeping a separate discounted cost below a prescribed threshold. C‑MDPs do not require prior knowledge of the cost functions, yet they typically guarantee constraint satisfaction only at test time and may produce stochastic optimal policies whose constraints hold for only a subset of states.  

Parallel to these developments, differentiable optimization layers have become a popular tool for embedding optimization problems within neural networks. Recent work has introduced layers that solve quadratic programs, SAT instances, submodular optimization problems, cone programs, and other convex formulations in a way that permits gradient‑based learning. By embedding such layers, networks can be endowed with inductive biases that respect hard constraints of the underlying domain, enabling the projection of network outputs onto feasible sets defined by stability or safety requirements.

This strategy has been applied to point‑cloud generation, bounding‑box prediction, and graph construction. Because the decoder treats the output as a sequence, it suffers from the “responsibility problem”: the loss landscape becomes discontinuous with respect to permutations of the target set, leading to unstable training. Some point‑cloud methods mitigate this issue by imposing domain‑specific assumptions, such as treating points as independent samples or arranging them on a regular grid, but these constraints limit applicability to more general set‑structured data.

A second line of work replaces the MLP with a recurrent neural network (RNN) decoder that generates set elements sequentially. When a canonical ordering can be defined—often by exploiting domain knowledge such as a breadth‑first traversal of a graph—this approach sidesteps the permutation issue. However, the requirement of a predefined order restricts the method to settings where such an ordering is natural or easy to compute, and it does not fully address the underlying set‑symmetry.

Iterative optimization‑based models constitute a closely related family. Mordatch introduced a framework that minimizes an energy function inside each forward pass and differentiates through the optimization loop. Their experiments demonstrated the ability to modify small 2‑D point sets, but the scalability of this approach to larger, more complex tasks such as object detection remains uncertain. The energy‑based formulation differs from direct set‑distance minimization, making it less transparent how the predicted set aligns with the target.

Auto‑encoding architectures that pool a set into a single feature vector and share this representation with a decoder have also been explored. By designing a permutation‑equivariant decoder, these models avoid the responsibility problem within an auto‑encoder setting. However, because inference requires an encoder to supply the pooled representation, they are unsuitable for direct set prediction where only a feature vector is available at test time. Related work on set‑structured latent spaces for images learns latent sets of variables that describe object compositions under strong task‑specific assumptions, offering insights for representation learning but not providing a general supervised prediction mechanism.

Nested optimization, where the outer loop differentiates through the inner loop, has been studied in earlier works on structured output prediction. Differentiating through a decoder rather than an encoder has been used to learn representations, while differentiating through an encoder has been employed to obtain structured predictions, illustrating the broader relevance of nested optimization to set‑valued outputs.

Finally, it is useful to distinguish vector‑to‑set mappings from set‑to‑set transformations. Methods such as Deep Sets and self‑attention focus on processing an input set to produce another set, often preserving the ordering induced by the input. Permutation‑matrix prediction techniques learn to reorder an input set into a list, but they still assume a set input. Tasks that require generating a set directly from a feature vector—such as object detection without an explicit set input—cannot be solved by set‑to‑set approaches alone and demand dedicated vector‑to‑set models.

[ANSWER]: Exhaustive computation of all pair‑wise distances between a query and a database quickly becomes prohibitive on most platforms, which has motivated a large body of work on approximate nearest‑neighbor (ANN) search.  The quality of ANN methods is typically quantified by recall, i.e., the fraction of true nearest neighbours that are retrieved by the algorithm.  Early surveys [1, 2] established recall as the standard metric for comparing speed‑recall trade‑offs across different techniques.

A prominent family of ANN methods reduces the computational burden by operating in a lossy‑compressed domain.  These approaches follow a two‑stage pipeline: first they search a compact representation of the data (such as trees, graphs, or hash tables) to generate a candidate set, and then they compute exact distances between the query and the candidates to obtain the final top‑k results.  Because only a subset of points undergoes full distance evaluation, the overall cost is lowered while preserving high recall.

Various concrete instantiations of the compressed‑domain pipeline have been proposed.  Locality‑sensitive hashing (LSH) uses hash functions to map nearby points to the same buckets, performing a quick lookup followed by exact scoring [3, 4].  Tree‑based methods recursively partition the space and apply the two‑stage process at each node [5, 6].  Graph‑based techniques iteratively explore a proximity graph, alternating between candidate selection and distance computation until a stopping criterion is met [7].  Inverted file (IVF) systems first cluster the data with k‑means, then restrict search to the posting lists of the nearest centroids, again followed by exact rescoring [8–11].

Despite their success, compressed‑domain approaches face two fundamental challenges.  First, fractional search typically yields poor cache reuse because the candidate sets for different queries overlap only minimally, leading to suboptimal memory bandwidth utilization on modern hardware.  Second, tuning the speed‑recall balance is highly data‑dependent; the distance contrast between neighbors diminishes as dimensionality grows—a phenomenon documented in [12] as the “curse of high dimensionality.”  Moreover, theoretical work [13, 14] has shown that, under the Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis, sub‑linear‑time NN search with high recall is impossible for Euclidean, Manhattan, or Hamming distances, underscoring intrinsic limits of pruning‑based strategies.

The rise of specialized accelerators for machine‑learning workloads has opened new avenues for NN search.  Platforms such as Google’s TPU V3 and V4, and NVIDIA’s GPUs (V100, A100), provide orders of magnitude higher floating‑point throughput than conventional CPUs, especially for dense matrix‑multiplication kernels.  These devices expose dedicated compute units—tensor cores in NVIDIA GPUs [15] and systolic arrays in TPUs [16, 17]—that deliver markedly higher operation throughput for matrix‑oriented workloads compared with scalar or element‑wise instructions.  Accurately modeling the differing throughputs of these instruction classes is therefore essential for performance‑aware algorithm design.

Even with abundant FLOP/s, devising efficient selection primitives (e.g., top‑k or arg‑min) on accelerators remains an active research topic.  Recent studies [18–21] investigate parallel reduction, hierarchical heap, and warp‑level primitives to extract the smallest distances without incurring excessive synchronization or memory traffic.  As accelerator peak performance increases, the relative cost of selection can dominate the overall runtime, making it crucial to minimize selection overhead while preserving high recall.

Building on these observations, the present work extends the roofline performance model to capture instruction‑level throughput differences on TPUs and GPUs, and leverages this model to design an ANN algorithm that eschews any pruning of the search space.  By computing all distances directly, the method avoids the cache‑reuse and dimensionality‑related limitations of compressed‑domain approaches and remains immune to the theoretical lower bounds on sub‑linear search.  The algorithm incorporates a novel, accelerator‑aware top‑k selection scheme that aligns with the modeled operation rates, thereby reducing selection overhead.  Empirical evaluation on TPU V3/V4 demonstrates peak‑theoretic performance and a recall‑in‑expectation guarantee, while achieving faster speed‑recall trade‑offs than the state‑of‑the‑art GPU‑based ANN methods.  The implementation is released as open‑source in JAX and TensorFlow, enabling reproducible research and practical deployment on modern accelerator hardware.

Causal‑fairness approaches similarly aim to purge encoders of spurious correlations by enforcing invariance to protected groups. While effective in many settings, these strategies presuppose abundant, instance‑level sensitive‑attribute information and assume that the encoder can be fully purified of fairness‑relevant signals—assumptions that are often unrealistic in practice. In contrast, our work departs from the encoder‑centric paradigm by demonstrating that fairness can be achieved by exclusively debiasing the task‑specific classification head, thereby sidestepping the need for costly annotations and the difficulty of completely erasing bias from deep representations.

A complementary strand of literature investigates the propensity of deep networks to rely on spurious correlations or shortcuts when trained on standard objectives. Empirical studies across vision and language tasks have shown that such shortcut learning harms generalization, robustness, and can amplify algorithmic discrimination. These findings motivate our central hypothesis: the classification head, rather than the encoder, is the primary conduit through which biased representations are linked to target labels. By neutralizing representations that share the same ground‑truth label but differ in protected attributes, our RNF framework directly attacks this conduit, reducing reliance on shortcuts without altering the underlying encoder.

The most closely related works also target the classification head, typically by leveraging true sensitive‑attribute annotations to regularize its parameters. These methods, however, inherit the annotation bottleneck of the broader bias‑mitigation literature and consequently have limited applicability in low‑resource environments. Our approach eliminates this dependency by generating proxy sensitive labels with a bias‑amplified teacher model, enabling representation neutralization without any external demographic information. Empirically, RNF matches or surpasses these head‑only baselines while remaining complementary to encoder‑level debiasing techniques, which can be combined with our head‑focused training for further fairness gains.

[ANSWER]: Analyzing the expressive power of coupling‑based normalizing flows has been an active research topic. A foundational result shows that any coupling‑based flow capable of approximating an arbitrary invertible function can learn any probability density in the weak sense [1]. This universality has been established for affine coupling flows [2, 3, 4], Flow++ [5], neural autoregressive flows [6] and SOS polynomial flows [7]. Similar universality statements for affine coupling flows in Wasserstein distance have also been proved [8]. These works, however, rely on couplings becoming increasingly ill‑conditioned as the approximation error diminishes, a phenomenon that is rarely observed in practice where learned functions tend to remain smooth. Moreover, the analyses are restricted to finite‑dimensional subspaces of the data domain and employ convergence criteria (weak convergence or Wasserstein distance) that do not guarantee convergence under the Kullback‑Leibler (KL) divergence, the loss actually optimized in maximum‑likelihood training. Indeed, an arbitrarily small distance in those metrics can correspond to an infinite KL divergence.

The relationship between conditioning of the coupling layers and the class of distributions that can be modeled has been examined in several studies. It has been shown that well‑conditioned affine couplings are sufficient to approximate log‑concave distributions that have been padded with additional dimensions, again with guarantees expressed in Wasserstein distance [9]. In contrast, Lipschitz‑constrained flows cannot capture arbitrary tail behaviours; this limitation can be mitigated by suitably adapting the latent distribution [10].

Beyond affine couplings, other families of normalizing flows have been investigated with respect to their convergence properties. SOS polynomial flows have been proven to converge in total variation to arbitrary probability densities [11], a mode of convergence that likewise does not imply KL convergence. Zero‑padded affine coupling flows have been shown to converge weakly [12], and Neural Ordinary Differential Equation (Neural ODE) based flows enjoy weak convergence guarantees as well [13, 14].

A more recent line of work focuses on the linear representational capacity of coupling blocks. It has been demonstrated that a stack of 48 linear affine coupling blocks can realize any invertible linear transformation [8], which in turn enables the exact mapping of any Gaussian distribution to the standard normal. This observation can be interpreted through the lens of KL divergence: the overall loss decomposes into the divergence to the nearest Gaussian (capturing non‑Gaussianity) and the divergence from that Gaussian to the standard normal (capturing non‑standardness). Consequently, the latter term can be controlled directly, suggesting that far fewer layers may be needed for accurate approximation than the worst‑case bounds implied by the universal representation result.

In this work we address the gap between existing universality results and the practical convergence criterion employed during training. By working directly with the KL divergence, we decompose the loss into its non‑Gaussianity and non‑standardness components and provide explicit bounds on the reduction of the non‑standardness term after a single coupling block, averaged over random orthonormal transformations. Leveraging these bounds, we prove that sequences of coupling blocks whiten the data covariance and that this whitening proceeds with a linear convergence rate in depth. Our analysis applies to all major coupling‑based architectures—including NICE, RealNVP, GLOW, Flow++, nonlinear‑squared flows, spline‑based flows, neural autoregressive flows, and monotonic neural networks—thereby offering a unified theoretical justification for their empirical success. Complementary numerical experiments confirm the theoretical predictions and highlight directions for further improvement.

Approaches that handle perfect pinyin have evolved from statistical language models [1] and statistical machine translation [2] to neural architectures. Notable neural systems include Moon IME, which combines an attention‑based network with an information‑retrieval module [3], an LSTM‑based encoder‑decoder enhanced by online vocabulary adaptation [4], and a variant that concatenates contextual words with abbreviated pinyin as input to an LSTM encoder‑decoder [5].  

A separate line of work has addressed the presence of typing errors in pinyin entry. One study introduced a typing model that jointly performs spelling correction within a sentence‑based pinyin input framework [1], while another proposed a joint graph model that simultaneously optimizes pinyin conversion and typo correction [6]. These methods aim to improve robustness against user mistakes, an aspect that remains less explored in the broader pinyin input literature.  

Recent advances in pretrained language models have incorporated pinyin information to enrich character representations. A general‑purpose Chinese BERT was extended with dedicated embedding layers for pinyin and glyph features [7]. Task‑specific BERT variants for grammatical error correction—where homophonic confusion is a major error source—have added pinyin embeddings to predict characters among similarly pronounced candidates [8]. To support comprehensive evaluation, we construct a new dataset of 270 K instances drawn from 15 news domains, covering diverse context lengths and pinyin types. Experiments show that both proposed strategies consistently improve abbreviated‑pinyin performance across all domains, and that longer character contexts further boost GPT‑based models. Our analysis confirms the individual contributions of context enrichment and pinyin‑constrained training, establishing a solid baseline for future research on GPT‑driven, error‑tolerant pinyin input systems.

[ANSWER]: Transfer‑learning research has traditionally focused on leveraging a single pre‑trained source model. Early approaches reused frozen features extracted from that model, and later studies demonstrated that fine‑tuning the entire network yields superior performance across a range of downstream tasks such as image classification, few‑shot learning, medical imaging, and object detection. Recent work has refined vanilla fine‑tuning by regularizing parameters or features, introducing auxiliary tasks to capture category relationships, or analysing layer‑wise transferability. Although these methods achieve strong results for a single source, they do not address how to exploit the abundant, heterogeneous knowledge that resides in a collection of pre‑trained models. Our Hub‑Pathway framework extends the fine‑tuning paradigm to a model hub, enabling data‑dependent activation of multiple pre‑trained models and joint optimization of pathway selection and aggregation, thereby filling the gap left by single‑model transfer techniques.

When multiple pre‑trained models are available, prior methods have typically estimated a scalar transferability score for each model and selected the single most promising candidate. Such model‑level selection can be unreliable because transferability is difficult to measure and it discards the complementary information present in the remaining models. Other approaches have attempted to fuse all models by aggregating their features or parameters, but they assume a homogeneous “model zoo” in which every model shares the same architecture and layer alignment—an assumption that does not hold for realistic model hubs composed of diverse architectures, training datasets, and learning paradigms. By contrast, our work removes these constraints: we treat the hub as an unrestricted set of heterogeneous models, employ a data‑driven gating mechanism to route each input to the most relevant subset of models, and aggregate their predictions without requiring any architectural correspondence. This positions our Hub‑Pathway framework as the most general solution for multi‑model transfer learning to date.

The design of our pathway mechanism is also related to the literature on conditional computation, where only a subset of network components is activated per example. Existing mixture‑of‑experts and sparsely‑gated expert layers rely on homogeneous expert networks that are randomly initialized and trained jointly from scratch. In contrast, our approach activates pre‑trained experts that already encode rich, domain‑specific knowledge, and it learns data‑dependent pathway weights through a noisy generator and an exploration loss that encourages the discovery of diverse and effective routing configurations. Moreover, we fine‑tune each activated model on the specific data that triggers it, ensuring that the transferred knowledge is fully exploited. Thus, while sharing the spirit of conditional computation, our Hub‑Pathway method uniquely combines heterogeneous pre‑trained experts, exploratory gating, and targeted fine‑tuning to achieve state‑of‑the‑art performance in model‑hub transfer learning.

[ANSWER]: Most existing continual‑learning approaches assume a class‑incremental setting in which all training samples for each new class are fully labeled and presented together in a single increment.  Methods that mitigate catastrophic forgetting by storing a subset of past examples and replaying them during training achieve strong performance, but their memory requirements grow linearly with the number of classes and quickly become impractical for real‑world robots.  Regularization‑based strategies avoid storing data but generally lag behind replay‑based methods in accuracy.  Recent few‑shot class‑incremental learning (FSCIL) works reduce the number of labeled examples per class, yet they still rely on a complete, labeled batch for every increment and cannot cope with streaming, mostly unlabeled data.  In contrast, our framework represents each learned class as a uniform Gaussian mixture model and employs pseudo‑rehearsal by sampling from these distributions, thereby eliminating the need to retain raw images while preserving discriminative feature representations.  This positions our method as a memory‑efficient solution that extends FSCIL to the online, few‑shot, and partially unlabeled regime required by robotic applications.  

Active‑learning research has largely focused on batch settings, training deep networks with uncertainty‑sampling criteria (e.g., predictive entropy or margin) to request labels for the most ambiguous instances.  Although such approaches reduce labeling effort, they are not designed for continual adaptation; when deployed in a sequential learning scenario they suffer from catastrophic forgetting and lose the ability to identify newly encountered unknown classes. While constraint‑based algorithms are attractive for their linear‑time scalability in the number of variables and their clear stopping criterion based on the maximal CI order, they are notoriously fragile: errors in high‑order CI tests, which are amplified in small‑sample regimes, can cascade into severely misspecified structures. Aitchison et al. argued that predictive coding can implement Bayesian inference but is not a necessary mechanism, emphasizing alternative computational routes [31]. This approach reveals non‑monotonic relationships between feedback utility, computational parameters, and environmental dynamics, leading to phase transitions in the optimal use of feedback. Early works demonstrated the feasibility of optimizing over fixed lists of molecules using acquisition functions such as expected improvement, but the approach is limited by the size of the library that can be enumerated in advance. Within this line of work, two complementary strands have emerged. The first strand focuses on improving the training objectives of the autoencoder or the surrogate model so that the latent representation better captures the structure of the target property; examples include the incorporation of supervised or semi‑supervised losses, triplet constraints, and other regularizers that align latent distances with property differences. The second strand concentrates on enhancing the decoder component, often by imposing syntactic or semantic constraints such as grammar‑based decoding, graph‑based generation, or domain‑specific validity checks. These decoder improvements have been extended to other discrete design domains, including neural‑network architectures and kernel design for Gaussian processes, illustrating the broad applicability of latent‑space Bayesian optimization.

Several studies have investigated alternative search strategies for molecular design that do not rely on conventional Bayesian optimization. Evolutionary algorithms, including genetic algorithms, have been adapted to traverse chemical space by mutating and recombining molecular fragments. Markov chain Monte Carlo techniques have been employed to sample high‑probability regions of the space, while reinforcement‑learning approaches have trained policies to construct molecules atom by atom or to generate complete SMILES strings using autoregressive models. [ANSWER]: Exhaustive computation of all pair‑wise distances is prohibitive on most hardware, which has motivated a large body of work on approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) search.  Prior studies evaluate ANN quality using recall metrics that compare the retrieved set 𝑅(q) with the true nearest‑neighbor set 𝑇(q) [1],[2].  While these works accept a loss in accuracy for speed, our algorithm departs from this trade‑off by preserving exact distance computation for every database point, thereby guaranteeing the same recall as exhaustive search while still attaining peak TPU performance through a principled performance model.

A dominant class of ANN methods reduces the search space by operating on a lossy‑compressed representation of the data.  Typical pipelines first locate a small candidate set using structures such as locality‑sensitive hashing [3],[4], hierarchical trees [5],[6], proximity graphs [7], or inverted file indices built on k‑means centroids [8]‑[11], and then refine the results by exact distance evaluation.  This two‑stage approach lowers computational cost but introduces several drawbacks that our work explicitly avoids: (i) candidate selection yields poor cache reuse because different queries rarely share the same subset of points, a limitation we quantify and exploit in Section X to achieve superior memory‑bandwidth utilization on TPUs; (ii) the speed‑recall balance is highly data‑dependent and requires costly tuning, whereas our method requires no index construction or hyper‑parameter search and delivers analytical recall guarantees.  By eliminating the pruning stage, our approach remains immune to the curse of dimensionality described in [12] and sidesteps the strong lower bounds on sub‑linear ANN search under the Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis [13],[14].

The hardware platforms that enable our contribution are modern machine‑learning accelerators, specifically Google TPU v3/v4 and NVIDIA GPUs V100/A100.  These devices provide specialized matrix‑multiply units—tensor cores on GPUs [15] and systolic arrays on TPUs [16],[17]—that deliver orders of magnitude higher throughput for dense linear algebra than for scalar operations.  Existing performance models for these accelerators treat all floating‑point operations as equal, which overlooks the pronounced throughput disparity between matrix‑multiply and element‑wise kernels.  We extend the classic roofline model [18] to capture these instruction‑level differences, a refinement that directly informs the design of our distance‑computation kernel and is absent from prior accelerator‑oriented ANN literature.

Even with abundant FLOP/s, selecting the top‑k nearest distances remains a bottleneck on accelerators, as evidenced by recent work on selection algorithms for GPUs and TPUs [19]‑[22].  Those studies focus on reducing the cost of the selection phase after a candidate set has been identified, but they do not address the situation where the selection must be performed over the entire dataset.  Our algorithm integrates selection into the same matrix‑multiply‑driven pipeline used for distance computation, thereby amortizing the selection cost across the same high‑throughput tensor operations and eliminating the extra overhead highlighted in [19]‑[22].  This integration is a key differentiator of our approach and enables the observed state‑of‑the‑art speed‑recall trade‑offs on TPU hardware.

[ANSWER]: Reduced‑precision deep neural networks have been studied extensively, especially for inference‑time efficiency. Early works such as BinaryConnect [4] and Ternary‑Weight Networks [5] focus on aggressively quantizing the weight tensors while keeping activations in full precision. These approaches demonstrate impressive memory savings but typically incur a noticeable drop in top‑1 accuracy (e.g., a 5 % loss on ImageNet [1]). More recent fine‑grained methods [6, 7] improve accuracy by applying per‑layer or per‑filter ternary quantization, yet they rely on post‑training fine‑tuning and are not suited for training networks from scratch. Our work departs from this line by jointly reducing the precision of both weights and activations during training, and compensating the potential accuracy loss through a systematic increase in network width, thereby preserving or surpassing the baseline performance without requiring a fine‑tuning stage.

A second strand of literature targets activation quantization, often in conjunction with weight quantization, to obtain end‑to‑end low‑precision pipelines. XNOR‑Net [12, 13] and related binary‑network approaches [9, 10, 11, 14, 15] quantize both weights and activations to a single bit, but report sizable accuracy degradations (8–12 % top‑1 loss on ImageNet). Subsequent refinements [16] achieve within‑1 % of full‑precision accuracy using 5‑bit logarithmic activations, yet they still depend on selective layer‑wise quantization and do not explore the trade‑off between activation precision and model capacity. By contrast, we demonstrate that a modest 4‑bit activation precision combined with a 2‑bit weight representation can match full‑precision accuracy when the network is made wider, and that even binary activations become viable when the width is appropriately scaled. This establishes a new accuracy frontier for activation‑aware quantization without resorting to complex, layer‑specific schemes.

Hardware‑friendly quantization is another important concern. Non‑power‑of‑two operand representations introduce misaligned memory accesses and can diminish the theoretical gains of low‑precision arithmetic [17]. Prior works therefore often adopt elaborate encoding or packing strategies that complicate hardware implementation and obscure end‑to‑end performance benefits. In our approach we employ a simple, uniform quantization that aligns naturally with memory boundaries, enabling efficient realization on GPUs, FPGAs, and ASICs. Empirical evaluations show that, unlike existing binary‑network implementations, our wide reduced‑precision networks achieve up to 100× energy savings on custom hardware while maintaining baseline accuracy, highlighting the practical advantage of our design.

Collectively, these observations motivate our contribution: we are the first to systematically study the interplay between reduced‑precision activations, reduced‑precision weights, and increased network width, and to prove that such “wide reduced‑precision networks” can attain state‑of‑the‑art accuracy on large‑scale benchmarks (e.g., 69.85 % top‑1 on ResNet‑34 with 2× width) at a lower computational cost than prior low‑precision methods. Our results thus redefine the accuracy‑efficiency trade‑off for both training and inference in deep learning.
