[ANSWER]: Score‑based and constraint‑based learning have long formed the two dominant paradigms for Bayesian network structure discovery.  Score‑based methods pair a decomposable scoring function such as BDeu with a heuristic search, e.g., Greedy Equivalence Search (GES) [2], to traverse the space of DAGs.  Constraint‑based approaches, exemplified by the PC and FCI algorithms [3, 4], rely on a series of conditional‑independence (CI) tests to infer the Markov equivalence class (CPDAG) that best fits the data.  While constraint‑based algorithms are attractive for their linear‑time scalability in the number of variables and their clear stopping criterion based on the maximal CI order, they are notoriously fragile: errors in high‑order CI tests, which are amplified in small‑sample regimes, can cascade into severely misspecified structures.  Hybrid techniques that interleave scoring and CI testing have been proposed to mitigate these weaknesses [5], yet they still inherit the sensitivity of the underlying CI tests.  Our contribution directly addresses this vulnerability by embedding a non‑parametric bootstrap within a recursive constraint‑based framework: low‑order independencies, which are empirically stable, are reused throughout the recursion, while higher‑order tests are protected by increasing the number of bootstrap replicates.  Consequently, the resulting B‑RAI algorithm retains the computational efficiency of constraint‑based learning while dramatically improving robustness to sampling noise, a property not achieved by existing hybrid methods.

Recent work on exact MAP learning has focused on expanding the searchable space through clever encodings and branch‑and‑bound strategies, yielding algorithms that can guarantee optimality for domains up to roughly two dozen variables [6‑9].  Parallel efforts have produced methods that enumerate the top‑k most probable networks [10‑12] by exploiting specialized search spaces.  Although these advances represent important theoretical progress, their practical applicability remains limited to modest‑size problems because the underlying combinatorial explosion is only partially alleviated.  In contrast, B‑RAI is designed for high‑dimensional settings with hundreds of variables.  By organizing the search as a generative tree whose nodes correspond to scored CPDAGs for variable subsets, the algorithm decomposes the global problem into a hierarchy of smaller subproblems.  This recursive decomposition, together with bootstrap‑driven stabilization, enables B‑RAI to scale far beyond the variable limits of exact MAP solvers while still delivering high‑quality MAP estimates.

Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) techniques have become the standard for Bayesian model averaging in structure learning, sampling DAGs from the posterior distribution [13‑17].  Although MCMC provides a principled way to approximate posterior expectations, finite‑run guarantees are lacking: poor mixing, autocorrelation, and the prohibitive cost of evaluating large numbers of candidate graphs restrict their use to relatively small domains.  Our approach offers a deterministic alternative for model averaging: after constructing the B‑RAI tree, we introduce an efficient algorithm that draws exact samples of CPDAGs from the posterior encoded by the tree.  This sampling procedure leverages the hierarchical organization of the tree to produce independent draws without the convergence concerns inherent to MCMC, and it does so at a computational cost comparable to a single pass of the recursive learning phase.  Thus, the proposed framework unifies MAP estimation and posterior sampling within a single scalable pipeline, filling the gap between exact MAP methods and stochastic model‑averaging approaches.

[ANSWER]: Diffusion probabilistic models (DPMs) were introduced as a class of generative models that can be interpreted as variational autoencoders (VAEs) with a specially structured latent space [1, 2, 3]. Their formulation permits the training of arbitrarily deep stochastic processes while retaining a tractable variational lower bound (VLB) on the data likelihood. The resurgence of interest in DPMs has been driven largely by their ability to produce high‑fidelity samples on image synthesis benchmarks [4, 5].

Early work on DPMs proposed a series of architectural and objective‑function refinements that substantially improved sample quality. In particular, the original discrete‑time diffusion model was shown to be equivalent to multi‑scale denoising score matching when diffusion variances are shared across dimensions, up to specific weightings per noise level [4]. Subsequent extensions introduced more expressive noise schedules and training tricks, leading to further gains in log‑likelihood performance [6].

A parallel line of research framed diffusion‑based generation as a multi‑scale denoising score‑matching problem and extended the methodology to continuous time. By interpreting the diffusion as a stochastic differential equation, these works derived sampling algorithms that reverse the forward diffusion process, enabling efficient generation without discretising the time axis [7, 8]. The continuous‑time perspective also opened the door to novel theoretical analyses of diffusion models.

Several recent studies derived variational lower bounds for continuous‑time diffusion models using stochastic differential equation formalisms. These works presented alternative derivations of the VLB, highlighted connections between the VAE‑style and score‑matching perspectives, and discussed conditions under which the two formulations coincide [9, 10, 11]. The analyses collectively deepened the understanding of how diffusion dynamics influence likelihood estimation.

By applying IntroD to the extractive QA setting, we use an ID‑teacher that captures the natural position distribution and an OOD‑teacher that imagines a uniform or counterfactual position distribution, enabling our student model to retain competitive SQuAD performance while substantially improving robustness to positional shifts.

Although these methods can be interpreted through a causal lens, they assume that training and test distributions are markedly different (often reversed), which explains why they excel on OOD benchmarks but degrade on ID data.  In contrast, IntroD treats the two teachers as complementary causal agents: the ID‑teacher provides factual knowledge while the OOD‑teacher supplies counterfactual insight. [ANSWER]: Previous research on continual learning (CL) has explored a variety of strategies to mitigate catastrophic forgetting. Memory‑based approaches retain data from earlier tasks and incorporate it during the training of new tasks, either by replaying raw samples [1–3] or by explicitly reducing gradient interference [4,5]. Generative methods train models such as GANs [6,7] or autoencoders [8] to synthesize examples from past distributions, thereby improving memory efficiency. Expanding network capacity by introducing additional parameters has also been proposed as a way to accommodate new tasks without overwriting old knowledge [15,16]. Meta‑learning, the paradigm of learning to learn, has been applied to sequence learning [22,23] and to continual‑learning settings [24–27]. For example, combining instance prototypes from prior tasks with tailored loss functions can adapt model parameters to reduce forgetting [28]. Conditioning mechanisms that modify network weights have also been investigated: linear functions that squeeze activation maps to normalize convolutional outputs [29], and task‑dependent conditioning of convolutional layers using external cues such as questions in visual‑question‑answering systems [30].

Early approaches represented the learning process with recurrent neural networks, allowing hidden states to persist across episode boundaries and to encode task information [5, 6, 7]. Within the meta‑RL paradigm, several studies have investigated experience relabeling as a means of sharing data across tasks. One line of work frames meta‑RL as a model‑identification problem, employing context‑dependent neural networks to parameterize transition dynamics and reward functions; this method applies relabeling only at meta‑test time to improve adaptation to out‑of‑distribution tasks, without any data sharing during meta‑training [17]. Another strand addresses offline meta‑RL, introducing reward relabeling to mitigate the “MDP ambiguity” that arises when learning from fixed datasets; the relabeling strategy is based on random task selection and is tailored to the offline setting [18]. The approach differs from prior meta‑RL relabeling techniques by operating in the online setting, using a maximum‑entropy‑derived utility to guide task selection, and being compatible with arbitrary reward structures. Empirical evaluation on a suite of robotic manipulation and locomotion benchmarks demonstrates that HFR outperforms existing relabeling methods from both the meta‑RL and multi‑task RL literature, establishing it as the first effective relabeling strategy designed specifically for the meta‑training phase.

[ANSWER]: Metric learning aims to learn a distance metric that brings examples from the same class (positive pairs) close together while pushing examples from different classes (negative pairs) apart. In deep metric learning, an explicit non‑linear mapping from raw inputs to a low‑dimensional embedding space is learned so that Euclidean distances in this space exhibit the desired properties. Although unsupervised formulations exist, the majority of work follows a supervised paradigm in which positive and negative pairs are defined by matching or mismatching class labels. Loss functions for deep metric learning are commonly divided into pair‑based and proxy‑based families. Pair‑based losses operate directly on pairs, triplets, quadruplets or higher‑order tuples of examples, capturing fine‑grained data‑to‑data relationships but often suffering from sensitivity to noisy labels, outliers, and a prevalence of zero‑gradient terms that motivate hard‑example mining strategies such as semi‑hard or distance‑weighted sampling. Proxy‑based losses introduce learnable class representatives (proxies) that summarize each class in the embedding space, reducing computational cost and typically providing more consistent gradients, which can lessen the reliance on mining and accelerate convergence.

Input mixup linearly interpolates two or more samples in the input space and simultaneously interpolates their target labels, serving as a simple yet effective data‑augmentation technique. In many distillation setups the teacher is either a fixed expert or a moving aggregation of experts [8, 9, 10, 3], whereas other methods generate targets by following a prescribed update rule rather than by aggregating existing models.

Trust‑region methods introduce an explicit distance function to regularize gradient updates, thereby controlling the step size and curvature of the optimisation landscape [11, 12, 13, 14].  These techniques have been applied in both supervised and reinforcement‑learning contexts to improve stability and convergence.

Building on these strands of research, the present work proposes a bootstrapped meta‑gradient (BMG) algorithm that generates future targets by continuing the learner’s own update rule (or an alternative rule) and then optimises the meta‑learner by minimising a chosen (pseudo‑)metric—such as Euclidean distance or KL divergence—between its current parameters and the bootstrapped target.  By formulating the meta‑objective in this way, BMG addresses the curvature and short‑horizon biases identified in earlier meta‑optimisation studies, provides theoretical guarantees of monotonic performance improvement, and enables the use of longer‑horizon information without back‑propagating through all intermediate updates. Another class of approaches addresses discrepancies between expert and learner environments that stem from differences in viewpoints, visual appearance, distracting elements, or morphological variations. [ANSWER]: Metric learning seeks embeddings in which examples sharing a class label (positive pairs) lie close together while examples from different classes (negative pairs) are pushed apart.  In deep metric learning this goal is achieved by learning a non‑linear mapping from raw inputs to a low‑dimensional space where Euclidean distance exhibits the desired behavior.  Most prior work follows a fully supervised paradigm that defines positives and negatives directly from class labels, and the literature has largely focused on two families of loss functions: pair‑based losses that operate on explicit pairs, triplets, quadruplets or higher‑order tuples, and proxy‑based losses that replace data points with learnable class proxies.  Pair‑based losses capture fine‑grained data‑to‑data relationships but are sensitive to noisy labels and often produce zero‑gradient constraints, which in turn motivates sophisticated hard‑example mining strategies.  Proxy‑based losses alleviate these issues by aggregating data through proxies, yielding denser gradients and faster convergence at the cost of reduced granularity.  Our contribution situates itself between these two streams: by formulating a generic loss abstraction that encompasses both pair‑based and proxy‑based objectives, we enable the seamless integration of mixup‑style augmentation into any existing metric‑learning loss, thereby unifying and extending the current landscape rather than replacing one family with the other.  

Mixup and its variants have become a staple of data augmentation for classification, where two or more inputs are linearly combined in either the raw pixel space (input mixup) or in intermediate feature spaces (manifold mixup), and the corresponding one‑hot class labels are interpolated in the same proportion.  The majority of mixup research targets cross‑entropy loss and assumes an additive label structure, while only a handful of works explore its interaction with pairwise objectives.  Existing studies on embedding‑level interpolation for metric learning either restrict themselves to deterministic synthesis within a single class or to proxy interpolation across classes, and they do not address the challenge of label interpolation for pairwise losses.  By extending the mixup principle to the metric‑learning setting, we introduce a principled way to interpolate not only inputs, features or embeddings but also the binary “positive/negative’’ label associated with each anchor‑pair.  This enables the model to receive smoothly varying supervisory signals that reflect the degree of mixing, a capability absent from prior mixup‑based metric‑learning methods.  

Prior attempts to apply interpolation to pairwise loss functions either avoid label interpolation altogether or rely on ad‑hoc heuristics that can generate false negatives when the mixing coefficient is extreme.  For example, embedding‑expansion and symmetric synthesis methods interpolate embeddings within the same class but keep labels binary, while proxy‑synthesis interpolates between class proxies without adjusting the underlying pairwise supervision, risking label corruption.  Contrastive representation approaches such as MoCHi and OptTransMix introduce thresholds to sidestep false negatives, and i‑mix linearly interpolates anchor embeddings and a single virtual class label, yet they cannot exploit the relative weighting of multiple positives and negatives per anchor.  In contrast, our proposed Metric Mix (Metrix) provides a unified formulation that supports both pair‑based and proxy‑based losses, permits mixing at any stage of the network (input, manifold or embedding), and interpolates the binary positive/negative label in a mathematically sound manner.  Consequently, the relative contribution of positives versus negatives is continuously modulated by the mixing factor, a property that directly addresses the shortcomings of earlier interpolation schemes and positions our work as the first general‑purpose mixup framework for deep metric learning.

Recent “sanity‑check’’ studies have demonstrated that many popular gradient‑based techniques—including guided backpropagation, gradient × input, and integrated gradients—can remain unchanged after randomizing model parameters or training data, indicating a lack of fidelity relative to vanilla input gradients.  Additional investigations using purpose‑built datasets have shown that several explanation approaches are prone to producing false‑positive attributions, whereas vanilla input gradients tend to be more reliable.  Relationships between vanilla gradients and other methods such as DeepLIFT have been identified, and recent work has linked the visual alignment of gradient‑based attributions to implicit density modeling, underscoring the importance of a deeper understanding of gradient fidelity.

A separate line of research focuses on quantitative metrics for explanation fidelity.  Many proposals measure the impact on model performance when the most or least important pixels, as identified by an explanation, are altered or removed.  However, such modification‑based metrics can conflate attribution quality with distribution shift effects introduced by masking, making it difficult to isolate the true contribution of the explanation.  Analyses have further revealed inconsistencies in ranking explanation methods when distribution‑shift penalties are applied.  The remove‑and‑retrain paradigm addresses this concern by retraining models on perturbed data, thereby accounting for distribution changes; yet studies employing this framework have found that even input gradients can underperform compared to random baselines, highlighting the need for more nuanced evaluation strategies.

Research on adversarial robustness has uncovered several side effects of adversarial training beyond increased resistance to perturbations.  Models trained with adversarial objectives have been shown to yield more transferable features, produce representations that align better with human perception, and generate input gradients with improved visual quality.  Moreover, evaluations using the remove‑and‑retrain approach have reported that the gradients of adversarially trained models exhibit markedly higher fidelity than random attributions.  These findings suggest a link between robustness and the reliability of gradient‑based explanations, motivating further analysis of how training regimes affect attribution behavior.

In this work we introduce a systematic framework for testing the core assumption that large‑magnitude input gradients reliably indicate task‑relevant features.  Building on the identified gaps in visual and modification‑based evaluations, we propose DiffROAR, a quantitative benchmark that measures attribution fidelity while explicitly controlling for distribution shift.  To enable controlled experiments with known discriminative features, we construct BlockMNIST, a semi‑real dataset that encodes ground‑truth signal coordinates.  Using DiffROAR, we reveal a phenomenon we term feature inversion in gradients (FIG), whereby standard models trained on natural data assign higher gradient magnitudes to irrelevant features, violating the assumed correspondence between gradient magnitude and importance.  Conversely, we show that adversarially robust models eliminate FIG, a behavior we label robustness‑fixes‑FIG (RF‑FIG).  Complementing empirical results on CIFAR‑10, ImageNet‑10, and BlockMNIST, we provide theoretical guarantees on a simplified version of the synthetic dataset, proving that standard one‑hidden‑layer networks inevitably exhibit FIG while adversarial training enforces RF‑FIG. A limitation of knowledge‑base‑centric methods is their dependence on the alignment between the target dataset and the underlying resource. Several benchmark datasets are derived from existing graphs—for example, CommonsenseQA originates from ConceptNet [13,14] and the NLI split used in ROC‑Stories [15,16]. When the dataset’s domain matches the source graph, incorporating the corresponding knowledge yields substantial gains [8]. A complementary strategy augments the input question with model‑generated text such as clarifications, explanations, or implications. [ANSWER]: Domain adaptation addresses the shift between source and target distributions by designing methods that align or transfer knowledge across domains [1]–[6]. Traditional approaches assume access to target data during training, an assumption that often does not hold in practice. To relax this requirement, recent studies have explored more challenging settings such as few‑shot and one‑shot domain adaptation, where only a limited number of target samples are available for model adjustment [7]–[9].

Domain generalization seeks to learn models that perform well on unseen target domains without any target data at training time. The problem was first introduced in [10] and formally defined in [11]. Early work focused on learning domain‑invariant representations by minimizing feature dissimilarities across source domains [11], [12]. This line of research has been extended by numerous methods that impose invariance constraints on learned features [13]–[17]. Several approaches treat domain generalization as a meta‑learning problem, training on a set of source domains and evaluating adaptation on held‑out domains [23]–[26]. Model‑agnostic meta‑learning (MAML) was introduced for this purpose in [27] and later enhanced with global and local regularization techniques [29]. Common experimental protocols partition source domains into meta‑source and meta‑target subsets to mimic the adaptation process during training [24], [25].

Test‑time adaptation methods aim to adjust a pretrained source model to unseen target data at inference time. Some approaches combine supervised and self‑supervised objectives during source training and then fine‑tune the model on target data using only the self‑supervised loss [31]. A different strategy learns a domain‑embedding network from unsupervised source data; the embedding is then estimated for a target domain using many unlabeled target samples, enabling adaptation without explicit fine‑tuning [33]. These techniques typically require additional steps such as fine‑tuning or processing batches of target samples. A prominent instance of this paradigm is Generative Adversarial Imitation Learning (GAIL), which casts imitation as a distribution‑matching problem and employs a generative‑adversarial network to minimize the Jensen–Shannon divergence between the expert and learner state‑action distributions. Building on GAIL, numerous works have explored alternative reinforcement‑learning back‑ends or substituted different statistical divergences to improve imitation performance, yet the majority of these approaches remain on‑policy, requiring fresh environment interactions at each policy update and consequently incurring high sample costs.

To address the sample inefficiency of on‑policy imitation, several off‑policy extensions have been proposed. Classical formulations often rely on linear matrix inequalities (LMIs) to encode stability and performance specifications, enabling the use of interior‑point or first‑order solvers for moderately sized problems. Because the stability proofs typically require simple (often linear) controllers, the resulting policies can be conservative in average‑case scenarios, prompting interest in methods that retain robustness while allowing richer controller structures.  

Deep reinforcement learning (deep RL) pursues optimal control policies represented by neural networks through interaction with an environment that may be unknown or partially known. This paradigm has achieved state‑of‑the‑art results on a variety of complex control benchmarks, leveraging the expressive power of deep networks to capture highly nonlinear behaviors. However, the absence of formal safety or stability guarantees limits the deployment of deep RL in safety‑critical domains where failures are costly or unacceptable.  

A substantial line of research seeks to combine control‑theoretic robustness with the flexibility of deep RL. These approaches integrate robust control concepts—such as Lyapunov‑based stability analysis, min‑max differential game formulations, or uncertainty‑aware policy optimization—into the learning process. By jointly learning policies and auxiliary certificates (e.g., Lyapunov functions) or by framing control synthesis as a game between a controller and an adversarial disturbance, these methods aim to inherit robustness properties while exploiting nonlinear function approximation. The scope of such techniques varies, with many focusing on specific uncertainty models or particular classes of systems.  

Safe reinforcement learning addresses the challenge of maintaining safety during learning and execution. Typical strategies constrain the exploration to regions of the state space that satisfy safety assumptions, often invoking smoothness or probabilistic models of the dynamics such as Gaussian processes or Lipschitz continuity. These frameworks can be more general in terms of admissible dynamics, but they rely on strong assumptions about model regularity and may incur substantial computational overhead, especially in high‑dimensional settings.  

Constrained Markov Decision Processes (C‑MDPs) formulate control as a reward maximization problem subject to cost constraints expressed as discounted expectations. While C‑MDPs do not require prior knowledge of the cost functions and can enforce constraints at test time, the resulting optimal policies are frequently stochastic, and the guarantees apply only to a subset of states, which can be limiting for safety‑critical applications.

[ANSWER]: Robust control provides rigorous worst‑case guarantees by formulating controller synthesis as linear matrix inequality (LMI) problems that can be solved with off‑the‑shelf interior‑point or first‑order solvers.  While these methods reliably produce stabilizing controllers, they typically restrict the policy to a simple (often linear) form, which limits performance on typical, non‑worst‑case trajectories.  Our work directly addresses this limitation: we retain the exact same LMI‑based stability certificates but replace the linear policy with a highly expressive neural‑network controller.  By projecting the network’s output onto the convex set of actions that satisfy the LMI constraints, we obtain a nonlinear controller that enjoys the original robust‑control guarantees while achieving substantially higher average‑case performance.

Deep reinforcement learning (RL) removes the need for analytic models by learning neural‑network policies through interaction with an environment, and it has demonstrated state‑of‑the‑art results on many challenging control benchmarks.  However, standard deep‑RL algorithms offer no explicit safety or robustness guarantees, which has confined their deployment to simulated or otherwise low‑risk settings.  A growing body of work attempts to combine RL with control‑theoretic ideas—such as jointly learning Lyapunov functions, solving min‑max differential games, or incorporating robust‑control specifications into the learning objective.  Compared with these approaches, our method is not tied to a specific formulation (e.g., stochastic stability or game‑theoretic objectives) and can be applied to any robust‑control problem that admits a convex description of stabilizing actions.  Consequently, we are able to handle a far broader class of uncertainty models, including polytopic and norm‑bounded disturbances, while still training the policy with standard RL algorithms.

Recent advances in differentiable optimization layers have enabled neural networks to embed hard constraints by back‑propagating through the solution of convex programs such as quadratic programs, cone programs, or SAT solvers.  These layers provide a powerful way to endow learned models with domain‑specific inductive bias.  We build on this line of work by designing custom, fast, differentiable projection layers that solve the convex feasibility problem defined by the robust‑control LMIs.  Unlike generic QP or cone‑program layers, our projection operators exploit the particular structure of stabilizing‑action sets, yielding polynomial‑time complexity that scales gracefully with state‑action dimension.  This makes it feasible to enforce provable stability in high‑dimensional systems such as quadrotors and microgrids, where generic differentiable‑optimization approaches would be computationally prohibitive.

Initial pruning techniques focused on removing individual neurons or connections, thereby reducing the total number of parameters and the storage footprint of the model.  While these unstructured approaches achieved substantial compression, they generally did not translate into faster inference because the sparse weight matrices could not be efficiently exploited by existing hardware accelerators.

More recent work has shifted toward structured pruning, which removes whole channels, filters, or even layers and therefore preserves the regular dense layout required for high‑throughput execution.  A widely used heuristic selects channels with the smallest ℓ₁‑norm, assuming that low‑magnitude filters carry less information.  Other methods evaluate the impact of each channel on the activations of the subsequent layer and prune those with minimal influence.  Regularization‑based approaches impose sparsity‑inducing penalties on the scaling factors of batch‑normalization layers, followed by global thresholding to discard insignificant channels.  Reinforcement‑learning strategies have been proposed to automatically learn the compression ratio for each layer, treating the selection of widths as a sequential decision problem.  Several single‑stage frameworks integrate training and pruning into a unified optimization, learning mask parameters jointly with the network weights and eliminating the need for a separate fine‑tuning phase.

A distinct line of research incorporates explicit resource constraints into the pruning process, enabling direct control over the size of the resulting model.  MorphNet introduces a sparsifying regularizer together with a uniform layer‑wise width multiplier, iteratively shrinking and expanding the network to satisfy a prescribed budget; however, it requires model‑specific hyper‑parameter searches to set the regularization strength. In contrast, the proposed approach delivers deterministic structured pruning by leveraging a continuous Heaviside projection and a novel crispness loss, enabling the extraction of highly sparse subnetworks directly from pretrained dense models without introducing auxiliary pruning parameters.  The method supports arbitrary budget specifications—including limits on parameters, FLOPs, channel counts, or activation volumes—and remains stable even when the target budget reduces the model to a few percent of its original size.  Experiments demonstrate consistent accuracy improvements over state‑of‑the‑art baselines across diverse budget settings, with gains of up to 16.1 % in extreme pruning scenarios.  Moreover, the learned binary masks transfer effectively between datasets, and in certain cases masks derived from a richly‑featured teacher dataset yield superior performance on a student dataset compared to masks obtained by pruning the student data directly.  This combination of deterministic mask generation, flexible budget handling, robustness under aggressive compression, and cross‑dataset mask transfer distinguishes the method from existing structured and budget‑aware pruning techniques.

[ANSWER]: Learning from Demonstrations (LfD) originated with behavior cloning, which pre‑trains a policy by minimizing prediction error on state‑action pairs collected from an expert. Although simple, behavior cloning suffers from distribution shift and error accumulation as the learned policy deviates from the demonstrated trajectories. To mitigate these issues, DAgger introduced a no‑regret framework that iteratively queries an oracle for corrective actions, at the cost of requiring online access to the expert. More recent LfD methods have embraced inverse reinforcement learning, which seeks a reward function that renders the expert behavior optimal; the recovered reward can then be optimized with standard reinforcement‑learning algorithms. A prominent instance of this paradigm is Generative Adversarial Imitation Learning (GAIL), which casts imitation as a distribution‑matching problem and employs a generative‑adversarial network to minimize the Jensen–Shannon divergence between the expert and learner state‑action distributions. Building on GAIL, numerous works have explored alternative reinforcement‑learning back‑ends or substituted different statistical divergences to improve imitation performance, yet the majority of these approaches remain on‑policy, requiring fresh environment interactions at each policy update and consequently incurring high sample costs.

To address the sample inefficiency of on‑policy imitation, several off‑policy extensions have been proposed. DAC adapts the GAIL objective to reuse past experiences stored in a replay buffer, thereby reducing the need for on‑policy data collection. Similar replay‑based strategies appear in other works that recycle cached transitions for policy improvement. A common limitation of these methods is that they often ignore the distributional discrepancy introduced when substituting the true on‑policy occupancy with an off‑policy approximation, which can lead to a drift from the intended objective. ValueDICE offers another off‑policy route by reformulating the on‑policy imitation loss using the DICE framework; however, it relies on access to expert actions, rendering it unsuitable for settings where only observations are available. Consequently, off‑policy imitation methods that do not require expert actions remain an open challenge.

Learning from Observations (LfO) tackles the more restrictive scenario in which expert action labels are absent. Model‑free LfO approaches typically extend the adversarial imitation paradigm to state‑only data. GAIfO applies the GAIL framework with a discriminator that receives only states, enabling imitation without action information. IDDM analyzes the theoretical gap between LfD and LfO objectives and shows that maximizing the mutual information between latent actions and observed states can partially bridge this gap, achieving performance comparable to GAIL while still relying on on‑policy data. Other model‑free methods assume a ranking over observation trajectories and construct reward functions accordingly; these techniques also inherit the sample‑inefficiency of on‑policy learning.

Model‑based LfO methods introduce dynamics models to compensate for the missing action signals. Forward‑model approaches learn a transition model and use it to synthesize pseudo‑actions or to plan directly; while effective for finite‑horizon tasks, they may struggle with long‑horizon or infinite‑horizon problems due to the need for time‑dependent policies. Inverse‑model approaches infer the missing actions by training a mapping from consecutive observations to the underlying action, after which standard behavior‑cloning can be applied. This strategy, exemplified by Behavior Cloning from Observations (BCO), inherits the limitations of behavior cloning and additionally requires strong assumptions such as deterministic, injective dynamics to guarantee accurate action recovery. Other recent works consider mismatched dynamics or viewpoints between expert and learner observations, further expanding the scope of LfO research.

In contrast to prior methods, the present work introduces a sample‑efficient LfO algorithm that operates fully off‑policy without requiring expert actions. By deriving an upper bound on the LfO objective, the approach enables principled off‑policy optimization while explicitly accounting for the distribution shift between on‑policy and replay‑buffer samples. To further accelerate learning, the method incorporates a regularization term that promotes mode‑covering distribution matching; under deterministic dynamics this regularizer is implemented via an inverse action model learned from the replay buffer. The resulting algorithm achieves state‑of‑the‑art performance on challenging locomotion benchmarks, matching or surpassing existing methods in both asymptotic return and sample complexity, thereby addressing the limitations of on‑policy dependence, action‑free requirements, and theoretical guarantees highlighted in earlier work.

[ANSWER]: FedAvg [1] is a widely adopted federated learning (FL) algorithm because of its simplicity and low communication cost. However, severe data heterogeneity can cause unstable training trajectories and lead to suboptimal models [2]–[4]. To mitigate the negative impacts of heterogeneity on a shared model, a variety of techniques based on variance reduction [2], [5], [4] and normalization [6] have been proposed. Most convergence analyses for these methods rely on strong technical assumptions such as bounded gradients or bounded Hessian similarity, which may not hold when the underlying data-generating process is considered [2], [5], [4]. Empirically, none of the approaches consistently outperforms the others across different heterogeneity settings [7]. In addition, the generalization error of the common model with respect to local data has received little attention, with the exception of recent work showing that a common model can tolerate a moderate level of model heterogeneity [8].

Federated multi‑task learning (MTL) aims to learn distinct models for each client [9], [10]. While conceptually appealing, the convergence behavior of federated MTL remains poorly understood because the objective is not jointly convex in model parameters and task relationships [9]–[12]. Early work focused on updating model parameters only [9]; even in centralized settings, convergence results require restrictive assumptions such as equal dataset sizes across tasks [12] or a small number of shared features [11]. Moreover, the analysis often concerns average excess error rather than task‑specific error, with the dominant term scaling with the homogeneous local dataset size [12]. Recent advances for linear representation learning and balanced local data have been reported [13], [14]. Parallel to federated MTL, model personalization has been studied under the model‑agnostic meta‑learning (MAML) framework [15], [16], where the global objective incorporates the cost of fine‑tuning a global model at individual clients. These works primarily analyze convergence of training errors and do not provide generalization‑error characterizations.

Clustered federated learning (CFL) can be viewed as a special case of federated MTL in which client tasks form cluster structures [17]–[22]. Several algorithms jointly learn clusters and models for each cluster. Some approaches perform clustering as a post‑processing step; for example, hierarchical clustering of clients is applied after training [17], which requires solving a sequence of empirical risk minimization problems to recover the clusters and can be time‑consuming. Other methods adopt a modular pipeline that first clusters clients in a one‑shot fashion and then conducts adversary‑resilient model training for each cluster [19]. These algorithms often scale poorly with input dimension, assume balanced and sufficiently large local datasets, and require each client to solve multiple empirical risk minimization problems. Soft‑clustering techniques have also been introduced to exploit information across clusters [22]; however, evaluations are limited to simple datasets such as MNIST and Fashion‑MNIST, and theoretical guarantees are lacking.

Generative replay approaches address the exemplar and feature storage issues by synthesizing past data with learned generators. Despite the success of these techniques, aligning distributions in parallel with the classification objective can sometimes diminish discriminative information. Meta‑learning strategies have been proposed to coordinate the optimization of alignment and classification objectives, reducing potential contradictions between them. [ANSWER]: Recovering private training data from shared gradients has become a central research theme in federated learning. Early work such as Deep Leakage from Gradients (DLG) introduced a gradient‑based inversion technique that can reconstruct individual training samples without auxiliary generative models or prior information. Although DLG demonstrated the feasibility of gradient inversion, its performance deteriorates sharply when the model architecture deviates from simple fully‑connected networks or when weight initialization is varied. By contrast, our proposed CAFE is designed to operate robustly across diverse VFL architectures and to remain effective under realistic initialization schemes, thereby overcoming the generalizability limitations of DLG.

Analytical approaches that extract information directly from gradients have also been explored. One line of work focuses on label recovery by exploiting the linear relationship between gradients and class logits, while another derives input features before the first fully‑connected (FC) layer through closed‑form solutions. These methods, however, are constrained to single‑sample settings and cannot be scaled to the batch regime that is typical in practical VFL training. CAFE extends the analytical insight to the batch scenario by jointly recovering the loss gradients with respect to the intermediate representations, enabling reliable reconstruction of many samples simultaneously.

A subsequent family of techniques formulates the inversion problem as a system of linear equations, attempting to solve for batch inputs before the FC layer. Such methods rely on strong assumptions—e.g., full rank of the activation matrix or independence among samples—that rarely hold in real‑world VFL deployments. Consequently, they lack guaranteed recovery when these assumptions are violated. In contrast, CAFE incorporates a theoretical analysis that quantifies the conditions under which batch recovery succeeds, and it relaxes the restrictive assumptions by leveraging the inherent alignment of data indices across parties in vertical FL.

Some researchers have argued that convolutional layers can be reshaped into equivalent FC layers, suggesting that gradient inversion could be applied uniformly across network types. Nevertheless, the gradients of the original convolutional operation differ from those of the reshaped FC representation, which hampers accurate inversion. CAFE explicitly addresses this mismatch by modelling the true convolutional gradient flow and integrating it into the recovery pipeline, thereby preserving fidelity when reconstructing data processed by convolutional components.

Building on DLG, later works introduced custom loss functions or regularizers—such as Gaussian‑kernel‑based gradient differences or recursive attack procedures—to improve stability across architectures. While these refinements enhance reconstruction quality for small batches, they still experience significant degradation as batch size grows. Our method departs from heuristic loss engineering by providing a principled three‑step recovery process (gradient of loss w.r.t. first FC output, input reconstruction to the FC layer, and final data recovery) that scales gracefully to large batches without sacrificing accuracy.

The most recent gradient inversion algorithms, exemplified by GradInversion, achieve batch reconstruction by iteratively optimizing noise vectors against gradient constraints. Their theoretical foundations, however, depend on strong assumptions about data distribution and gradient linearity, and empirical evaluations have been limited to modest batch sizes (≤ 48). CAFE not only surpasses these batch limits—demonstrating successful recovery on substantially larger batches in vertical FL—but also supplies explicit recovery guarantees that clarify when and why the attack succeeds.

Overall, the existing literature either targets horizontal FL, assumes single‑sample inputs, or imposes impractical conditions that restrict batch scalability. By integrating vertical federated learning specifics, offering rigorous theoretical guarantees, and proposing a practical defense based on fake gradients, CAFE positions itself as the first comprehensive solution that both reveals the severity of large‑batch data leakage in VFL and provides actionable mitigation strategies.

In many “cheap‑talk’’ settings agents discover protocols by transmitting real‑valued vectors, but a substantial line of work concentrates on discrete communication in which each message must be chosen from a finite set of vectors.  Early approaches introduced binary discrete messages and later converged on one‑hot encodings, treating each possible token as an orthogonal basis vector that agents emit without sharing gradients or weights during training or execution.  

A recurring limitation of emergent protocols is their lack of interpretability for humans or for agents that have not co‑trained on the same communication system, which manifests as a “zero‑shot’’ learning problem.  Several studies have identified environmental and architectural factors that promote zero‑shot continuous communication, while other efforts adopt bottom‑up strategies that explicitly align emergent tokens with human language, demonstrating that people can infer the meaning of certain agent symbols in novel contexts.  Complementary top‑down approaches integrate pre‑trained, task‑specific language models to facilitate natural‑language interaction between agents and humans.  

Parallel developments in natural‑language processing have transitioned from naïve one‑hot word representations to dense embedding methods such as Word2Vec and GloVe.  These embeddings map discrete lexical items into a continuous semantic space where proximity reflects similarity of meaning, yielding faster training and superior generalization compared with orthogonal one‑hot encodings.  The success of such continuous representations has motivated the view that emergent communication tokens might benefit from a similar embedding‑based treatment rather than remaining as isolated one‑hot symbols.  

Research on zero‑ and few‑shot classification further illustrates how side information—often derived from language—enables models to recognize novel classes with little or no labeled data.  Techniques that leverage auxiliary linguistic knowledge to guide classification decisions provide a conceptual bridge to emergent communication, where aligning learned tokens with external word embeddings can furnish the side information needed for zero‑shot understanding of unseen messages.  

In this work we introduce a neural‑agent architecture that learns a finite vocabulary of discrete tokens embedded in a continuous semantic space, thereby relaxing the conventional one‑hot constraint.  A decision‑theoretic analysis demonstrates that this embedding‑based communication is optimal across a broad range of task conditions, whereas one‑hot messages are only optimal under restrictive assumptions.  Self‑play experiments reveal that agents spontaneously cluster tokens into semantically meaningful regions, leading to robust performance in noisy environments where one‑hot baselines fail.  By aligning the emergent token space with pre‑trained word embeddings, the agents acquire zero‑shot capabilities: they correctly interpret novel human utterances and generate appropriate responses without additional training.  Human‑subject studies confirm that participants can reliably decode the unlabeled emergent symbols, outperforming prior one‑hot communication schemes.  Together, these contributions extend emergent discrete communication beyond orthogonal symbols, integrate ideas from modern word‑embedding and zero‑shot learning literature, and enable both agent‑agent and human‑agent interaction without reliance on external language models.

[ANSWER]: Marginal‑likelihood approximations have long been a cornerstone of Gaussian‑process (GP) modeling. Early work on sparse GP approximations relied on selecting subsets of the training data to reduce the cubic cost of exact inference, a strategy formalized in the subset‑of‑data (SoD) and subset‑of‑regressors frameworks. The introduction of pseudo‑inputs (or inducing points) provided a more flexible alternative, allowing the inducing locations to be placed anywhere in the input space and leading to variational formulations that yield an evidence lower bound (ELBO) on the marginal likelihood. Stochastic approximations to the ELBO were subsequently proposed, enabling mini‑batch training and scaling to larger datasets. These stochastic ELBO methods can be viewed as Bayesian counterparts to earlier deterministic sparse approximations, preserving the probabilistic treatment while improving scalability.

Active‑set methods, which fix the inducing variables to be a subset of the training inputs, were investigated empirically and shown to produce stable approximations even when the active set comprised only a small fraction of the data. However, random selection of active points was observed to induce non‑smooth fluctuations in the objective, complicating convergence under exact gradient ascent. This instability motivated the development of pseudo‑input approaches, where the inducing variables are optimized continuously rather than chosen discretely, resulting in smoother optimization dynamics. Recent stochastic optimization techniques have revisited active‑set ideas, proposing to average over active‑set configurations rather than optimize a single deterministic subset, thereby mitigating the fluctuations associated with random selection.

The relationship between cross‑validation (CV) and GP marginal‑likelihood estimation has been explored as an alternative avenue for model selection. Initial studies highlighted CV as a practical tool for assessing predictive performance, while later theoretical work established an equivalence between exhaustive CV and the log‑marginal likelihood, offering a novel perspective on Bayesian model evidence. Building on this equivalence, recent research has integrated CV‑based objectives into GP training pipelines. In the context of GP latent‑variable models, back‑constraints have been introduced to regularize the latent space when using inducing points, employing doubly stochastic variational inference to handle the resulting intractabilities. Parallel advances in supervised GP settings have leveraged amortization networks to drastically reduce the number of required inducing points, further enhancing scalability.

In this work we introduce a stochastic active‑set (SAS) framework that unifies these strands of prior research. By exploiting the established link between exhaustive cross‑validation and the log‑marginal likelihood, we derive a stochastic estimator of the marginal likelihood that can be evaluated efficiently using randomly sampled active sets. Unlike traditional active‑set methods, SAS does not seek a single optimal subset; instead, it averages over many subsets, eliminating the non‑smooth fluctuations observed with random selection and obviating the need for costly combinatorial optimization. This stochastic estimation also sidesteps the optimization challenges associated with pseudo‑inputs, while retaining the computational benefits of fixed active points. Moreover, SAS integrates naturally with back‑constraint ideas, providing a principled way to encourage structure in the latent space without additional variational parameters. Empirically, the SAS‑GP decoder attains superior latent representations, scales to substantially larger datasets, and outperforms both variational autoencoders and competing GP‑based decoders in terms of robustness, computational efficiency, and representation quality.

Several works propose specially trained base models to improve the tightness of the certificates, yet they cannot exploit any internal structure of the classifier.  A subset of the literature designs particular randomization schemes—such as discrete patch corruptions or limited‑norm perturbations—that admit exact enumeration of outcomes and therefore yield deterministic certificates for those restricted settings. Research on robustness for tree‑based models has largely focused on settings where each feature may be perturbed independently.  Within this framework, a number of methods have been introduced to train and certify robust decision trees and decision stumps, often by leveraging the combinatorial structure of the tree to obtain exact or over‑approximated certificates.  These techniques, however, are typically confined to ℓ∞‑type perturbations and do not directly extend to other ℓp norms that better capture realistic disturbances.  Alternative certification strategies formulate the problem as a mixed‑integer linear program, achieving complete ℓ∞ certification but incurring Co‑NP‑complete computational costs that render them impractical for large ensembles.  More scalable dynamic‑programming‑based algorithms have been proposed for stump ensembles, providing fast but incomplete certificates by over‑approximating the maximal effect of perturbations.  Additional incomplete methods compute distances from sample points to leaf pre‑images of trees, yet they tend to produce weaker guarantees compared with approaches that exploit the specific structure of stumps.

Building on these lines of work, the present contribution introduces a deterministic smoothing framework tailored to ensembles of decision stumps.  By exploiting the additive independence of feature‑wise contributions, the method computes exact output distributions under arbitrary isotropic continuous randomizations using dynamic programming, thereby delivering deterministic ℓp‑norm certificates that jointly cover numerical and categorical attributes.  An MLE‑optimal training criterion is proposed for individual stumps to align them with the smoothing distribution, and two boosting procedures are developed to enhance the certified robustness of the entire ensemble.  Empirical evaluation on vision and tabular benchmarks demonstrates substantially higher certified accuracies than existing tree‑based certification methods, establishing a new state‑of‑the‑art. [ANSWER]: Model‑based reinforcement learning (MBRL) has been widely studied because it can achieve higher sample efficiency than model‑free methods. Existing approaches are often grouped into four categories based on how the learned dynamics model is used: (i) Dyna‑style algorithms employ the model to generate imagined transitions and then apply off‑the‑shelf model‑free RL algorithms to update a policy with a mixture of real and imagined data; (ii) shooting methods use model‑predictive control to plan actions directly without learning an explicit policy; (iii) analytic‑gradient techniques back‑propagate through the model to compute policy gradients; and (iv) model‑augmented value‑expansion methods incorporate short model rollouts into temporal‑difference targets. The Dyna family is distinguished by its ability to reuse advances in model‑free RL while leveraging a learned model to boost data efficiency, and it therefore constitutes a major focus of recent research.  

Within Dyna‑style methods, several lines of work have sought to improve individual components of the learning loop. For model learning, deep ensembles have become a standard technique to mitigate overfitting and quantify uncertainty. Imagined data generation is commonly constrained to short rollouts to limit compounding model error, and uncertainty estimates are used to select reliable imagined transitions. Policy optimization has been explored with different data‑mixing strategies: some algorithms rely exclusively on imagined data, others fix a constant proportion of real versus imagined samples, and still others adapt this proportion dynamically based on the estimated uncertainty of the value function. A game‑theoretic formulation has also been proposed, casting model and policy updates as a two‑player game to encourage coordinated improvement.  

Research on automatic hyperparameter tuning for MBRL has explored population‑based training for shooting methods and meta‑learning frameworks that treat the scheduling of sampling and training operations as a reinforcement‑learning problem. These approaches aim to alleviate the manual burden of selecting rollout lengths, model‑training frequencies, and data‑mixing ratios, but they typically do not provide theoretical insight into why particular schedules are beneficial, and they often assume access to idealized initial states or rely on reward signals that differ from the true return of the underlying task.  

In contrast, the present work provides a principled analysis of how the proportion of real data influences the error bound of model‑based value iteration, showing that a gradually increasing real‑data ratio yields a tighter theoretical guarantee than a fixed ratio. Experiments on a suite of continuous‑control benchmarks demonstrate that the automatically tuned schedules substantially improve performance over manually designed configurations, and the discovered schedules corroborate the theoretical prediction that increasing reliance on real data over time is advantageous. This contribution advances the understanding of hyperparameter dynamics in Dyna‑style MBRL and offers a practical, theory‑guided solution for robust, sample‑efficient learning.

[ANSWER]: A substantial body of research has explored the incorporation of output constraints into structured‑prediction models through constrained decoding. In this paradigm, a model is trained without regard to constraints, and the decoding procedure is modified to produce outputs that satisfy a prescribed set of conditions, typically by conditioning the model’s distribution on the constraint set. Early work on constrained conditional random fields introduced positive and negative token‑wise constraints and developed a constrained Viterbi algorithm for maximum‑a‑posteriori inference as well as a constrained forward–backward algorithm for marginal inference, focusing on settings where constraints are unavailable during training.  

Other approaches treat constrained decoding as a search problem. For example, neural networks that predict token‑wise probabilities for semantic‑role labeling have been combined with exact A* search to enforce the BIO label schema and additional task‑specific constraints. In the context of autoregressive models, constrained beam search variants have been proposed to impose regular‑language constraints during decoding, guaranteeing that generated sequences belong to a predefined formal language.  

Beyond decoding, several lines of work have sought to weaken the Markov assumption of linear‑chain CRFs in order to capture long‑distance dependencies directly within the model. Semi‑Markov CRFs replace the first‑order Markov property with a semi‑Markov one, allowing each segment to depend on its immediate neighbors while permitting arbitrary internal structure within a segment. Skip‑chain CRFs augment the linear chain with explicit edges linking distant nodes that share particular properties (e.g., identical input values), thereby introducing loops into the factor graph. Because exact inference becomes intractable in such loopy models, approximate methods such as belief propagation and Gibbs sampling have been employed.  

A related research direction concerns the discovery of constraints from data, often framed as structure learning in probabilistic graphical models. Since a graph’s edges encode conditional independence relationships, learning the graph structure can be interpreted as learning latent constraints. Both global structure‑learning methods and local independence‑estimation techniques have been investigated, providing mechanisms to infer the underlying dependency topology without pre‑specified constraints.

The model‑based likelihood framework we adopt—Gaussian mixture components endowed with AR(1) autocorrelation—extends the static mixture‑of‑Gaussians setting to multivariate panel data. Coresets for clustering on static data are now a mature research area.  Results for k‑median, k‑means, and k‑center [10–19] show that, under mild assumptions, a weighted subset of points can approximate the original objective arbitrarily well.  These constructions rely on the fact that the objective decomposes as a sum of independent point contributions.  In contrast, the log‑likelihood of a Gaussian mixture with autocorrelations couples observations across time, preventing a naïve point‑wise decomposition.  Our contribution is to adapt the Feldman‑Langberg framework to this non‑separable setting by (i) proving that the influence of covariance and autocorrelation parameters can be uniformly bounded, and (ii) reducing the time‑series mixture problem to a b‑means clustering problem on a transformed point set.  This reduction enables us to bound the total sensitivity of entities and obtain a coreset whose size is independent of the number of entities N and the length of each series T.

Prior work on coresets for Gaussian‑mixture models with static observations [22, 23] achieves size bounds of order O(k d ε⁻²) under a bounded‑condition‑number assumption (and, in [23], additional integrality constraints).  These methods treat each observation as an isolated datum and therefore cannot capture temporal dependence.  Our algorithm extends the static‑GMM coreset theory to the multi‑observation, autocorrelated regime while retaining the same dependence on k, d, and ε.  By handling the full panel of observations per entity, we obtain a coreset whose size does not grow with N or T, a property absent from the static‑GMM results.

Coreset constructions for time‑series regression, notably the GLSE framework of [24], address a supervised learning problem where each entity‑time pair carries a label and the objective is additive over observations.  Their approach relies on a single weight function per entity‑time pair and assumes boundedness of the regression loss.  In our unsupervised clustering setting the log‑likelihood contains a product of Gaussian density terms and a mixing‑weight term, which together yield an unbounded per‑entity loss when means are far from the data.  To overcome this, we introduce a pair of weight functions—one for entities and one for time periods—allowing us to capture the interaction between the mixing weights and the Gaussian terms.  Moreover, by bounding the effect of covariances and autocorrelations we avoid the restrictive bounded‑loss assumption of [24] and prove a sensitivity bound that underpins our coreset size guarantee.

Finally, recent coresets for piecewise‑linear segmentation of a single time series [25, 26] exploit the additive nature of the segmentation loss across time points, which permits a reduction to static‑data coreset techniques.  Those works consider only one entity and an objective that is linear in the number of observations, whereas our problem involves many entities simultaneously clustered into latent mixture components.  Consequently, their techniques do not address the cross‑entity mixture structure or the autocorrelation coupling that we handle.  Our results thus broaden the applicability of coreset methodology from single‑series segmentation to multi‑entity, autocorrelated mixture clustering.

In summary, our work bridges three previously disconnected strands of research—time‑series model‑based clustering, static Gaussian‑mixture coresets, and coreset constructions for time‑dependent objectives—by providing the first provably accurate, size‑optimal coreset for Gaussian‑mixture clustering of multivariate panel data with autocorrelation.

[ANSWER]: Deep generative models, and in particular variational auto‑encoders (VAEs), formulate unsupervised representation learning as a probabilistic inference problem by introducing an approximate posterior over latent representations. Although VAEs have become a standard tool, their model parameters remain deterministic, which makes them vulnerable to poor local minima and over‑fitting to the training data. This deterministic treatment can limit generalisation performance and lead to unreliable uncertainty estimates.  

Bayesian neural networks (BNNs) address these shortcomings by placing probability distributions over the network weights, thereby propagating weight uncertainty to the data space. While BNNs can in principle provide calibrated uncertainties, their practical adoption for autoencoder‑style architectures has been hampered by high computational cost, the need for careful tuning, and complex implementation requirements. Consequently, alternative approaches such as deep ensembles, stochastic weight averaging (SWAG), and Monte‑Carlo dropout have been proposed as scalable approximations to the weight posterior. These methods, however, typically increase training time, may suffer from sub‑optimal empirical performance, or lack a rigorous Bayesian interpretation.  

The Laplace approximation (LA) offers a tractable post‑hoc strategy for approximating the intractable weight posterior after maximum‑a‑posteriori (MAP) training. Early work demonstrated that LA can be applied to classification and regression tasks, providing scalable uncertainty estimates and enabling marginal‑likelihood‑based model selection and invariance learning. To make LA computationally feasible, researchers have introduced diagonal, Kronecker‑factored, and other structured Hessian approximations, which have also found use in second‑order optimisation schemes. These approximations reduce the memory and runtime burden of handling full Hessian matrices while preserving many of the benefits of a Gaussian weight posterior.  

A fully Bayesian treatment of VAE weights was explored in prior work that combined VAEs with Hamiltonian Monte‑Carlo sampling to obtain posterior samples over the parameters. This line of research highlighted the potential of exact Bayesian inference for generative models but also underscored the difficulty of scaling Hamiltonian dynamics to large‑scale training regimes and the associated computational overhead.  

In this paper we introduce a Bayesian autoencoder framework that integrates a variational Laplace‑style approximation directly into the training objective, rather than applying it post‑hoc. By deriving a variational lower bound on the autoencoder evidence and maximising it with Monte‑Carlo EM, we obtain a tractable objective that jointly learns representations and weight uncertainty. [ANSWER]: Unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) seeks to transfer knowledge from labeled source domains to unlabeled target domains. Early theoretical analyses demonstrated that learning domain‑invariant representations can make a classifier trained on the source applicable to the target. Accordingly, many methods pursue domain invariance by directly minimizing a discrepancy between source and target distributions, using metrics such as the Maximum Mean Discrepancy, Central Moment Discrepancy, or other statistical distances. An alternative and increasingly dominant line of work employs domain‑adversarial learning, in which a domain discriminator is trained to distinguish source from target features while the feature extractor is encouraged to produce representations that confuse the discriminator. This adversarial formulation has become the backbone of most recent high‑performing UDA approaches.

Building on the seminal domain‑adversarial neural network (DANN), a large family of variants has been proposed to strengthen the alignment signal. Conditional adversarial networks condition the discriminator on class predictions, thereby injecting label‑related information into the alignment process. Multi‑discriminator designs allocate a separate domain classifier per class to achieve class‑wise alignment. Other extensions perform simultaneous alignment at multiple granularities (e.g., class, group, and domain) and enforce gradient consistency across these levels. Heuristic‑driven methods introduce domain‑specific representations or curriculum‑based sample selection to guide the alignment toward more transferable source instances. Collectively, these techniques refine the adversarial objective but retain the fundamental paradigm of aligning whole feature vectors across domains.

Despite the progress, most adversarial UDA methods treat domain alignment as an auxiliary task that runs in parallel with the primary classification objective. This separation can cause the alignment process to interfere with discriminative information, leading to a loss of class‑specific features. Several recent works have highlighted this issue: restoration modules have been added to recover discriminative cues after alignment; meta‑learning strategies have been employed to harmonize the optimization directions of alignment and classification; and explicit coordination mechanisms have been introduced to prevent contradictory updates. These efforts acknowledge the tension between alignment and classification but generally do not specify which components of the feature space should be aligned to best support the classification task.

A distinct line of research investigates feature decomposition as a means to separate domain‑related from domain‑unrelated information. For example, approaches that decouple features into domain‑invariant and domain‑specific parts have been applied to tasks such as unsupervised person re‑identification. However, such decompositions are typically driven by domain considerations rather than by the requirements of the downstream classification task, and they do not explicitly guide alignment toward task‑relevant sub‑features.

In this work we address the gap identified above by proposing a task‑oriented alignment framework. First, we emphasize that selecting the “right” features for alignment—those that are intrinsically discriminative for the classification task—is crucial for effective adaptation. To this end, we introduce a mechanism that decomposes each source feature into a task‑discriminative component and a task‑irrelevant component, using meta‑knowledge derived from the classification objective itself. Alignment is then performed exclusively on the discriminative components, while the irrelevant components are ignored, ensuring that domain alignment directly reinforces classification performance. The proposed approach can be seamlessly integrated with existing adversarial UDA methods, incurs negligible additional training cost, and does not affect inference complexity. Extensive experiments on standard benchmarks (Office‑Home, VisDA‑2017, DomainNet) demonstrate that the task‑oriented alignment consistently improves performance and achieves state‑of‑the‑art results across diverse adaptation settings.

ACM complements these approaches by explicitly providing a diversification channel that isolates high‑frequency information, and by mixing it with aggregation and identity channels through node‑wise learned coefficients, achieving comparable or superior performance without the instability associated with signed attention.

Early work in the “model‑retraining’’ family (e.g., [2]–[5]) imposes a dual objective: remain close to the original black‑box while satisfying a fairness constraint.  These methods typically rely on constrained optimisation or adversarial training, which limits their flexibility to accommodate many fairness notions and often requires access to the original training data.  In contrast, our technique operates purely as a wrapper around a fixed predictor, requiring no retraining or data access, and therefore directly addresses desideratum (a) – the ability to handle a broad spectrum of fairness metrics – while also satisfying (b) through provable proximity guarantees between the original and modified posteriors.

A second line of research modifies the classifier’s outputs at inference time, either by adjusting decision thresholds ([6]–[10]) or by learning a mapping from predictions to fair outcomes ([5], [6]).  These approaches achieve pointwise fairness guarantees but rarely provide systematic bounds on how far the transformed distribution deviates from the original, nor do they offer composability when multiple fairness corrections are applied sequentially.  Our contribution fills this gap: by learning an α‑tree wrapper based on the α‑loss, we obtain explicit KL‑divergence bounds (addressing (b) and (c)), a clean composability property (addressing (e)), and an interpretable tree‑shaped representation (addressing (d)). Our approach differs fundamentally: rather than combining multiple black‑boxes, we construct a single, lightweight α‑tree that directly modifies the output of any black‑box. Our empirical evaluation on conditional value‑at‑risk, equality of opportunity, and statistical parity further confirms that the proposed α‑tree boosters outperform existing baselines across diverse datasets.

A prominent family of offline RL algorithms avoids value functions altogether by framing the problem as conditional behavior cloning. Goal‑conditioned behavior cloning learns policies that map states and desired goals to actions, demonstrating strong performance on benchmark suites [11, 12, 13]. Reward‑conditioned behavior cloning similarly conditions on scalar reward values or reward functions, enabling a single policy to serve multiple tasks [14, 15, 16]. These methods treat the offline dataset as supervised training data, leveraging simple imitation objectives to produce competent policies without explicit value estimation.

Beyond goals and rewards, prior work has explored conditioning on richer contextual information. Some approaches condition on multiple past timesteps, providing the policy with a short history of observations and actions to capture temporal dependencies [17, 18]. Other studies infer task representations through inverse reinforcement learning, then condition the policy on these latent task embeddings [19]. Additional task‑specific signals, such as language instructions or symbolic descriptors, have also been incorporated as conditioning inputs [20, 21].

A subset of conditional imitation methods extends to interactive settings by coupling policy learning with iterative data collection. In these frameworks, the learned policy is periodically deployed to gather new trajectories, which are then added to the training set [15, 11]. While effective in online or semi‑online regimes, such iterative refinement is incompatible with the strict offline RL setting where only a fixed dataset is available.

Reward‑conditioned policies have been examined specifically within the offline context. One line of research reported that reward conditioning alone was insufficient for high performance, arguing that additional advantage weighting—where trajectories are re‑weighted by estimated advantage values—was necessary to achieve competitive results [14, 22, 23]. More recent work introduced high‑capacity autoregressive Transformer policies for conditional imitation learning in offline RL. Moreover, the analysis shows that conditioning on goals versus rewards leads to complementary strengths across environments, underscoring the importance of task‑specific conditioning decisions. These findings clarify the essential ingredients of reinforcement learning via supervised learning, delineate its limitations on datasets with scarce near‑optimal trajectories, and provide a practical guide for deploying simple yet effective offline RL algorithms.

[ANSWER]: Hierarchical reinforcement learning (HRL) builds on the success of macro‑operators and abstraction in classical planning, inspiring a substantial body of work that decomposes control across multiple levels of abstraction.  Early approaches emphasized the intuitive benefits of such decompositions—simpler sub‑problems and the ability to make long‑term decisions—but more recent analyses have highlighted that, for modern neural‑network‑based agents, the principal advantage of HRL often lies in its enhanced exploration capabilities.  By separating the acquisition of low‑level policies (options or skills) from high‑level decision making, HRL can dramatically accelerate learning on downstream tasks.

A diverse set of methods has been proposed for discovering low‑level primitives.  Some techniques rely on random walk data to identify useful behaviours, while others formulate mutual‑information objectives that encourage diversity among options.  Additional strands of research exploit datasets of agent or expert trajectories, motion‑capture recordings, or dedicated pre‑training tasks to shape the skill space.  These approaches differ in the source of supervision and the assumptions they make about the environment, yet they share the goal of producing reusable behaviours that can be composed by higher‑level policies.

The usefulness of learned skills across many downstream tasks is constrained by a trade‑off between generality and specificity.  Many prior works resolve this trade‑off in favour of specificity, often by selecting benchmark domains that align closely with the induced prior.  Classic navigation problems in grid‑world mazes and simulated robotic locomotion tasks dominate the evaluation landscape, where translating the robot’s centre of mass is the primary required skill.  In such settings, skills are frequently defined by partitioning the state space according to the agent’s position or by leveraging position‑heavy reward signals, thereby embedding an explicit locomotion prior.  Other studies that address non‑navigation environments introduce tailored pre‑training objectives or rely on in‑domain motion‑capture data to bias skill acquisition toward particular behaviours.

In contrast, recent efforts have begun to explore skill discovery without external supervision or task‑specific pre‑training designs, aiming to learn low‑level behaviours that do not encode a fixed bias toward any single type of motion.  These works seek to retain flexibility in the skill set, allowing downstream tasks to select the most appropriate behaviours dynamically rather than being constrained by a predetermined prior.  

Building on these lines of research, the present work proposes an unsupervised pre‑training framework that generates a hierarchy of skills with increasing complexity, each controlling a variable subset of the robot’s configuration.  A three‑level hierarchical policy is introduced to automatically select among these skills, determine target configurations, and execute the corresponding low‑level actions, thereby enabling dynamic trade‑offs between generality and specificity during downstream learning.  To evaluate the approach, a benchmark suite of sparse‑reward tasks for bipedal robots is released, extending assessment beyond traditional navigation problems and facilitating systematic comparison of motor‑skill and HRL methods.  Extensive experiments demonstrate how prior knowledge embedded in skills affects exploration efficiency, and show that the proposed hierarchical skill framework achieves superior performance relative to existing unsupervised skill discovery and hierarchical RL baselines.
