[ANSWER]: Tagger introduced an unsupervised perceptual‑grouping framework that employs multiple copies of a neural network to reconstruct distinct portions of an input and explicitly outputs a grouping mask. By learning the segmentation masks jointly with the reconstruction, Tagger attains fine‑grained control over the segmentation process and has been applied successfully to complex texture‑segmentation problems. A recurrent extension, RTagger, later incorporated temporal recurrence to enable the model to process sequential data, thereby broadening the scope of Tagger‑style grouping to video and other time‑varying domains.

The binding problem, first articulated in neuroscience, concerns how distributed, feature‑based representations can be combined without ambiguity. Early computational approaches addressed the issue with oscillatory neural networks that exploited synchronization as a grouping cue, and subsequent work replaced explicit oscillations with complex‑valued activations to achieve similar effects. More recent studies have shown that generic recurrent networks can, in principle, learn binding mechanisms, but practical training often requires additional inductive biases such as competitive interactions, fast‑weight memories, or dedicated perceptual‑grouping modules to facilitate reliable binding.

Unsupervised segmentation has been explored across a range of settings, from random‑vector clustering and texture segmentation to full‑image decomposition. Early video‑segmentation methods applied generalized Expectation‑Maximization to infer object splits in moving sprite sequences. Later approaches leveraged optical‑flow cues to train convolutional networks for figure‑ground segmentation, while the multi‑causal modelling literature formalized perceptual grouping as inference in compositional generative models of images. Masked Restricted Boltzmann Machines extended the RBM framework with latent masks inferred via block‑Gibbs sampling, providing another probabilistic route to unsupervised part discovery.

Gradient back‑propagation through inference procedures has been investigated primarily in the context of sparse coding. Algorithms such as (Fast) Iterative Shrinkage/Thresholding (ISTA/FISTA) have been unrolled into fixed‑depth computational graphs, and recurrent neural networks have been trained to predict sparse codes directly, effectively learning to approximate the iterative updates. Building on this idea, recurrent variants of Expectation‑Maximization have been derived by unrolling the EM steps into trainable recurrent modules, yielding architectures that retain the structure of iterative pursuit while exposing learnable parameters; some designs further untie weights across iterations to increase flexibility, whereas others keep weights shared to preserve stability.

In this work we formalize perceptual grouping as inference in a spatial mixture model whose components are parameterized by neural networks, and we derive a fully differentiable clustering algorithm based on the Expectation‑Maximization principle. The resulting Neural Expectation‑Maximization (N‑EM) method learns to both discover and represent individual entities without supervision, using the posterior of the E‑step as an implicit grouping signal. By keeping the inference mechanism tightly coupled to EM, the approach admits a clear theoretical analysis and permits the use of comparatively small networks relative to Tagger, while still achieving accurate segmentation. Extending N‑EM with recurrent hidden‑state dynamics yields a sequential model capable of next‑step prediction, addressing the limitations of Tagger’s static architecture and matching the temporal capabilities introduced by RTagger. Moreover, the method integrates insights from the binding‑problem literature by providing a principled mechanism for separating distributed representations, and it connects to the broader unsupervised segmentation and inference‑through‑back‑prop literature by unrolling EM updates in a trainable recurrent framework. Empirical results demonstrate that the learned representations are both faithful to the underlying objects and useful for downstream predictive tasks, positioning the proposed approach as a compact, theoretically grounded alternative to existing perceptual‑grouping and unsupervised‑segmentation models.

Existing methods are commonly divided into two-stage and one-stage paradigms. Two-stage pipelines typically begin by pre‑training a strong object detector, such as Faster‑RCNN [13], to obtain bounding boxes and visual features for all object categories in the dataset. A separate graph generation network is then built on top of these detector outputs, with the detector parameters frozen during graph learning. Various architectures have been employed for the second stage, including bi‑directional LSTMs [12], Tree‑LSTMs [8], graph neural networks [10], and other message‑passing schemes [6], [9]. A limitation of this design is that the graph generation component cannot influence the detector or the extracted object features. One-stage approaches address this issue by enabling end‑to‑end training of detection and graph generation modules. Examples include fully convolutional networks [4] and transformer‑based models [14], [3], which allow joint optimization and have been shown to produce more coherent scene graphs. However, many of these methods rely on fixed factorized models that impose conditional independencies, which may not be optimal in all settings.  

The long‑tail distribution of object and predicate categories poses a significant challenge for scene graph generation, as the combinatorial space of relational triplets leads to highly skewed class frequencies. Long‑tail recognition has been extensively studied across visual tasks, with data sampling strategies such as oversampling tail classes or undersampling head classes being widely adopted [15]–[21]. In the context of scene graphs, works such as [1] and [22] have applied sampling techniques to improve performance on rare predicates. Complementary to sampling, loss re‑weighting methods assign larger weights or enforce wider decision boundaries for under‑represented classes [23]–[26]. A recent contribution [27] introduced a re‑weighting scheme that leverages correlations between predicate classes to address the imbalance in scene graph generation.  

Transformers, originally introduced for machine translation as an attention‑based architecture that dispenses with recurrent or convolutional components [28], have since been adapted to numerous vision tasks, including object detection [29]–[31], image captioning [32], [33], and image generation [34]. Their capacity for parallel processing and end‑to‑end training has motivated their adoption in scene graph generation as well [14], [3]. In visual relation detection, [14] employs a composite decoding strategy that jointly predicts the subject, predicate, and object of a relationship triplet. Another line of work [3] first generates a set of entity and predicate proposals independently and then assembles them into triplets via a graph matching procedure, which does not condition entity predictions on predicate estimates. Both approaches illustrate the flexibility of transformer‑based designs for modeling visual relationships.

[ANSWER]: Early ensemble‑distillation methods focused on reproducing only the average output of a teacher ensemble.  These works showed that a single neural network can be trained to mimic the mean predictions of a large collection of models, typically by minimizing a cross‑entropy loss against the ensemble’s soft targets or by using a convex combination of the teachers’ outputs.  While effective for improving speed at test time, such approaches do not preserve the variability among ensemble members, which limits their usefulness for uncertainty quantification.  Representative examples include the original demonstrations that a student network can learn the knowledge of a big ensemble, methods that augment the standard loss with a convex combination of teacher predictions, and online student‑teacher schemes where the teacher is obtained via Markov‑chain Monte‑Carlo training.  

Subsequent research introduced techniques aimed at capturing the diversity of the teacher ensemble.  Ensemble Distribution Distillation (EnDD) was among the first to model the full predictive distribution by fitting a Dirichlet‑parameterized network to the ensemble outputs.  Building on this idea, later works also assumed a Dirichlet form for the predictive distribution, learning separate networks for the Dirichlet mean (class probabilities) and concentration (confidence).  To mitigate over‑confidence and low diversity on the training set, these methods employed unsupervised auxiliary data and temperature‑annealing schedules.  Although these approaches improve uncertainty estimates, they remain restricted to classification tasks and rely on the Dirichlet assumption, which can be overly limiting for more general predictive scenarios.  

Another line of work extended the basic distillation framework by assigning each teacher member a dedicated task head while sharing a common backbone.  In this setting the backbone learns a shared representation, and each head is trained to reproduce the predictions of a specific ensemble member using standard cross‑entropy loss.  Weight‑sharing strategies such as BatchEnsemble have also been incorporated, together with data‑perturbation schemes—including Gaussian noise, Output‑Diversified Sampling (ODS), and confidence‑aware ODS—to increase diversity among the heads on the training data.  These perturbation‑based methods, however, introduce additional computational overhead because they require per‑iteration generation of adversarial‑like perturbations, making training slower and less scalable to large ensembles.  

In contrast, the proposed approach introduces a flexible functional ensemble distillation framework that captures both the predictive mean and the full covariance structure of the teacher ensemble without restricting the predictive distribution to a Dirichlet form.  By transferring stochasticity to a latent noise variable, the distilled model can generate diverse function samples and compute inter‑prediction covariances, which are valuable for downstream tasks such as correlated object‑detection decisions.  To address the common over‑fitting regime where ensemble members achieve near‑zero training loss yet exhibit divergent test‑time behavior, the method leverages mixup augmentation to create an auxiliary dataset that is both sufficiently different from the original training set to elicit diverse teacher predictions and sufficiently close to preserve performance on the target domain.  This auxiliary data is generated without requiring any external unlabeled samples, keeping the pipeline simple and scalable.  Extensive experiments on several image‑classification benchmarks demonstrate that the resulting distilled model attains superior accuracy, calibration, and uncertainty estimation compared with prior ensemble‑distillation techniques, while remaining computationally efficient at inference time.

A parallel line of research framed diffusion‑based generation as a multi‑scale denoising score‑matching problem and extended the methodology to continuous time. By interpreting the diffusion as a stochastic differential equation, these works derived sampling algorithms that reverse the forward diffusion process, enabling efficient generation without discretising the time axis [7, 8]. The continuous‑time perspective also opened the door to novel theoretical analyses of diffusion models.

These datasets enable the training of deep networks that predict heatmaps for predefined joint or landmark locations, achieving high accuracy when sufficient labeled examples are provided. The reliance on extensive manual annotation, however, limits the scalability of such approaches to new object categories or domains where annotated data are scarce.  

Unsupervised landmark discovery methods avoid explicit keypoint labels by exploiting geometric or photometric consistency. Early work introduced equivariance constraints, enforcing that landmark coordinates remain stable under synthetic transformations or across video frames. Subsequent approaches learned viewpoint‑independent representations that are equivariant to a variety of transformations, or used optical‑flow coherence as a self‑supervisory signal. Other methods imposed structural properties on learned landmarks, such as separability and concentration, while generative models encouraged reconstruction of the original image from predicted heatmaps of transformed copies. More recent techniques enforce inter‑instance consistency by swapping descriptor vectors between images of the same object class. These unsupervised strategies have primarily been evaluated on facial images, which exhibit limited pose variability compared with full‑body human or animal joints.  

Semi‑supervised learning has been extensively studied for image classification, where unlabeled data are leveraged alongside a small labeled subset. Pseudo‑labeling assigns model predictions as artificial targets for unlabeled examples, while consistency regularization penalizes changes in predictions under realistic input perturbations. Variants such as Temporal Ensembling and Mean Teacher maintain moving averages of predictions or model weights to provide stable targets. State‑of‑the‑art frameworks like UDA, ReMixMatch, and FixMatch combine consistency losses with sophisticated data augmentations, including color jittering and spatial transformations, to improve performance on classification benchmarks.  

Applying semi‑supervised ideas to keypoint localization remains relatively under‑explored. One line of work extends consistency‑based pseudo‑labeling to facial landmarks by introducing a teacher model and multiple student networks that generate more reliable pseudo‑labels for unlabeled images. While effective for faces, the limited pose diversity in facial datasets raises concerns about the robustness of pseudo‑labels when confronted with the larger variations typical of human or animal bodies. Other studies incorporate auxiliary annotations—such as action labels for human joints or emotion tags for facial keypoints—to guide semi‑supervised learning, but these approaches depend on additional class information that is not always available.  

In contrast, the present work proposes a semi‑supervised keypoint localization framework that jointly learns heatmap predictions and low‑dimensional semantic keypoint representations. By enforcing a transformation‑equivariant constraint on heatmaps and a transformation‑invariant constraint on semantic vectors, the method captures both spatial precision and pose‑agnostic identity of landmarks. A semantic consistency loss further encourages features of the same anatomical point to be similar across diverse images, without requiring any auxiliary class labels. The approach can be attached to existing keypoint detectors with minimal architectural changes and computational overhead. Extensive experiments on both human and animal benchmark datasets demonstrate that, even with a modest amount of labeled data, the proposed method surpasses prior fully supervised, unsupervised, and semi‑supervised techniques, establishing a new state of the art for keypoint localization under limited annotation conditions.

[ANSWER]: Post‑processing of pretrained classifiers is one of the three principal families of approaches that have been proposed to reconcile accuracy with fairness requirements in machine learning systems [1]. Within this family, researchers have distinguished three sub‑categories: (I) methods that learn a new model while enforcing proximity to the original black‑box and fairness constraints; (II) techniques that modify the predictions of the black‑box at inference time in order to satisfy a fairness criterion; and (III) strategies that combine multiple models to obtain a fair aggregate predictor [11].

The first sub‑category comprises approaches that jointly optimize a fidelity term measuring the distance between the new model and the pretrained predictor and a fairness regularizer. Early work on this theme introduced convex formulations that enforce statistical parity or equalized odds while penalizing deviation from the original decision boundary [2, 3]. Subsequent papers extended the idea to richer notions of fairness, such as conditional value‑at‑risk and demographic parity, and explored kernel‑based and neural‑network implementations that preserve predictive performance [4, 5]. All of these methods rely on access to the training data and often require solving a constrained optimization problem that couples the fairness and proximity objectives.

The second sub‑category focuses on altering the output distribution of a fixed classifier at classification time. A line of work proposes deterministic or stochastic post‑processing maps that reweight or relabel predictions so that the resulting decisions satisfy a prescribed fairness metric [6, 7, 8, 9, 10]. Some techniques operate by learning a calibrated score‑adjustment function, while others employ linear programming or optimal transport to redistribute probability mass across protected groups. These methods are attractive when the underlying model is a black‑box or when training data are unavailable, but they typically target a single fairness definition and provide limited theoretical guarantees beyond empirical fairness improvement.

The third sub‑category exploits ensembles of classifiers to achieve fairness. By aggregating the outputs of several models—often trained with diverse fairness constraints—or by selecting a subset of models that together satisfy a fairness criterion, these approaches aim to inherit the strengths of each constituent predictor [11]. Ensemble‑based methods have been shown to improve trade‑offs between accuracy and multiple fairness notions, yet they introduce additional computational overhead and may require access to the internal predictions of each model in the pool.

Across the three sub‑categories, several desiderata identified in the literature have been addressed to varying extents. Works such as [12] and [4] provide mechanisms that are flexible enough to accommodate multiple fairness metrics (point a) and, in some cases, derive analytic conditions that guarantee the applicability of new fairness definitions (point c). However, the algorithmic cost of these guarantees is often high, relying on convex‑optimization solvers or large‑scale linear programs, which can hinder scalability (point d). Consistency and generalization results have been established for a subset of post‑processing schemes, notably those based on calibrated score adjustments, thereby offering assurances related to proximity between the original and modified predictors when fairness constraints are mild (point b) [6, 5]. Composability—i.e., the ability to apply successive post‑processing steps for different fairness notions—has received limited attention, and existing proposals typically lack formal composition theorems (point e). Generalization bounds based on Rademacher complexity or uniform convergence have been derived for certain convex formulations, but they often assume restrictive model classes or specific loss functions (point f).

To the best of our knowledge, none of the prior post‑processing methods have leveraged the α‑loss (an improper loss function) and its theoretical property of being able to correct any systematic twist in probability estimates, including unfairness. This observation motivates a new line of investigation that exploits the corrective potential of improper losses for fairness‑aware post‑processing.

In this work we introduce a family of post‑processing techniques that build on the α‑loss to obtain fair predictions from any black‑box classifier. We define α‑trees, a class of interpretable tree‑shaped correction functions, and present two generic boosting algorithms for learning them. Our analysis establishes (a) flexibility across a broad range of fairness notions, (b) proximity guarantees between the original and corrected posteriors when fairness requirements are light, (c) strong algorithmic guarantees on achieving the desired fairness constraints, (d) interpretability through the explicit tree structure of the correction, (e) composability of successive α‑tree wrappers, and (f) generalization bounds derived via Rademacher complexity of the α‑tree class. These techniques follow a general blueprint that allows for arbitrary base classifiers, though they often rely on specially trained models. More generally, isotropic continuous randomization schemes have been employed to leverage comprehensive results on randomized smoothing, providing robustness guarantees against a broad spectrum of \(\ell_p\)-norm bounded adversaries.

This interdependence limits the applicability of approaches that exploit feature independence.

Complete robustness certification of tree ensembles in the \(\ell_p\)-norm setting has been explored via mixed‑integer linear programming (MILP). While MILP provides exact certificates, its Co‑NP‑complete complexity renders it intractable for most practical settings. These methods achieve fast certification but may produce weaker certificates compared to alternatives that exploit more refined analyses. Additional incomplete certification techniques for tree ensembles have been proposed, based on computing distances between the pre‑image of all tree leaves and the original sample; however, empirical evaluations have shown these approaches to yield comparatively poorer results.

[ANSWER]: FedAvg is the canonical algorithm for federated learning because of its simplicity and low communication overhead.  However, when client data are highly heterogeneous, FedAvg can exhibit unstable training dynamics and converge to sub‑optimal solutions.  Existing analyses of FedAvg under heterogeneity rely on restrictive assumptions such as bounded gradients or similarity of local Hessians, which are violated in many realistic settings.  In contrast, our work establishes global convergence of a two‑phase federated algorithm for mixed‑regression problems without requiring any of these assumptions, and it remains provably effective even when a substantial fraction of clients possess only a constant number of data points.  

A large body of work seeks to mitigate heterogeneity by learning a single global model and augmenting FedAvg with variance‑reduction, normalization, or adaptive stepsizes.  While these techniques improve empirical stability, their theoretical guarantees typically depend on strong technical conditions (e.g., uniform gradient boundedness) and they seldom address the generalization gap between the global model and heterogeneous local distributions.  By moving away from the common‑model paradigm, our approach directly targets the underlying cluster structure of the data, providing a provably optimal trade‑off between communication efficiency and statistical accuracy that holds for arbitrary initializations and unbalanced local sample sizes.  

Methods that aim for fully personalized models, such as federated multi‑task learning and model‑agnostic meta‑learning, face fundamental challenges: the joint optimization problem is non‑convex, convergence results are limited to balanced or highly constrained settings, and they often ignore per‑client generalization error.  Our algorithm sidesteps these difficulties by clustering clients that share the same regression parameter, thereby reducing the effective problem dimension while still delivering individualized models.  Crucially, we prove that each client’s model converges to the true cluster parameter even when the client contributes as few as one or two samples, a regime that lies beyond the reach of existing personalized‑learning guarantees.  

Prior clustered federated learning methods either perform clustering as a post‑processing step, require sequential solution of multiple empirical risk minimization problems, or assume balanced, large local datasets and strong convexity.  Many of these approaches are heuristic, lack convergence proofs, or scale poorly with input dimension.  Our contribution is a unified algorithm that simultaneously learns cluster assignments and refines cluster‑specific models in an alternating fashion.  The method leverages a small set of “anchor” clients with modest sample sizes to obtain coarse estimates via federated moment descent, after which all clients iteratively update their cluster labels and model parameters using FedAvg or FedProx.  This design eliminates the need for balanced data, avoids costly sequential optimization, and is supported by a rigorous analysis that guarantees convergence from any starting point.  

The mixed‑regression formulation that underlies our problem has been studied in the statistics literature, often assuming that each client supplies only a single observation or that the data are evenly distributed across clusters.  Recent works on mixed regression in federated or meta‑learning contexts impose strong initialization requirements, balanced data, or rely on sample‑splitting across iterations, leading to exponential dependence on dimension and cluster count.  Our analysis departs from these assumptions by introducing an eigengap‑free bound for subspace estimation and a novel uniform bound on clustering errors derived from VC‑dimension arguments for polynomial concept classes.  These technical innovations enable us to isolate the dominant source of error—uniform deviation of clustering decisions—and to prove that the overall estimation error scales favorably with the number of anchor clients, irrespective of the extreme imbalance in the remaining population.  

Together, these contributions position our work as the first federated learning framework for clustered personalized models that offers global convergence guarantees under minimal data‑balance assumptions, provides explicit uniform error controls for clustering, and operates effectively with arbitrarily poor initializations.

[ANSWER]: Temporal side information and non‑stationarities have recently been exploited to obtain identifiability in nonlinear ICA.  The earliest result of this line, time‑contrastive learning (TCL) [1], showed that independent sources can be recovered from non‑stationary data segments by enforcing a contrastive objective.  Subsequent work introduced permutation‑based contrastive learning (PCL) [2], which leverages temporal dependencies to separate independent sources under a uniformly‑dependent assumption.  More generally, a hidden‑Markov‑model formulation was combined with nonlinear ICA to model non‑stationarity without manual segmentation [3], and a VAE‑based approach incorporated auxiliary non‑stationary variables, assuming exponential‑family conditionals for identifiability [4].  All of these methods share the restriction that the latent factors must be jointly independent; they do not address the recovery of latent variables that interact causally over time.  In contrast, our framework lifts the independence requirement and establishes identifiability for latent processes that are conditionally independent given their time‑delayed causal parents, thereby broadening the applicability of nonlinear ICA to settings with genuine temporal causality.

A parallel strand of research has focused on using temporal structure to separate independent sources through contrastive objectives.  The PCL method [2] learns to discriminate between correctly ordered and permuted time windows, achieving identifiability when the sources satisfy a uniformly‑dependent condition.  Other approaches have extended this idea by incorporating non‑stationary segmentation or hidden‑Markov dynamics [3], yet they remain limited to independent latent variables and typically require strong assumptions about sparsity or the number of observed children per latent factor.  Our contribution diverges from these works by explicitly modelling time‑delayed causal relations among the latent processes.  We prove that, under either a non‑parametric non‑stationary regime or a parametric regime with known functional forms, the causal latent processes and their directed influences are uniquely recoverable from invertible nonlinear mixtures, without relying on sparsity or minimality constraints.

Recent efforts have begun to integrate causal structure into nonlinear ICA.  A linear causal layer was introduced to transform independent exogenous factors into endogenous causal variables [5], and several VAE‑based models have incorporated auxiliary variables to aid identifiability [4].  However, these approaches either assume linear causal mechanisms, retain the joint‑independence of the underlying sources, or lack rigorous identifiability guarantees for nonlinear, time‑delayed causal dynamics.  Our work advances this line by embedding a causal‑process prior within a variational auto‑encoding architecture (LEAP) that enforces the Independent Noise condition and captures non‑stationarity via flow‑based estimators.  This design yields provable identifiability of temporally causal latent processes from their nonlinear mixtures and demonstrates superior empirical performance on synthetic and real‑world datasets, marking one of the first successful unsupervised recoveries of time‑delayed latent causal dynamics without sparsity or minimality assumptions.

[ANSWER]: Combining reinforcement learning with behavior cloning has been explored as a way to accelerate learning from demonstrations. Early works used behavior‑cloning losses as regularizers for policy‑gradient methods, natural‑policy‑gradient, and actor‑critic algorithms, often augmenting the replay buffer with demonstration data or pre‑training the policy before RL updates. More recent baselines such as SAC + BC and PPO + BC have demonstrated that a simple imitation term can improve performance on offline benchmarks, although they typically rely on additional engineering such as separate pre‑training phases or modified buffer sampling strategies.

Imitation learning has also been integrated with reinforcement learning through a variety of mechanisms beyond direct behavior cloning. Adversarial imitation techniques, for example, train a discriminator to shape the reward signal, while other approaches employ demonstrations for pre‑training, alter the replay buffer composition, or modify the value‑function updates to incorporate imitation cues. These methods generally aim to mitigate exploration challenges or to speed up convergence by leveraging expert trajectories, but they often introduce extra components such as adversarial networks or specialized training schedules.

Offline reinforcement learning algorithms predominantly address the extrapolation error that arises from out‑of‑distribution actions by constraining the learned policy to remain close to the behavior policy. Strategies include explicit behavior‑policy parameterizations, divergence‑based regularizers (e.g., KL, MMD, or Wasserstein penalties), and weighted behavior‑cloning objectives that prioritize high‑advantage actions. Some methods restrict the action space using count‑based or learned behavior‑policy masks, while others embed pessimism directly into the value estimates through conservative Q‑learning or similar techniques. Across these approaches, additional hyper‑parameters and auxiliary models (such as generative networks) are commonly employed to enforce the constraint.

A growing body of meta‑analyses has examined the impact of implementation details on the performance of both online and offline RL algorithms. Studies have highlighted how subtle choices—such as network architecture, optimizer settings, or data normalisation—can account for apparent algorithmic improvements, sometimes obscuring the true source of gains. Analyses of off‑policy methods have shown that co‑adapted implementation tricks are crucial for reproducing reported results, and that many high‑performing offline methods rely on extensive engineering beyond the core algorithmic ideas.

In this work we introduce a minimalist offline RL method that augments the TD3 algorithm with a single behavior‑cloning term in the policy update and applies standard state normalisation. By adding only one hyper‑parameter to balance the imitation loss, we retain the original TD3 dynamics while enforcing proximity to the dataset, thereby addressing extrapolation error without resorting to explicit behavior‑policy models, divergence penalties, or auxiliary networks. Our approach eliminates the need for complex replay‑buffer manipulations, generative components, or extensive hyper‑parameter tuning, resulting in a method that matches or exceeds state‑of‑the‑art performance on benchmark tasks while halving computational overhead. This contribution demonstrates that careful, low‑complexity modifications can achieve competitive offline performance, complementing prior work on RL + BC, imitation‑augmented RL, and constrained offline RL, and underscores the importance of scrutinising implementation simplicity in future algorithmic design.

[ANSWER]: Recent advances in neural machine translation (NMT) have yielded outputs that approach professional human quality in constrained domains, yet the inherent uncertainty of automatically generated text remains a concern. Studies have shown that even high‑performing NMT systems can produce errors that are difficult for end‑users to detect without additional verification mechanisms, motivating research on user‑facing feedback that can signal translation reliability and suggest corrective actions.

Interactive machine translation (IMT) has primarily been investigated in post‑editing environments, where translators revise machine‑generated drafts, and in computer‑assisted translation settings that aim to accelerate or enhance human translation effort. This body of work emphasizes tight coupling between the user and the translation output, assuming that the user possesses sufficient proficiency in the target language to make substantive edits. Consequently, most IMT approaches focus on scenarios in which the user can directly manipulate the target‑side text.

A distinct line of research addresses outbound translation, in which authors must convey messages in a language they do not speak. Early work explored Czech–German translation for question‑asking and reformulation tasks, highlighting the challenges of providing useful cues to non‑target‑language speakers. A subsequent preliminary study examined the impact of translation cues such as backward translation and word‑level quality estimation, but its limited participant pool, reliance on non‑native English speakers, and small annotation set constrained the generalizability of its findings, particularly regarding the effectiveness of fine‑grained quality signals.

Building on these strands of literature, the present study extends the investigation of outbound translation by (i) evaluating three feedback mechanisms—backward translation, quality estimation with alignment, and source‑side paraphrasing—across multiple MT system quality levels; (ii) employing a substantially larger and more diverse participant sample in an e‑commerce context; (iii) collecting both self‑reported confidence scores and expert assessments of fluency and adequacy; and (iv) analyzing how each cue influences user confidence and objective translation quality. This comprehensive experimental design addresses the gaps identified in prior work on feedback effectiveness, user proficiency assumptions, and scalability of outbound translation evaluations.

[ANSWER]: Since the introduction of multi‑hop reasoning benchmarks such as HotpotQA, a variety of architectures have been proposed. Graph‑based networks construct explicit reasoning graphs over retrieved sentences or entities, enabling the model to propagate information across multiple hops (e.g., Graft‑Net, Graph‑based Reasoning Network). External‑knowledge retrieval methods first select a set of relevant passages from large corpora and then perform reasoning over the retrieved texts, often using dense retrieval or TF‑IDF based heuristics. Supporting‑fact selection approaches treat the identification of the sentences that justify the answer as a supervised sub‑task, training classifiers to predict which sentences constitute the gold supporting facts.

A separate line of work has highlighted that models can achieve high answer accuracy by exploiting superficial patterns rather than performing genuine multi‑step inference. Similar “shortcut” phenomena have been reported in object detection, natural language inference, and multi‑hop QA, where models learn heuristic rules that correlate answer types or surface cues with the correct label. These shortcuts undermine the interpretability and robustness of the systems.

To counteract shortcut behavior, researchers have explored adversarial training and data augmentation. Synthetic adversarial examples that break spurious correlations are generated to force the model to rely on deeper reasoning. Another strategy augments supervision with paragraph‑level sufficiency signals, teaching the model to recognize whether a pair of paragraphs jointly contain enough information for a correct answer. This binary classification task is relatively easy to learn and has been shown to reduce paragraph‑level shortcuts.

More fine‑grained supervision has been pursued through sentence‑level evidence annotation. Early approaches train models to predict supporting sentences using human‑annotated evidence, treating evidentiality as a supervised classification problem. While effective, such methods require costly annotation pipelines and are limited to the coverage of the annotated data.

Despite these advances, there remains a gap between coarse paragraph‑sufficiency supervision and fully supervised sentence‑level evidence selection: a need for methods that can assess the evidential contribution of individual sentences without relying on explicit annotations. Existing attention‑based pseudo‑labels provide a weak signal but lack causal grounding, and recent critiques emphasize the importance of counterfactual analysis to establish true sentence causality.

In this work, we introduce a framework that learns evidentiality without any human evidence annotations. By constructing evidence‑positive and evidence‑negative training instances through counterfactual manipulation of answer confidence, we generate pseudo‑evidentiality labels that capture the causal impact of sentence groups on predictions. Our approach leverages an interpreter module to remove and aggregate candidate evidences, comparing model behavior in observational and counterfactual settings. To encourage the model to be confident on evidence‑positive instances while remaining uncertain on evidence‑negative ones, we formulate two complementary objectives and employ selective regularization that decorrelates the target model from a deliberately biased auxiliary model. Evaluated on HotpotQA and its challenge set, our method achieves higher accuracy and robustness to reasoning shortcuts than prior graph‑based, retrieval‑based, and evidence‑selection baselines, and it can be combined orthogonally with existing state‑of‑the‑art systems for further gains.

[ANSWER]: Early flow-based variational inference methods such as planar flows introduced simple, analytically tractable bijections that operate on low‑dimensional vectors [1]. Sylvester flows extended this idea by employing upper‑triangular and orthogonal matrices, enabling the Jacobian determinant to be computed efficiently via Sylvester’s identity [2]. While both families share the goal of preserving tractable likelihoods, they are limited to vector‑valued inputs and rely on matrix structures (triangularity, orthogonality) that complicate the inverse computation, often requiring iterative solvers [3, 4, 5]. In contrast, our Woodbury transformations act directly on matrix‑shaped data (e.g., images), avoid restrictive matrix parametrizations, and provide a closed‑form inverse through the Woodbury matrix identity. This makes our approach a true matrix‑level generalization of planar‑type flows that retains exact invertibility without resorting to approximation or costly iteration.

A large body of work has sought to enrich the expressiveness of normalizing flows by introducing invertible convolutions that couple spatial and channel dimensions. 1 × 1 convolutions [6] and their variants (emerging convolutions [7], periodic convolutions [8]) increase representational power by using dense kernels, yet they incur either non‑parallelizable inverses or expensive Fourier‑domain operations, limiting scalability to high‑dimensional data. Our Woodbury transformations share the same high‑level goal—modeling rich interactions across both spatial and channel axes—but achieve linear‑time inversion and determinant evaluation by exploiting Sylvester’s determinant identity alongside the Woodbury identity. Consequently, we obtain the three desiderata emphasized in modern flow architectures (high‑dimensional interactions, efficient sampling, and efficient likelihood computation) simultaneously, whereas prior convolution‑based layers can satisfy at most two of them.

Beyond convolutional designs, recent advances such as invertible residual networks [9, 10] and continuous‑time flows [11, 12] broaden the class of bijections but typically require iterative solvers or ODE integration to evaluate inverses and Jacobians, which introduces additional computational overhead. Our contribution situates Woodbury transformations as a complementary building block: they can be incorporated into existing flow pipelines (including residual‑type or hybrid architectures) to provide exact, low‑cost inverses and determinants, thereby reducing the reliance on approximation methods. Empirically, we demonstrate that integrating Woodbury layers yields higher test log‑likelihoods on image benchmarks while preserving the fast training and sampling speeds characteristic of flow‑based models. This positions our work as a practical, mathematically grounded enhancement to the repertoire of invertible transformations available for deep generative modeling.

[ANSWER]: Most continual‑learning research has focused on the class‑incremental setting, where a model—typically a neural network—receives data from new classes in successive stages and is evaluated on all classes learned so far. Early class‑incremental learning (CIL) methods mitigate catastrophic forgetting by retaining a subset of exemplars from previously seen classes and interleaving them with new data during training. While effective, exemplar‑based approaches scale poorly because memory constraints become prohibitive as the number of classes grows, limiting their applicability in real‑world scenarios. To address memory limitations, a line of work adopts regularization‑based strategies that constrain parameter updates to preserve knowledge of earlier tasks. Although these techniques eliminate the need for stored examples, they generally lag behind exemplar‑based methods in terms of accuracy.

A smaller body of literature has examined few‑shot class‑incremental learning (FSCIL), which seeks to incorporate new classes from only a few labeled examples while operating under strict memory budgets. These studies explore various mechanisms—such as prototype adaptation, metric learning, and dynamic network expansion—to balance the competing demands of sample efficiency and stability. Nonetheless, a common assumption across most continual‑learning frameworks is that each incremental batch contains fully labeled data for the classes introduced at that stage. In many robotic and embodied settings, data arrive as a continuous stream, are often unlabeled, and must be processed online, highlighting a gap between existing methods and practical deployment.

Parallel to continual learning, active learning has been widely investigated for object recognition. Approaches based on uncertainty sampling train deep networks with specialized loss functions that encourage the model to assign high uncertainty scores to ambiguous samples, thereby guiding the selection of informative instances for annotation. These methods, however, are generally designed for batch learning and do not incorporate mechanisms to prevent forgetting when the model is updated repeatedly. Moreover, while active‑learning systems can identify unknown classes during an initial batch training phase, they tend to lose this capability in subsequent increments, as newly learned categories absorb previously unknown samples.

Open‑set recognition and out‑of‑distribution (OOD) detection constitute another related research area. In this setting, a model trained on a known set of classes must identify test samples that belong to unseen categories. Numerous OOD detection techniques have been proposed, ranging from confidence‑based thresholds to generative‑model approaches, enabling the recognition of unknown inputs during inference. However, these methods typically treat unknown samples as static test‑time anomalies and do not incorporate them into the training process for continual improvement. Comprehensive surveys have highlighted the conceptual overlap among continual learning, active learning, and open‑set recognition, suggesting that integrating insights from these domains could provide a natural bridge for systems that must both select informative unlabeled data and adapt continuously to newly encountered classes.

A substantial body of work focuses on learning a single common model for all clients. Techniques based on variance reduction and normalization have been proposed to mitigate the adverse effects of heterogeneity. Most convergence analyses for these methods rely on strong technical assumptions such as bounded gradients or bounded Hessian similarity, which are often violated when the true data‑generating process exhibits substantial variation across clients. Empirically, no single approach consistently outperforms the others across different heterogeneity regimes, and the generalization error of the common model on local data has been largely overlooked, with the notable exception of a recent study that quantifies the moderate level of model heterogeneity that a common model can tolerate.  

Another line of research investigates fully personalized models, where each client learns its own predictor. Federated multi‑task learning (MTL) proposes to learn a distinct model for each client, but the resulting objective is not jointly convex in the model parameters and their relationships, leaving the convergence behavior poorly understood. Existing convergence results for federated MTL typically assume equal dataset sizes across tasks or a small number of shared features, and they often bound only the average excess error rather than the error of individual tasks. Parallel efforts under the model‑agnostic meta‑learning (MAML) framework modify the global objective to account for the cost of fine‑tuning a global model at individual clients; however, these works concentrate on training‑error convergence and do not provide generalization‑error guarantees.

[ANSWER]: Navigation in simulators has been the dominant paradigm for learning indoor navigation policies.  Existing methods typically fall into two categories: tasks where the goal location is known a priori, requiring limited exploration, and tasks where the goal is unknown, demanding efficient exploration of the environment.  The latter includes finding specific objects, rooms, or images, as well as pure exploration.  Most recent work leverages large‑scale simulators such as Habitat, Matterport, and AI2‑Thor to generate billions of interaction frames and to provide ground‑truth maps for reward design.  This reliance on simulated environments enables end‑to‑end reinforcement learning (RL) approaches but constrains the methods to the set of scenes for which high‑fidelity 3D assets have been constructed.

A line of research has investigated navigation when only passive experience is available in the test environment.  Several studies exploit video trajectories recorded in the target scene to extract semantic cues for exploration‑based navigation, while a smaller subset trains policies without any simulator at all.  Within the image‑goal navigation setting, some works consider unseen environments where the agent has no prior experience and no map information.  Neural Topological SLAM (NTS) builds a topological map and learns a distance estimator to a target image, but it requires panoramic observations and ground‑truth maps for training the distance function.  A related approach for object‑goal navigation incorporates YouTube videos to learn a Q‑function, yet it relies on a memory‑less distance predictor that operates only on the current observation rather than on the full episodic history.  These methods differ in their data requirements, the type of observations they assume, and whether they learn distance functions that aggregate past experiences.

Learning from demonstration (LfD) and offline RL constitute another family of approaches that avoid online interaction.  LfD methods typically assume access to action annotations—often obtained via teleoperation in a simulator—and to optimal human demonstrations, using either imitation or reward shaping to match the demonstrated behavior.  Offline RL, by contrast, learns a policy from a fixed dataset of trajectories but still relies on reward signals derived from those trajectories.  Both paradigms thus depend on either action labels or reward computation, distinguishing them from methods that forgo explicit policy learning and instead focus on modeling the distance to the goal.

Map‑based navigation strategies employ various spatial representations.  Metric maps encode precise occupancy information and have been widely used for visual navigation, but they can suffer from scalability issues and sensitivity to sensor noise.  Topological maps have gained attention as a more compact alternative, often constructed from pre‑collected video data or assumed to be available at test time.  Some works generate topological maps from a short video of the test environment, while others assume access to a ground‑truth map.  There are approaches that build topological maps on‑the‑fly without prior test‑time experience, yet they still depend on simulators to compute shortest‑path distances between image nodes.  The cognitive map hypothesis from neuroscience, which posits that humans and animals use landmark‑based internal representations, provides motivation for topological over metric maps.

Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have been applied to relational reasoning on non‑Euclidean structures and have seen limited use in visual navigation.  Prior work employs GNNs for sub‑tasks such as localizing an agent within a ground‑truth topological map, but comprehensive integration of GNNs for distance‑to‑goal estimation over an exploration frontier remains uncommon.  Recent advances in attention‑based graph architectures enable weighted aggregation of neighboring node information, offering a promising avenue for modeling navigation graphs.

In this work we introduce a self‑supervised navigation framework that eliminates the need for simulators, reinforcement learning, and explicit policy learning.  The method learns a geodesic distance estimator and a target prediction model solely from passive egocentric RGB‑D videos, using SLAM to obtain relative poses.  By treating the predicted distance as a proxy for value, a greedy navigation strategy selects frontier nodes with minimal estimated distance to the goal.  Obstacle avoidance is addressed locally with depth information, removing the requirement for collision data in the training videos.  The approach can be viewed as model‑based control, where both the environment model and cost function are derived from passive data.  Extensive experiments demonstrate that the proposed system outperforms end‑to‑end RL baselines even when those baselines are trained with substantially more data and compute, and it operates directly on real‑world video collections, thereby avoiding the sim‑to‑real gap.  Consequently, the method provides a scalable and effective baseline for future image‑goal navigation research that previously relied on simulation and reinforcement learning.

[ANSWER]: Much research effort has been devoted to extracting and processing event chains. Early work introduced the modern interest in narrative chains by modeling event co‑occurrence using pointwise mutual information, establishing a foundation for unsupervised chain discovery. Subsequent extensions brought this approach to cross‑document settings, applying the resulting chains to news prediction and timeline construction. In the biomedical domain, methods have extracted relations among events and entities in biological processes to support reading‑comprehension tasks through structure‑matching techniques. More recent studies have attempted to infer the type of action and object associated with a chain, requiring recognition of goals or intentions embedded in the sequence. Probabilistic graphical models have also been employed to capture common patterns from analogous chains and to induce new chains from these patterns. Across this body of work, the focus has remained on modeling event co‑occurrence and relations, without explicit consideration of event salience or discourse structure.  

A parallel line of research has examined event salience and discourse structure as means of identifying the most important content in a document. Several studies have explored dominant‑event detection in news articles by leveraging mined event coreference relations, while others have introduced sequence‑tagging models for event‑salience detection and released large‑scale salience corpora derived from news sources. Further work has sought richer representations of events and their interactions, evaluating salience modeling in the context of extractive summarization. On the discourse side, annotated corpora have been created that treat paragraphs as units for discourse‑label prediction, and sentence‑level discourse‑structure datasets spanning multiple domains have been released to facilitate fine‑grained identification of sentences relevant to a main topic. These contributions collectively define two complementary notions of salience—event‑level and discourse‑level—that have informed subsequent attempts to filter or prioritize information in narrative texts.  

Event‑centric language modeling has emerged as another prominent research direction, aiming to capture sequences of events within neural language models. A number of approaches extract raw event chains directly from text and train neural language models for tasks such as narrative prediction or script generation. Some recent work has sought to induce event schemas by training autoregressive language models on salient paths extracted from event‑event relation graphs, explicitly attempting to reduce noise in schema construction. While these methods recognize the importance of salient information, they typically rely on raw chains or graph‑based paths rather than integrating explicit salience and discourse cues during model fine‑tuning.  

Building on these strands of literature, this work introduces a discourse‑aware, salience‑aware method for extracting principal event chains from natural‑language texts. By jointly leveraging event‑level salience detection and sentence‑level discourse profiling, the approach filters out peripheral and supportive sentences, yielding cleaner chains that better reflect the core narrative flow. Event language models trained on the filtered chains achieve notable improvements on narrative‑prediction benchmarks, surpassing prior models that use unfiltered chains, and attain state‑of‑the‑art performance on temporal‑ordering question answering. The contributions are threefold: (1) a novel extraction pipeline that incorporates both event salience and discourse structure to isolate primary event sequences; (2) empirical evidence that salience‑guided filtering enhances narrative prediction, demonstrated on the Story Cloze Test; and (3) validation that the resulting discourse‑rich chains improve temporal understanding, establishing new performance levels on the TORQUE temporal QA dataset. These results underscore the value of integrating salience and discourse information when constructing event‑centric representations for downstream language‑understanding tasks.

FedAvg, introduced as a variant of local gradient descent/SGD, pioneered this idea and demonstrated empirical gains in communication efficiency.  Theoretical analyses of local SGD subsequently established linear convergence rates for strongly‑convex smooth losses with a small number of communication rounds, and later extended to non‑convex objectives, adaptive step‑sizes, and heterogeneous data partitions.  Tightened bounds for general convex functions and heterogeneous data have been derived, and further work examined local GD/SGD in fully decentralized networks as well as the impact of non‑i.i.d. data on convergence for strongly‑convex problems.  Comparative studies have also highlighted the trade‑offs between local SGD and mini‑batch SGD under both homogeneous and heterogeneous settings.

A complementary line of research addresses distributional robustness in learning, which is particularly relevant when data are imbalanced or non‑i.i.d.  DRO formulations cast robustness as a minimax problem over mixtures of local loss functions.  Early algorithms such as bandit mirror descent and top‑k loss minimization tackled the DRO minimax structure, providing guarantees for robustness against adversarial or skewed data distributions.  Within federated learning, the first proposals introduced a worst‑case (agnostic) empirical loss that seeks a model performing uniformly well across all clients, thereby mitigating the adverse effects of data heterogeneity.  These works established convergence rates for convex‑linear and strongly‑convex‑strongly‑concave settings, but typically required communication at every iteration to update the mixing weights, limiting scalability.

A third body of literature studies smooth minimax optimization, where one seeks saddle points of objectives that are convex (or strongly convex) in one variable and concave (or strongly concave) in another.  Stochastic gradient descent‑ascent (SGDA) was shown to converge efficiently for non‑convex‑concave problems, while extra‑gradient and optimistic gradient methods have become standard tools for training generative adversarial networks and other bilevel models.  More recent algorithms combine mirror descent with Nesterov‑type acceleration to achieve optimal rates for strongly‑convex‑concave and non‑convex‑concave problems.  Proximal and variance‑reduced variants have further improved convergence in non‑convex‑concave settings, and linear convergence has been obtained for strongly‑convex‑strongly‑concave objectives using accelerated schemes.  Decentralized minimax methods have also been explored, though none of these works consider a setting in which one variable is trained locally across clients while the other variable is updated only intermittently at a central server.

Building on these strands of research, this work proposes a communication‑efficient federated algorithm that simultaneously addresses distributional robustness and the minimax structure of robust federated objectives.  By integrating periodic model averaging with adaptive client sampling, the method reduces the number of synchronization rounds required for updating the mixing weights, overcoming the communication bottleneck identified in earlier DRO‑FL approaches.  The algorithm leverages a randomized snapshotting mechanism to approximate the accumulated history of local gradients for the mixing parameter, enabling convergence guarantees comparable to those of centralized minimax methods while accommodating heterogeneous, non‑i.i.d. client data.  Convergence analyses are provided for both convex‑linear and non‑convex‑linear regimes, establishing rates that improve upon prior federated DRO results by requiring significantly fewer communication rounds.  A proximal variant extends these guarantees to regularized robust objectives, and additional analysis covers strongly‑convex‑strongly‑concave and PL‑condition‑based non‑convex settings. Existing methods typically fall into two categories: tasks where the goal location is known a priori, requiring limited exploration, and tasks where the goal is unknown, demanding efficient exploration of the environment. Several studies exploit video trajectories recorded in the target scene to extract semantic cues for exploration‑based navigation, while a smaller subset trains policies without any simulator at all.  Within the image‑goal navigation setting, some works consider unseen environments where the agent has no prior experience and no map information.  Neural Topological SLAM (NTS) builds a topological map and learns a distance estimator to a target image, but it requires panoramic observations and ground‑truth maps for training the distance function.  A related approach for object‑goal navigation incorporates YouTube videos to learn a Q‑function, yet it relies on a memory‑less distance predictor that operates only on the current observation rather than on the full episodic history.  These methods differ in their data requirements, the type of observations they assume, and whether they learn distance functions that aggregate past experiences.

Learning from demonstration (LfD) and offline RL constitute another family of approaches that avoid online interaction.  LfD methods typically assume access to action annotations—often obtained via teleoperation in a simulator—and to optimal human demonstrations, using either imitation or reward shaping to match the demonstrated behavior.  Offline RL, by contrast, learns a policy from a fixed dataset of trajectories but still relies on reward signals derived from those trajectories.  Both paradigms thus depend on either action labels or reward computation, distinguishing them from methods that forgo explicit policy learning and instead focus on modeling the distance to the goal.

Map‑based navigation strategies employ various spatial representations.  Metric maps encode precise occupancy information and have been widely used for visual navigation, but they can suffer from scalability issues and sensitivity to sensor noise.  Topological maps have gained attention as a more compact alternative, often constructed from pre‑collected video data or assumed to be available at test time.  Some works generate topological maps from a short video of the test environment, while others assume access to a ground‑truth map.  There are approaches that build topological maps on‑the‑fly without prior test‑time experience, yet they still depend on simulators to compute shortest‑path distances between image nodes.  The cognitive map hypothesis from neuroscience, which posits that humans and animals use landmark‑based internal representations, provides motivation for topological over metric maps.

Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have been applied to relational reasoning on non‑Euclidean structures and have seen limited use in visual navigation.  Prior work employs GNNs for sub‑tasks such as localizing an agent within a ground‑truth topological map, but comprehensive integration of GNNs for distance‑to‑goal estimation over an exploration frontier remains uncommon.  Recent advances in attention‑based graph architectures enable weighted aggregation of neighboring node information, offering a promising avenue for modeling navigation graphs.

[ANSWER]: The design of sample‑efficient sequential decision‑making agents has long been grounded in principled approaches to information acquisition and information representation. Early work demonstrated how information‑theoretic tools, particularly rate‑distortion theory, can formalize the trade‑off between the amount of information an agent must gather and the performance loss incurred by adopting a simplified learning target. By interpreting the complexity of a learning problem as the number of bits required to identify a target, these studies provided a theoretical foundation for constructing satisficing objectives that balance efficiency and near‑optimality.

A central difficulty in achieving sample efficiency is the exploration–exploitation dilemma that arises in multi‑armed bandit settings. The information‑directed sampling (IDS) principle was introduced as a systematic way to navigate this dilemma. IDS defines an information ratio as the squared expected regret divided by the expected information gain, and prescribes selecting the policy that minimizes this ratio at each timestep. This framework yields elegant theoretical guarantees and has been extended in numerous directions, including refined analyses of the information ratio, adaptations to contextual and combinatorial bandits, and connections to posterior sampling methods. However, the majority of IDS‑based research measures information gain exclusively with respect to the optimal action, thereby limiting its applicability when the learning objective extends beyond a single optimal policy.

Rate‑distortion concepts have been operationalized in sequential decision‑making through the Blahut‑Arimoto algorithm, which provides an alternating‑optimization procedure for computing optimal trade‑offs between information cost and distortion. The algorithm has been widely studied in the information‑theory literature for its convergence properties, computational efficiency, and extensions to various channel models. In the bandit context, the Blahut‑Arimoto approach has enabled agents to compute satisficing targets that adapt as more data are collected, but prior implementations have primarily combined these targets with probability‑matching action selection such as Thompson sampling, leaving the integration with more sophisticated information‑acquisition strategies unexplored.

Building on these strands of literature, we introduce a unified framework that couples the optimal computation of learning targets via rate‑distortion theory with the optimal acquisition of information through an information‑directed sampling lens. Leveraging the Blahut‑Arimoto algorithm to obtain dynamic learning targets, we redefine the information ratio to capture expected regret and information gain about these targets, thereby extending IDS beyond the optimal‑action focus. The resulting algorithm, which we term Blahut‑Arimoto Information‑Directed Sampling (BLAIDS), retains a single real‑valued hyperparameter that governs the designer’s preference for target fidelity versus learning speed. We provide a computationally tractable instantiation of BLAIDS that mirrors the efficiency gains observed in prior Blahut‑Arimoto‑based methods while inheriting the stronger exploration guarantees of IDS. Theoretical analysis establishes regret bounds that reflect the combined effect of target compression and directed information acquisition, and extensive experiments on multi‑armed bandit benchmarks demonstrate that BLAIDS outperforms both standard IDS and Blahut‑Arimoto‑guided Thompson sampling across a range of distortion levels. This work therefore bridges the gap between rate‑distortion‑based target design and optimal information‑directed exploration, offering a flexible and principled tool for constructing sample‑efficient agents in complex environments.

[ANSWER]: Bootstrapping has long been a cornerstone of temporal‑difference (TD) reinforcement‑learning algorithms, where an agent treats its own future predictions as training targets.  Recent self‑supervised works have imported this idea to representation learning, but none have explored its use for learning update rules themselves.  Our work extends bootstrapping to the meta‑learning setting: the meta‑learner generates a future target by continuing to apply either its own learned update rule or an alternative rule, and then optimises to reach that target in fewer steps.  This “meta‑bootstrap” transforms the meta‑learner into its own teacher and directly addresses the myopia that plagues conventional meta‑optimisation.

Matching a learner’s parameters to a target has been employed in multi‑task meta‑learning, where methods such as MAML‑style initialisation learning minimise the Euclidean distance between the adapted parameters and task‑optimal solutions.  Those approaches are restricted to a single distance metric and to initialisation‑only meta‑parameters.  In contrast, Bootstrapped Meta‑Gradient (BMG) generalises this paradigm by (i) allowing arbitrary pseudo‑metrics (e.g., KL divergence) to shape the optimisation landscape, (ii) supporting any differentiable meta‑parameterisation beyond simple initialisations, and (iii) using bootstrapped targets that encode information about future learning dynamics.  This broader formulation yields tighter curvature control and empirically stronger performance across few‑shot and multi‑task benchmarks.

Self‑referential meta‑learning studies have shown that a meta‑learned update rule can be used to improve its own objective, yet prior formulations either rely on hand‑crafted regularisers or lack provable improvement guarantees.  BMG builds on this line of work by explicitly constructing a meta‑objective that minimises a distance to a bootstrapped future state, and by proving that each meta‑update provably reduces the learner’s loss under mild conditions.  The resulting acceleration mirrors classic optimisation schemes such as Nesterov momentum, but arises naturally from the meta‑bootstrap rather than from externally imposed heuristics.

Distillation and trust‑region methods also inspire our design.  Traditional knowledge‑distillation pipelines employ a fixed or slowly moving teacher network to shape a student’s predictions, while trust‑region algorithms constrain updates with a distance‑based penalty to improve stability.  BMG differs fundamentally: the “teacher’’ is a dynamically generated target produced by extending the learner’s own update trajectory, and the distance function serves both as a curvature‑regulariser for meta‑optimisation and as a bridge to the future target.  This dual role enables us to achieve state‑of‑the‑art results on Atari model‑free agents and to meta‑learn efficient exploration strategies without back‑propagating through the underlying update rule.

[ANSWER]: Adding stochastic perturbations during training has long been recognized as a practical regularization technique for neural networks.  Dropout and its variants such as DropConnect randomly zero out activations or weights, thereby preventing co‑adaptation of neurons.  Denoising autoencoders inject noise into the input while learning to reconstruct the original signal, encouraging the model to capture robust features.  These empirical strategies have demonstrated improvements in both training stability and test performance across a variety of architectures.  

Theoretical investigations of noise in learning systems have focused on its impact on convergence and generalization.  Analyses of additive and multiplicative noise in recurrent neural networks have shown that appropriately scaled perturbations can accelerate convergence toward minima of the loss surface.  Formal studies of noisy recurrent networks have further established that such perturbations increase stability and robustness to input variations.  For feed‑forward models, researchers have derived Rademacher‑complexity bounds for networks trained with dropout, revealing a dependence on the product of layer‑wise norms and the dropout probability.  These results indicate that substantial noise levels are required for the bounds to improve upon traditional uniform‑convergence estimates.  

The sample‑complexity theory of PAC learning provides a foundational framework for assessing the capacity of hypothesis classes.  Classical VC‑dimension and related combinatorial measures have been applied to neural networks, yielding generalization bounds that scale with the number of parameters.  Subsequent work has refined these analyses for specific architectures, producing a rich literature of parameter‑count‑based guarantees for deep models.  

Beyond combinatorial quantities, a substantial line of research has sought capacity measures that reflect the geometry of the function class rather than its sheer size.  Norm‑based and Lipschitz‑based analyses bound generalization error in terms of weight magnitudes, group norms, or spectral norms, often producing tighter estimates for networks with controlled weight growth.  These approaches exploit the fact that compositions of Lipschitz functions remain Lipschitz, albeit with an enlarged constant, and they have been used to derive covering‑number and Rademacher‑complexity bounds that depend on norm constraints rather than parameter counts.  

Despite these advances, many of the resulting bounds remain vacuous for modern architectures and datasets.  PAC‑Bayesian techniques and compression‑based arguments have been introduced to obtain non‑vacuous guarantees, typically by constructing data‑dependent priors or by explicitly compressing trained models.  Parallel lines of inquiry question whether uniform‑convergence theory can fully explain the empirical success of over‑parameterized networks, proposing instead that implicit algorithmic biases—such as those induced by gradient descent—lead to benign over‑fitting.  These perspectives highlight the limitations of traditional capacity measures and motivate alternative analytic tools.  

Information‑theoretic analyses have recently linked generalization to the mutual information between training data and learned parameters.  Bounds based on conditional mutual information show that algorithms with low information leakage, including stochastic gradient Langevin dynamics and noisy stochastic gradient descent, enjoy favorable generalization properties.  By interpreting noise injection as a mechanism for reducing information flow, these works provide a complementary viewpoint to norm‑ or VC‑based approaches, though they typically yield algorithm‑specific rather than hypothesis‑class‑specific guarantees.  

In this work we introduce a systematic method for controlling the capacity of composed function classes by adding a vanishing amount of Gaussian noise at the interface between modules.  We define uniform covering numbers for random functions with respect to total‑variation and Wasserstein distances, and we prove a composition lemma that leverages the data‑processing inequality for total variation.  Our analysis yields translation theorems between these stochastic covering numbers and conventional uniform covering numbers, enabling us to bound the capacity of noisy multi‑layer sigmoid networks in terms of the original layerwise capacities.  We further propose the NVAC metric, which quantifies the sample size required for a bound to become non‑vacuous, and we demonstrate empirically that even noise with an infinitesimal standard deviation (e.g., 10⁻²⁴⁰) markedly improves NVAC compared to existing VC‑, norm‑, PAC‑Bayesian, and information‑theoretic bounds without degrading training or test accuracy.  By bridging stochastic perturbations, covering‑number theory, and practical deep‑learning architectures, our results provide a novel, modular recipe for designing high‑capacity models whose generalization can be rigorously controlled.

[ANSWER]: Several strands of research have explored how to make deep neural networks more transparent by generating human‑interpretable explanations.  Some approaches derive explanations directly from the model’s internal states, such as gradients, hidden activations, or learned attention maps, and present these as visual or textual rationales for a decision [1, 2].  Other methods focus on producing post‑hoc justifications that are consistent with the model’s output but are not necessarily rooted in the underlying computation [3, 4].  A widely used family of techniques visualizes the regions of the input that most influence a prediction, either by training explicit attention mechanisms that highlight relevant image patches [5, 6] or by exposing implicit attention weights that emerge during inference [7].

A parallel line of work has examined how to evaluate the usefulness of such explanations.  Many studies assess whether explanations increase users’ trust in a system or help them accomplish a downstream task, often using offline questionnaires, rating scales, or controlled experiments in which participants judge the quality of the explanations [3, 8, 9].  These evaluations typically measure perceived trustworthiness, satisfaction, or task performance, but they rarely investigate whether explanations make a model’s behavior more predictable to a human collaborator in an interactive setting.

Research on failure prediction has mainly focused on algorithmic approaches that estimate a model’s likelihood of error.  Statistical or meta‑learning classifiers are trained on features such as confidence scores, uncertainty estimates, or historical performance to flag inputs that are likely to be misclassified [10, 11].  While effective in automated settings, these methods do not address how a human observer might learn to anticipate a model’s failures through experience or interaction.

The concept of legibility has been studied in robotics, where the expressiveness of a robot’s trajectory is analyzed as a means of communicating its intent to observers [12].  This work treats the observable intermediate states of a system as signals that can convey the ultimate goal, emphasizing the importance of transparent behavior for human interpretation.

Finally, investigations of how humans adapt to imperfect AI agents have highlighted the strategies people employ when collaborating with systems that have limited capabilities.  Observational studies of interactive language games reveal that users form mental models of an AI’s strengths and weaknesses and adjust their behavior accordingly [13].  These findings underscore the role of familiarization and experiential learning in shaping effective human‑AI teamwork.

Building on these bodies of literature, we evaluate whether existing explanation modalities—ranging from attention visualizations to post‑hoc rationales—actually improve a human’s ability to predict the outputs and failures of a visual question‑answering model.  By introducing two interactive tasks, Failure Prediction and Knowledge Prediction, we measure participants’ performance after a brief familiarization phase and after exposure to various explanation types.  Our results show that, although people can learn to anticipate the model’s behavior above chance, the explanations commonly proposed in prior work do not enhance this predictability, whereas simple training that acquaints users with the model’s patterns does.  This work therefore bridges the gap between explanation generation, evaluation of trust, failure prediction, legibility, and human adaptation, demonstrating that transparent internal signals alone are insufficient for improving human‑model predictability in interactive VQA settings.
